seo.description: How ClaimValuator handles your data: calculators run in your browser, what the case review form collects, cookies, analytics and your privacy choices.
seo.focus: claimvaluator privacy policy

posts.content:
The short version

Calculators do not collect your name, email or phone number, and the numbers you type stay in your browser. We collect personal information only when you send a form.

What we collect

  • Forms: when you request a case review or contact us, the details you enter, the page you sent it from and the time
  • Usage data: standard server logs (IP address, browser, pages visited), kept for security and to keep the site working
  • Cookies: the site does not need cookies to work. If we add analytics, we will list them here.

How we use it

To respond to your request, to share a case review request with participating attorneys in your state when you ask us to, to keep records of consent, and to secure the site.

Sharing

We share case review requests only with participating law firms and service providers who help us run the site, such as hosting and email. We do not sell form information to data brokers.

Retention

Form submissions are kept for as long as needed to handle the request and meet legal record-keeping duties, then deleted.

Your choices

You can ask for a copy of your information or ask us to delete it by contacting us. Depending on your state, you may have additional rights under privacy laws such as the California Consumer Privacy Act.

Children

The site is not directed at children under 13, and we do not knowingly collect their information.

Last updated: October 13, 2026

posts.content:
Free · 50 states + DC · No sign-up

What is your injury claim worth in your state?

Free settlement calculators that apply your state’s fault rule, filing deadline and insurance minimums, then show the math line by line.

  • No name, email or phone needed
  • Rules cited to each state’s statutes
  • Numbers stay in your browser

Most-used calculators

See all 35 tools

How every estimate is built, in this order

Step 1

Add up what the injury cost you

Medical bills, past and future, plus income you lost. Vehicle damage is valued as its own property claim.

Step 2

Price the pain and suffering

A multiplier from 1.5× to 5× on those costs, set by how serious and how lasting the injury is.

Step 3

Apply your state’s rules

Cut by your share of fault, barred past your state’s limit, then checked against the insurance actually available.

Your state’s fault rule can cut a claim to zero

Same crash, same $100,000 claim, you 30% at fault. Here is what each rule leaves you.

South Dakota compares “slight” and “gross” negligence instead. See every state’s fault rule

Enter the offer next to your estimate to see where it falls in your state’s range, and get a counteroffer figure to start from.

Check my offer

Each state page lists its fault rule, deadlines, insurance minimums and damage caps, with links to every calculator set up for that state.

posts.content:
Actual cash value

What a vehicle was worth just before a crash, based on comparable local sales. The basis of a total loss payment.

Adjuster

The insurance company employee who investigates a claim and negotiates the settlement.

At-fault state

A state where the driver who caused a crash, through their liability insurance, pays the other people’s injury claims. Most states are at-fault states.

Bodily injury liability

The part of an auto policy that pays injury claims of people the policyholder hurts, up to the policy limit.

Comparative negligence

A rule that reduces an injured person’s award by their own share of fault. Pure comparative applies at any fault level; modified versions bar recovery at 50% or 51%.

Contingency fee

A lawyer’s fee paid as a percentage of the recovery, owed only if there is one.

Contributory negligence

A strict rule, used in five jurisdictions, that can bar recovery if the injured person was even slightly at fault.

Damages

Money awarded for a loss. Economic damages have a receipt (bills, wages); non-economic damages do not (pain, suffering).

Demand letter

A letter to the insurer setting out the claim, the damages and the amount needed to settle.

Diminished value

The resale value a vehicle loses because of its accident history, even after repairs.

Economic damages

Losses with a dollar figure: medical bills, future care, lost wages and lost earning capacity.

Lien

A legal claim on settlement money by someone who paid for your care, such as a hospital, health plan or Medicare.

MedPay

Optional auto coverage that pays medical bills after a crash regardless of fault.

Multiplier method

Estimating pain and suffering by multiplying economic damages by a number, usually 1.5 to 5.

No-fault state

A state where your own PIP coverage pays your injury costs first, and you can sue the at-fault driver only above a threshold.

Non-economic damages

Losses without a receipt: pain, emotional distress, loss of enjoyment of life and loss of companionship.

Per diem method

Estimating pain and suffering as a daily rate times the number of days in pain or recovery.

Personal injury protection (PIP)

Auto coverage that pays your medical bills and part of your lost income regardless of fault. Required in no-fault states.

Policy limit

The most an insurer will pay under a policy, written as per person, per crash and property damage, such as 30/60/25.

Release

The document you sign to accept a settlement. It ends the claim for good.

Statute of limitations

The deadline to file a lawsuit. Missing it almost always ends the claim.

Strict liability

Liability without proof of fault, such as dog owners’ liability for bites in many states.

Subrogation

An insurer’s right to be repaid from your recovery for what it paid on your behalf.

Threshold

In no-fault states, the injury severity or medical bill amount you must reach to sue the at-fault driver for pain and suffering.

Underinsured motorist (UIM) coverage

Your own coverage that pays when the at-fault driver’s policy is too small for your injuries.

Uninsured motorist (UM) coverage

Your own coverage that pays when the at-fault driver has no insurance or cannot be found.

Wrongful death claim

A claim by family members for losses caused by a death due to someone else’s negligence.

posts.content:
ClaimValuator exists for the person staring at a medical bill and an insurance adjuster’s phone number, wondering what their claim is worth. Most settlement calculators online give one national number. Real claims depend on state law: who can recover when both sides share the blame, how long you have to sue, what insurance drivers must carry and whether damages are capped.

What we build

Free calculators for injury claims, insurance coverage, settlement money, workplace benefits and employment claims. Each state version applies that state’s rules, cites the statute or case behind each one and shows the math line by line, so you can see how an estimate was built and argue with any part of it.

What we do not do

We are not a law firm and we do not give legal advice. Our estimates are not predictions or offers. Calculators never ask for your name, email or phone number, and the numbers you enter stay in your browser.

How we keep it accurate

Every rule in our data has a source and a date it was last checked. State pages name their reviewing attorney once one is confirmed for that state. Read how we calculate, our editorial policy and the legal review board.

How we make money

When someone asks for a free case review, we may be paid by a participating law firm. That never changes a calculator result. See our advertising disclosure.

posts.content:
Every settlement calculator on this site follows the same steps in the same order. This page explains each step, the assumptions we make and where our rules data comes from.

Step 1: Economic damages

We add medical bills already incurred, future medical care you enter, income lost so far and future lost income. Vehicle damage is valued separately, because it is paid under a different coverage and settles on a different timeline.

Step 2: Pain and suffering

Non-economic damages are estimated with the multiplier method most adjusters start from: economic damages times a range set by injury severity.

The pain and suffering calculator also shows the per-diem method (a daily rate times days in recovery) side by side.

Step 3: No-fault rules

In the 12 no-fault states, we subtract the medical bills and lost income your own PIP coverage pays, up to the state minimum. If you say your injury does not meet the state’s threshold to sue, we set pain and suffering to zero and keep only economic losses beyond PIP.

Step 4: Damage caps

Where a state caps non-economic damages in ordinary injury cases with a clear dollar figure, we apply the cap, including higher caps for catastrophic injuries where the law provides them. Caps with broad exceptions are shown but not applied.

Step 5: Your share of fault

We apply the state’s fault rule to the total:

  • Pure comparative: reduce by your percentage at any level
  • 51% bar: reduce by your percentage; zero above 50%
  • 50% bar: reduce by your percentage; zero at 50% or more
  • Contributory negligence: zero at any fault above 0%
  • Slight/gross (South Dakota): reduce by your percentage, with a warning that a jury may bar the claim; zero at 50% or more
  • Michigan: above 50%, pain and suffering is removed and economic damages are reduced

Where a state changed its rule, such as Florida in 2023 and Louisiana in 2026, we use the date you enter to pick the rule in force.

Step 6: Insurance available

We compare the estimate with the at-fault party’s policy limit you choose, plus your UM/UIM coverage for vehicle claims. When the range passes the coverage, we say so.

Step 7: Take-home

At the midpoint, capped at available insurance, we subtract the attorney fee you choose, an estimate of case costs (2% of the recovery, at least $1,000, when a lawyer is used) and medical bills still owed. Real fees, costs and lien reductions vary.

Filing deadlines

We add the state’s statute of limitations to the date you enter, using the vehicle crash or wrongful death deadline where the state sets a different one, and rules in force on that date. Exceptions can change the real deadline.

Our rules data

Each state’s fault rule, deadlines, minimum insurance, no-fault threshold, damage cap and dog bite rule is stored once and used by every page. Each value cites its statute or case and has a “last checked” date. The full data is published as a JSON feed.

Limits of any calculator

No formula captures credibility, the quality of medical records, local jury attitudes or the strength of the evidence. Use the estimates to understand the range and judge offers. For advice on your claim, talk to a lawyer licensed in your state.

Each state’s rules data and the articles that discuss them are reviewed by an attorney licensed in that state. Reviewers check that every rule matches the current statute or controlling case, that the plain-English summaries are accurate, and that the examples do not mislead.

What reviewers check

  • The fault rule, filing deadlines, insurance minimums, no-fault threshold, damage caps and dog bite rule for their state
  • The citations behind each value
  • State-specific questions and answers on calculator pages

What reviewers do not do

Reviewers do not review individual users’ claims through this site, and their review is not legal advice to anyone using the calculators.

Corrections

If you believe a rule or article is wrong, please tell us. We log every correction and update the “last checked” date when a fix goes live.

posts.content:
Sources first

Every legal rule we state comes from a primary source: a statute, a regulation or a court decision. We cite it next to the rule. Secondary sources are used only to find primary ones.

Plain language

We write for people dealing with an injury, not for lawyers. Short sentences, defined terms and worked examples with real numbers.

Review

Articles and state rules are checked against their sources before publishing and reviewed by a licensed attorney where one is assigned for that state. Each page shows when it was last updated or checked.

Independence

Advertising and referral partnerships never affect a calculator result or what an article says. Writers and reviewers do not know which firms participate in the referral program.

Updates

We re-check every state’s rules at least twice a year and whenever a legislature changes one of them. Pages are updated, not quietly rewritten: material changes are noted.

posts.content:
What this calculator covers

Use it for any injury caused by someone else’s carelessness: a crash, a fall on someone’s property, a defective product, an assault at a poorly secured business. For car, truck, slip and fall or dog bite claims, the dedicated calculators ask a few extra questions that matter for those cases.

The three parts of an injury claim

Economic damages are losses with a receipt: medical bills, future treatment your doctors expect, lost wages and lost earning capacity. Non-economic damages cover pain, emotional distress and loss of enjoyment of life. They have no receipt, so they are usually estimated as a multiple of economic damages or as a daily rate. Punitive damages punish extreme conduct and are rare in ordinary negligence cases, so the calculator leaves them out.

How your state changes the number

Three state rules do most of the work. The fault rule decides how much your own share of blame costs you, and whether it bars the claim. The statute of limitations decides how long you have to sue. A handful of states cap non-economic damages in ordinary injury cases, including Alaska, Colorado, Maryland, Mississippi, Ohio and Tennessee. Pick your state in the calculator and those rules are applied for you. The damage caps table lists every state.

Insurance decides what can be collected

A $300,000 claim against someone with a $100,000 policy and no assets is, in practice, a $100,000 claim. Ask early which insurer covers the at-fault party and what the limits are. The calculator shows where available coverage sits against your estimate.

Why real settlements differ from any calculator

Adjusters weigh things no formula captures: how believable you are, whether your treatment was consistent, what a local jury tends to award, and how strong the proof of fault is. Use the estimate to understand the range and to judge offers, not as a promise of what you will receive.

What the numbers look like in practice

National data gives a rough sense of scale. Auto insurers paid an average of $28,278 per bodily injury liability claim in 2024 (Insurance Information Institute). Dog-related injury claims averaged $65,450 in 2025 (Triple-I and State Farm). Workers’ compensation claims averaged $47,316 for injuries in 2022–2023 (National Safety Council, using NCCI data), although workers’ comp pays no pain and suffering.

Averages blend minor and catastrophic injuries, so they say little about any single claim. Your medical records, the length of your recovery and the insurance available matter far more.

Settlement value versus what you keep

A gross settlement is not your take-home figure. A typical deduction order is:

  1. The attorney’s contingency fee, often 33⅓% before a lawsuit and up to 40% after
  2. Case costs: records, filing fees, expert reports
  3. Medical liens from health plans, Medicare, Medicaid or hospitals

On a $60,000 settlement with a one-third fee, $1,200 in costs and a $9,000 health plan lien, you would keep about $29,800. Run your own numbers with the attorney fee calculator and the medical lien calculator.

Calculators for specific claims

This calculator works for any injury. For more specific estimates, use the car accident, truck accident, motorcycle, pedestrian, bicycle, rideshare, slip and fall, dog bite or wrongful death calculator. Work injuries follow different rules; see the workers’ comp settlement calculator.

Questions people ask

How are personal injury settlements calculated?

Most start with economic damages, add pain and suffering as a multiple of those costs or a daily rate, subtract your share of fault, and check the result against the insurance available. Read the full walkthrough in how injury settlements are calculated.

Is a personal injury settlement taxable?

Compensation for a physical injury, including the pain and suffering that comes with it, is generally not taxable under federal law. Interest and punitive damages are. Try the settlement tax calculator.

How long does a personal injury claim take?

Simple claims often settle a few months after treatment ends. Claims with surgery, disputed fault or a lawsuit can take one to three years.

Do I need a lawyer for a personal injury claim?

Not for every claim, but studies and insurer data consistently show represented claimants recover more on serious injuries, even after fees. Most injury lawyers offer a free review and work on contingency.

What is the average personal injury settlement?

There is no reliable single average because personal injury covers everything from minor sprains to catastrophic injuries. As one benchmark, auto insurers paid an average of $28,278 per bodily injury claim in 2024 (ISO data via the Insurance Information Institute).

How long does a personal injury settlement take?

Simple claims often settle in three to nine months once treatment ends. Claims that need a lawsuit commonly take one to three years. See our guide to settlement timelines for each stage.

posts.content:
How a car accident claim is valued

Most adjusters start from the same rough math. Add up the economic damages: medical bills, past and future, and income you lost. Then estimate pain and suffering as a multiple of those costs, about 1.5× for a minor injury and up to 5× for one that is permanent or disabling. The total is reduced by your share of fault. Damage to your car is a separate property claim, paid under the other driver’s property damage coverage.

What moves the number up or down

Pushes value up

  • Surgery, imaging or other objective proof
  • A permanent injury, scarring or disability
  • Months of consistent treatment
  • Clear fault on the other driver, such as a citation or video

Pulls value down

  • Gaps in treatment or a late first visit
  • A pre-existing condition in the same area
  • Your own share of fault
  • A low policy limit on the at-fault driver

The other driver’s policy usually sets the ceiling

A claim is only worth what can be collected. Most car accident claims settle within the at-fault driver’s bodily injury limit. In Texas the minimum is written 30/60/25: $30,000 per injured person, $60,000 per crash, $25,000 for property. When your damages run past the limit, your own underinsured motorist (UIM) coverage can pay the gap. Every state calculator shows this ceiling next to your estimate. See minimum car insurance by state.

No-fault states work differently

In 12 states your own personal injury protection (PIP) pays your medical bills and lost wages first, whoever caused the crash. You can claim pain and suffering from the at-fault driver only after your injury passes the state’s threshold, either a serious-injury definition or a dollar amount in medical bills. The calculators for these states ask about the threshold before they price pain and suffering.

Florida, Hawaii, Kansas, Kentucky, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, New York, North Dakota, Pennsylvania and Utah use no-fault insurance. In Kentucky, New Jersey and Pennsylvania drivers can choose a no-fault or a traditional policy. Details are in no-fault states and thresholds.

Don’t miss the filing deadline

Every state sets a statute of limitations for injury lawsuits, most often two or three years from the crash. File one day late and the court will almost always dismiss the case, which also ends your leverage to settle. Claims against a city, county or state agency can require a written notice within months. Each state calculator works out your last day to file from the crash date you enter, or use the statute of limitations calculator.

What to keep while the claim is open

  • The police report number and the other driver’s insurance details
  • Photos of the vehicles, the scene and your injuries
  • Every medical bill, record and receipt, including mileage to appointments
  • Pay stubs or a letter from your employer showing time missed
  • A short weekly note on pain, sleep and what you could not do

What is the average car accident settlement?

Insurers don’t publish settlement averages by state, but the closest national benchmark is claim severity: the average amount paid per bodily injury liability claim. Auto insurers paid an average of $28,278 per bodily injury claim in 2024, up from $26,178 in 2023, according to ISO data published by the Insurance Information Institute. That figure includes small soft-tissue claims and large surgical ones, so the median claim is lower and serious injuries run far higher.

Use the average as a sanity check, not a target. Two claims with the same medical bills can settle for very different amounts depending on fault, documentation and the insurance available. The calculator above shows how each of those inputs moves your own number. For a deeper look at the data, read average car accident settlement amounts.

Car accident settlement examples by injury

These are illustrations built with the same formula the calculator uses, not reported settlements. Read more about specific injuries in our guides to whiplash, herniated discs and broken bones.

Other crash calculators

Different crashes bring different insurance and fault questions. Use the truck accident, motorcycle accident, pedestrian accident, bicycle accident or Uber and Lyft accident calculator when one fits better. For the car itself, see the total loss, diminished value and rental car reimbursement calculators.

Questions people ask

What is the average car accident settlement?

No single average means much. Minor soft-tissue claims often settle for a few thousand dollars, while claims with surgery or permanent injury can reach six or seven figures. A state-specific range built from your own bills is more useful than any national average.

Does my own fault reduce my settlement?

In almost every state, yes. Most cut the award by your percentage of fault and bar recovery at 50% or 51%. Alabama, Maryland, North Carolina, Virginia and DC can bar a claim for almost any fault on your side. See comparative negligence by state.

Should I accept the insurer’s first offer?

First offers tend to sit at the low end of the range. Once you sign a release you cannot ask for more, so compare the offer with your estimate first using the settlement offer checker.

Is my vehicle damage part of the settlement?

It is usually handled as a separate property damage claim, often settled within weeks. The injury claim waits until your treatment ends, so you know its full cost.

Is this calculator legal advice?

No. It is a free estimate to show how claims are valued. ClaimValuator is not a law firm.

How much is a car accident claim worth without a lawyer?

The same injury has the same value, but people without a lawyer often settle for less because they accept early offers or leave out future costs. Without a lawyer you also keep the 33% to 40% fee, so compare your likely net figure both ways with the attorney fee calculator.

Does a rear-end collision settle for more?

Not automatically, but fault is usually clearer, so less is taken off for comparative fault and claims tend to resolve faster. The injury still drives the value.

File one day late and the court will almost always dismiss the case, which also ends your leverage to settle. Claims against a city, county or state agency can require a written notice within months. Each state calculator works out your last day to file from the crash date you enter, or use the statute of limitations calculator.

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: What to keep while the claim is open

blocks.name: core/list
blocks.html:
• The police report number and the other driver’s insurance details
  • Photos of the vehicles, the scene and your injuries
  • Every medical bill, record and receipt, including mileage to appointments
  • Pay stubs or a letter from your employer showing time missed
  • A short weekly note on pain, sleep and what you could not do

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: What is the average car accident settlement?

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: Insurers don’t publish settlement averages by state, but the closest national benchmark is claim severity: the average amount paid per bodily injury liability claim. Auto insurers paid an average of $28,278 per bodily injury claim in 2024, up from $26,178 in 2023, according to ISO data published by the Insurance Information Institute. That figure includes small soft-tissue claims and large surgical ones, so the median claim is lower and serious injuries run far higher.

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: Use the average as a sanity check, not a target. Two claims with the same medical bills can settle for very different amounts depending on fault, documentation and the insurance available. The calculator above shows how each of those inputs moves your own number. For a deeper look at the data, read average car accident settlement amounts.

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: Car accident settlement examples by injury

blocks.name: core/table
core/paragraph
blocks.html: These are illustrations built with the same formula the calculator uses, not reported settlements. Read more about specific injuries in our guides to whiplash, herniated discs and broken bones.

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: Other crash calculators

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: Different crashes bring different insurance and fault questions. Use the truck accident, motorcycle accident, pedestrian accident, bicycle accident or Uber and Lyft accident calculator when one fits better. For the car itself, see the total loss, diminished value and rental car reimbursement calculators.

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: Questions people ask

blocks.name: core/details
blocks.html:
What is the average car accident settlement?

No single average means much. Minor soft-tissue claims often settle for a few thousand dollars, while claims with surgery or permanent injury can reach six or seven figures. A state-specific range built from your own bills is more useful than any national average.

blocks.name: core/details
blocks.html:
Does my own fault reduce my settlement?

In almost every state, yes. Most cut the award by your percentage of fault and bar recovery at 50% or 51%. Alabama, Maryland, North Carolina, Virginia and DC can bar a claim for almost any fault on your side. See comparative negligence by state.

blocks.name: core/details
blocks.html:
Should I accept the insurer’s first offer?

First offers tend to sit at the low end of the range. Once you sign a release you cannot ask for more, so compare the offer with your estimate first using the settlement offer checker.

blocks.name: core/details
blocks.html:
Is my vehicle damage part of the settlement?

It is usually handled as a separate property damage claim, often settled within weeks. The injury claim waits until your treatment ends, so you know its full cost.

blocks.name: core/details
blocks.html:
Is this calculator legal advice?

No. It is a free estimate to show how claims are valued. ClaimValuator is not a law firm.

blocks.name: core/details
blocks.html:
How much is a car accident claim worth without a lawyer?

The same injury has the same value, but people without a lawyer often settle for less because they accept early offers or leave out future costs. Without a lawyer you also keep the 33% to 40% fee, so compare your likely net figure both ways with the attorney fee calculator.

blocks.name: core/details
blocks.html:
Does a rear-end collision settle for more?

Not automatically, but fault is usually clearer, so less is taken off for comparative fault and claims tend to resolve faster. The injury still drives the value.

posts.content:
Why truck claims are valued differently

Injuries from a crash with an 80,000-pound tractor-trailer tend to be more severe, the medical bills higher and the recovery longer. The bigger difference is insurance. A car driver may carry only the state minimum, but interstate motor carriers must carry far more under federal rules, so the ceiling on what can be collected is usually much higher.

Many carriers buy $1 million to $5 million or more. Trucks that never leave one state may follow lower state limits.

More than one party can pay

A truck crash claim can run against the driver, the motor carrier, the company that loaded the cargo, the owner of the trailer, a maintenance shop or a parts maker. Each may have its own insurance. That is why truck cases often settle for more than a car case with the same injuries.

Evidence disappears quickly

Trucks carry electronic logging devices, engine control modules and dash cameras, and carriers must keep driver logs, inspection reports and drug test results. Some of that data can be overwritten in weeks. A lawyer’s preservation letter early in the claim keeps it from being lost.

Federal safety rules matter for fault

Hours-of-service limits, inspection duties and driver qualification rules from the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration set the standard of care. A driver over their hours or a truck with brakes out of adjustment can make fault much easier to prove. Your state’s fault rule then decides how any share of blame on your side affects the award.

Why truck settlements run higher

Truck crashes tend to cause more serious injuries because of the weight difference, and there is usually more insurance to pay for them. Federal rules require interstate carriers hauling general freight to carry at least $750,000 of liability coverage, $1 million for oil and $5 million for most hazardous materials (49 CFR § 387.9). A car driver in many states may carry only $25,000.

Higher limits mean the injury, not the policy, usually sets the ceiling. It also means the carrier’s insurer and lawyers move quickly after a crash, so preserve evidence early: photos, the truck’s DOT number, witness names and a letter asking the carrier to keep its driver logs and electronic data.

Questions people ask

What is the average truck accident settlement?

Truck claims vary too widely for an average to help. Because injuries are often serious and the insurance is higher, many settle in the six figures and some in the millions. Build a range from your own bills with the calculator.

Who pays in a truck accident claim?

Usually the motor carrier’s liability insurer, because the company is responsible for its driver. Other parties, such as a shipper or maintenance company, may share liability.

How long do I have to file a truck accident claim?

The same statute of limitations as other injury claims in your state, usually two or three years. Check yours with the statute of limitations calculator.

Who can be sued after a truck accident?

Often more than one party: the driver, the motor carrier that employs or contracts the driver, and sometimes the company that loaded the cargo, the broker or a maintenance shop. Each may have its own insurance.

posts.content:
Motorcycle claims start from the same math

Medical bills and lost income, plus pain and suffering as a multiple of those costs, reduced by your share of fault. What changes is the typical injury: riders have no steel frame or airbags, so fractures, road rash, head injuries and surgery are common. Many claims sit in the severe range of the multiplier.

Expect a fight about fault

Insurers often argue a rider was speeding, lane splitting or hard to see. Your state’s fault rule decides what that argument is worth. In a pure comparative fault state a 30% share cuts the award by 30%. In a contributory negligence state, any share can bar the claim. Witness statements, helmet camera footage and crash reconstruction carry extra weight.

Helmets and damages

Not wearing a helmet does not usually bar a claim, but in some states the defense can argue it made a head injury worse and ask for a reduction. Wearing one, and keeping it, helps. Laws on helmet use and on whether non-use can be raised in court vary by state.

Insurance gaps are common

The car driver’s policy may carry only the state minimum, which a serious motorcycle injury can exceed many times over. Your own uninsured and underinsured motorist coverage on the bike is often the second source of money. Motorcycles are also often outside no-fault rules, so check whether PIP applies to you. Run the policy limits and UM/UIM gap calculator to see what your coverage adds.

Questions people ask

Is the rider always blamed in a motorcycle accident?

No. Many crashes happen when a driver turns left across the rider’s path or changes lanes without seeing the bike. Fault is decided on the evidence, not on who rode the motorcycle.

Does no-fault insurance cover motorcycle riders?

Often not. Several no-fault states exclude motorcycles from PIP, which can also mean the threshold to sue does not apply. Check your state and policy.

What if the driver who hit me had no insurance?

Your uninsured motorist coverage on the motorcycle policy can pay, up to its limit. Some states also let you use UM coverage from a car policy in your household.

posts.content:
Pedestrians can claim against the driver and their own policy

A pedestrian hit by a car claims against the driver’s liability insurance like any other crash victim. Your own auto policy usually still helps even though you were on foot: PIP in no-fault states, MedPay in others, and uninsured or underinsured motorist coverage if the driver has too little insurance or drives off.

Crosswalks do not settle fault on their own

Drivers must yield to pedestrians in marked and unmarked crosswalks in every state, but insurers still look at where you crossed, the signal, lighting and whether you were distracted. Under your state’s fault rule, a share of blame reduces the claim and can bar it in contributory negligence states. In DC, pedestrians and cyclists can recover unless they were more at fault than the driver.

Injuries are often serious

With no protection, pedestrians suffer leg and pelvic fractures, head injuries and long recoveries. That pushes claims toward the higher multipliers, and also makes it more likely the driver’s policy limit becomes the ceiling. The calculator adds your UM/UIM coverage to show the realistic maximum.

Hit-and-run crashes

If the driver leaves, report it to police at once. Your uninsured motorist coverage usually treats a hit-and-run driver as uninsured, but many policies require a police report within a short time.

Questions people ask

Does my car insurance cover me if I was hit while walking?

Usually yes. PIP or MedPay can pay medical bills, and UM/UIM coverage can pay for injuries when the driver is uninsured, underinsured or unknown.

Can I recover if I was jaywalking?

Often yes, but your share of fault reduces the award. In contributory negligence states, any fault can bar the claim, so the evidence matters a great deal.

posts.content:
Cyclists are treated as road users

In every state a cyclist has the rights and duties of a vehicle driver on the road. When a driver turns across a bike lane, opens a door into a rider or passes too close, the driver’s liability insurance pays the injury claim. Your own auto policy may add PIP, MedPay or UM/UIM coverage even though you were on a bike.

Fault arguments to expect

Insurers look for lights at night, riding direction, lane position and signals. Under your state’s fault rule, any share of blame reduces the award. DC lets cyclists recover unless they were more at fault than the driver, a narrow exception to its otherwise strict contributory negligence rule.

Document the bike and the gear

Keep the damaged bike, helmet and clothing. A bike shop’s written estimate supports the property claim, and a cracked helmet is strong evidence of the force of a head impact.

Questions people ask

Who pays when a car hits a cyclist?

The driver’s liability insurer pays for injuries and the bike. Your own auto coverage can fill gaps when the driver has too little insurance.

Does not wearing a helmet hurt my claim?

It does not usually bar a claim, but some states allow the defense to argue it made a head injury worse.

posts.content:
The app status decides the insurance

Rideshare drivers use personal cars, so which policy pays depends on what the driver was doing in the app at the moment of the crash.

State laws set the minimums for each period, and they differ. The calculator lets you pick the status to set the insurance ceiling.

Passengers, other drivers and pedestrians

A passenger hurt during a trip usually claims against the $1 million policy, whether the rideshare driver or another driver caused the crash. If another driver was at fault, that driver’s insurance pays first and the rideshare UM/UIM coverage can pay the rest. Other drivers and pedestrians hit by a rideshare car claim against whichever policy applied at that moment.

Get the trip record

Screenshots of the ride receipt, the driver’s name and plate, and the trip route establish the period. The companies keep trip data, and a lawyer can request it formally.

Questions people ask

Can I sue Uber or Lyft directly?

Usually the claim is against the driver and paid by the company’s insurance. The companies treat drivers as contractors, which limits direct claims against them in most cases.

How much does Uber or Lyft insurance pay?

Up to $1 million of liability coverage during a trip. With the app on but no trip accepted, much lower contingent limits apply.

posts.content:
Proving the owner knew is half the case

A property owner is not automatically liable because you fell. You must show the owner, or its employees, created the hazard, knew about it, or should have found it with reasonable inspections, and failed to fix it or warn you. A spill that had been there for an hour is a strong claim. A spill seconds old, with no one aware of it, is a weak one.

Evidence that wins premises claims

  • Photos of the hazard before it is cleaned up, with something for scale
  • The store’s incident report and the name of the manager you spoke to
  • Names and phone numbers of witnesses
  • Your shoes and clothing from that day
  • Surveillance video, which stores often overwrite within days: ask for it in writing

Your own care matters

Owners argue the hazard was open and obvious or that you were looking at your phone. Your state’s fault rule turns that argument into a percentage. In a 51% bar state, being found 40% at fault cuts the award by 40%. In a contributory negligence state it can end the claim.

Who pays

A store, restaurant or apartment complex usually carries commercial general liability insurance of $1 million or more. A homeowner’s policy usually covers falls at a private home. Claims against cities, schools or public housing need written notice within a short time, sometimes 30 to 180 days.

Questions people ask

What is a typical slip and fall settlement?

It depends on the injury. A sprain may settle for a few thousand dollars, while a hip fracture needing surgery, common in older adults, can settle for well into six figures.

Can I sue if I fell at a friend’s house?

Yes, the claim is usually paid by their homeowner’s insurance, not by your friend personally.

What if I fell on a public sidewalk?

The city may be responsible, but government claims have short notice deadlines and special rules. Act quickly.

A spill that had been there for an hour is a strong claim. A spill seconds old, with no one aware of it, is a weak one.

blocks.html: Evidence that wins premises claims

blocks.name: core/list
blocks.html:
• Photos of the hazard before it is cleaned up, with something for scale
  • The store’s incident report and the name of the manager you spoke to
  • Names and phone numbers of witnesses
  • Your shoes and clothing from that day
  • Surveillance video, which stores often overwrite within days: ask for it in writing

blocks.html: Your own care matters

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: Owners argue the hazard was open and obvious or that you were looking at your phone. Your state’s fault rule turns that argument into a percentage. In a 51% bar state, being found 40% at fault cuts the award by 40%. In a contributory negligence state it can end the claim.

blocks.html: Who pays

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: A store, restaurant or apartment complex usually carries commercial general liability insurance of $1 million or more. A homeowner’s policy usually covers falls at a private home. Claims against cities, schools or public housing need written notice within a short time, sometimes 30 to 180 days.

blocks.html: Questions people ask

blocks.name: core/details
blocks.html:
What is a typical slip and fall settlement?

It depends on the injury. A sprain may settle for a few thousand dollars, while a hip fracture needing surgery, common in older adults, can settle for well into six figures.

blocks.name: core/details
blocks.html:
Can I sue if I fell at a friend’s house?

Yes, the claim is usually paid by their homeowner’s insurance, not by your friend personally.

blocks.name: core/details
blocks.html:
What if I fell on a public sidewalk?

The city may be responsible, but government claims have short notice deadlines and special rules. Act quickly.

posts.content:
Strict liability or the one-bite rule

States split on when an owner must pay. In about 36 states a statute makes owners strictly liable for bites, so you do not have to prove the dog had bitten before. Other states follow the one-bite rule and negligence: you must show the owner knew or should have known the dog was dangerous, or was careless, for example by breaking a leash law. Several states mix the two. Pick your state in the calculator to see its rule, or compare all states in dog bite laws by state.

What a dog bite claim is worth

Medical bills for wound care, infections and plastic surgery, lost income and pain and suffering drive the value. Scarring, especially on the face or on a child, raises it sharply. Emotional trauma and fear of dogs are part of the claim too.

Homeowner’s insurance usually pays

The owner’s homeowner’s or renter’s policy covers most bites, commonly with $100,000 to $300,000 of liability. Some policies exclude certain breeds or dogs with a bite history, and some owners have no insurance, which limits what can be collected.

Steps after a bite

  • Get medical care and ask about rabies and tetanus
  • Report the bite to animal control
  • Photograph the wounds as they heal
  • Get the owner’s name, address and insurance details

Average dog bite settlement

Insurers paid $1.86 billion on 28,450 dog-related injury claims in 2025, an average of $65,450 per claim, according to Triple-I and State Farm. That average was $69,272 in 2024. New York had the highest average cost per claim in 2025, at $92,154.

The average is pulled up by severe attacks on children and facial injuries that need reconstructive surgery. A bite treated with stitches and antibiotics usually settles for far less. Our guide to dog bite settlement amounts breaks down what drives the number.

Questions people ask

How much is a dog bite settlement worth?

Insurers paid an average of more than $50,000 per dog bite claim in recent years, according to industry data, but serious scarring cases run much higher and minor bites lower.

Can I claim if a dog knocked me over without biting?

In many states, yes. Some strict liability statutes cover only bites, so other injuries follow negligence rules.

What if I was bitten by a friend’s dog?

The claim is against their homeowner’s or renter’s insurance, not their savings, in most cases.

Does homeowners insurance cover dog bites?

Usually yes, through the liability part of a homeowner’s or renter’s policy. Some insurers exclude certain breeds or dogs with a bite history, so ask the owner for the policy details early.

seo.title: Wrongful Death Settlement Calculator ()

seo.focus: wrongful death settlement calculator,wrongful death settlement amounts,average wrongful death settlement

posts.content:
What a wrongful death claim pays for

A wrongful death claim compensates the family for what they lost when someone died because of another’s negligence. Most states allow:

  • Lost financial support: the income the person would have earned and spent on the family
  • Household services: childcare, chores, repairs and other work the person did
  • Final expenses: medical bills from the final injury, funeral and burial costs
  • Loss of companionship, care and guidance for a spouse, children and sometimes parents

Many states also allow a separate survival claim for the person’s own pain before death and their estate’s losses.

How future losses are valued

Economists project the person’s earnings to retirement, subtract what they would have spent on themselves, and discount the result to today’s value, because money received now can be invested. The calculator uses a 3% discount rate and lets you set the personal consumption share, commonly 20% to 40% depending on family size.

Who can file and when

State law decides who brings the claim, usually the personal representative of the estate on behalf of the spouse, children or parents. The filing deadline usually runs from the date of death and is often two or three years, but can be as short as one. Enter the date in the calculator to see your state’s deadline.

Limits that can apply

A few states cap non-economic damages in death cases, and the at-fault party’s insurance limit often sets the practical ceiling. A death claim against a government agency can face both caps and short notice deadlines.

Questions people ask

How are wrongful death settlements calculated?

By adding the present value of lost support and services, final expenses and an amount for the family’s loss of companionship, then applying the state’s fault rule and checking the insurance available.

Who receives a wrongful death settlement?

Usually the surviving spouse, children or parents, divided according to state law or a court order.

Is a wrongful death settlement taxable?

Compensation for a death caused by physical injury is generally not taxable under federal law. Punitive damages and interest are.

seo.description: Free pain and suffering calculator. Compare the multiplier method (1.5x to 5x) with the per diem method to estimate non-economic damages in an injury claim.

posts.content:
What counts as pain and suffering

Pain and suffering covers the physical pain of an injury and what comes with it: anxiety, sleep loss, depression, scarring, and the loss of activities you used to enjoy. These are non-economic damages, so there is no bill to add up. Insurers and juries estimate them, usually in one of two ways.

The multiplier method

Add up economic damages, mainly medical bills and lost income, then multiply by a number from about 1.5 to 5. The multiplier rises with the seriousness of the injury, how long recovery takes, whether there is permanent harm, and how well your records document it. On $20,000 of bills and lost income, a 2× to 3× multiplier gives $40,000 to $60,000.

The per-diem method

Pick a daily rate and multiply by the number of days you were in pain or recovering. Many people use a day’s take-home pay as the rate, on the reasoning that living with the injury was at least as hard as a day’s work. At $150 a day for 120 days, that is $18,000. The method works best for injuries with a clear recovery date.

What pushes the number up

  • Surgery, imaging or other objective proof of injury
  • A permanent limitation, scarring or disfigurement
  • Consistent treatment without gaps
  • A journal and statements from family or co-workers about the change in your life

State caps

A few states cap non-economic damages in ordinary injury cases. Maryland, Mississippi, Tennessee, Colorado, Alaska and Ohio do; most states do not. The calculator applies the cap when your estimate passes it.

Questions people ask

What multiplier should I use?

About 1.5× to 2× for minor injuries that heal in months, 2× to 3× for fractures or longer treatment, 3× to 4× for surgery or permanent impairment, and up to 5× for catastrophic injuries.

Do insurers really use a multiplier?

Many use claims software that weighs injury codes and treatment rather than a single multiplier, but the result usually lands in the same range. The multiplier is a useful way to check an offer.

Is pain and suffering taxable?

Not when it comes from a physical injury or illness. Emotional distress damages without a physical injury generally are taxable.

seo.title: Attorney Fee Calculator: Your Net Settlement After Fees
seo.description: See what you take home from a settlement. Subtract the contingency fee (often 33% to 40%), case costs and medical liens from the gross award to find your net.
seo.focus: attorney fee calculator,contingency fee calculator,net settlement calculator,how much do lawyers take from a settlement

posts.content:
How a contingency fee works

Most injury lawyers work on contingency: no fee unless you recover money, and then a percentage of the recovery. One-third (33⅓%) is the most common rate. Many agreements rise to 40% if a lawsuit is filed or the case goes to trial, and some states cap fees in certain cases, such as medical malpractice.

Gross or net makes a real difference

Your agreement says whether the fee is taken from the gross settlement (before case costs) or the net (after case costs). On a $100,000 settlement with $3,500 of costs, a one-third fee is $33,333 on the gross and $32,167 on the net. Ask which one your agreement uses before you sign.

The order money comes out

Case costs are separate from the fee

Costs are the out-of-pocket expenses of the case: filing fees, medical records, expert reports, depositions and court reporters. They are small in a claim that settles early and can reach tens of thousands of dollars in a case that goes to trial. Ask for an itemized closing statement.

Liens can often be reduced

Hospitals, health plans and Medicare must be repaid from the settlement, but many will reduce their claim, especially when the recovery is limited by insurance. Lawyers negotiate these reductions routinely. Model yours with the medical lien calculator.

Example

A $90,000 settlement before a lawsuit is filed, with a 33⅓% fee, $1,800 in case costs and a $12,000 health plan lien:

  • Attorney fee: $30,000
  • Case costs: $1,800
  • Medical lien: $12,000, often reduced through negotiation
  • Your net: $46,200

If the lawyer negotiated the lien down by a third, to $8,000, your net would rise to $50,200. Lien reductions are one of the places a lawyer can add money that the fee percentage doesn’t show.

Sliding-scale fees

Many contingency agreements raise the percentage at each stage: for example, 33⅓% if the claim settles before a lawsuit, 40% after suit is filed and up to 45% if the case goes through trial or appeal. Some states cap contingency fees for certain claims, such as medical malpractice. Read the fee agreement before you sign, and ask whether costs come out before or after the fee is calculated, since that changes your net.

Questions people ask

What percentage do personal injury lawyers take?

Usually 33⅓% of the recovery, often rising to 40% if a lawsuit is filed or the case goes to trial. Rates as low as 25% are sometimes offered for claims that settle quickly.

Do I pay the lawyer if I lose?

Not a fee under a contingency agreement. Check whether you would owe case costs; many firms waive them if there is no recovery.

Is the attorney fee negotiable?

Often, yes, especially for clear liability cases with high policy limits. Get the terms in writing.

Are case costs taken out before or after the attorney fee?

It depends on the agreement. Taking costs out first lowers the amount the percentage applies to, which slightly increases your net.

Can I negotiate a lawyer’s contingency fee?

Often yes, especially for a clear liability claim with high value. Ask about a lower percentage if the case settles quickly.

seo.title: Medical Lien Calculator: Liens on a Settlement
seo.description: Estimate how much of your settlement goes to hospital, health plan and Medicare liens, and how a pro rata reduction for legal fees can lower what you repay.

posts.content:
What a medical lien is

When a health plan, Medicare, Medicaid or a hospital pays for treatment of an injury someone else caused, it can claim repayment from your settlement. That claim is a lien or a right of reimbursement (subrogation). It must be resolved before the settlement money is paid out.

Medicare’s procurement-cost reduction

Medicare reduces its claim by its share of what it cost to get the recovery: the attorney fee and case costs. The formula is in the federal regulations (42 C.F.R. § 411.37). On a $100,000 settlement with a one-third fee and $3,000 of costs, procurement costs are about 36%, so a $20,000 Medicare claim drops to about $12,700.

Other lien holders

  • Medicaid can recover only from the part of a settlement that pays medical costs, and most states also reduce for procurement costs.
  • Self-funded employer plans (ERISA) follow the plan document, which often demands full repayment. Reductions are possible but depend on negotiation and the plan terms.
  • Private insurers are often subject to the common fund doctrine and state anti-subrogation rules, which can cut their share.
  • Hospital liens are governed by state lien laws, which can cap the amount or require reasonable charges.

Why reductions matter

When insurance limits keep a settlement below the full value of the claim, lien holders are often asked to take less so the injured person is not left with nothing. Every dollar saved on a lien goes to you.

Example: a pro rata reduction

You settle for $75,000. Your lawyer’s fee is one-third ($25,000) plus $1,500 in costs, so procurement costs are 35.3% of the settlement. Your health plan paid $15,000 and claims a lien.

Many plans and state laws reduce a lien by the same share it cost to get the money: $15,000 × 35.3% = $5,300 off, leaving a lien of about $9,700. Your net rises from $33,500 to about $38,800.

Who can claim a lien

  • Medicare must be repaid under federal law, reduced for procurement costs, and the case can’t close until Medicare’s final demand is resolved
  • Medicaid can recover from the part of the settlement that represents medical expenses
  • Employer health plans governed by ERISA follow the plan document, and self-funded plans often claim full repayment
  • Hospitals in many states can file liens under state law
  • Your own insurer may claim MedPay or PIP reimbursement in some states

Reducing what you repay

Ask for an itemized lien and check every charge relates to the injury. Ask for a procurement cost reduction. In some states, the made-whole doctrine limits recovery when the settlement doesn’t cover all your losses. Lawyers negotiate these reductions routinely.

Questions people ask

Do I have to pay back my health insurance from a settlement?

Often yes, if your plan has a reimbursement clause or the law gives it a lien. The amount is frequently negotiable.

How much does Medicare take from a settlement?

Medicare claims what it paid for injury-related care, reduced by its share of attorney fees and costs. It can also waive or compromise the claim in hardship cases.

Do I have to pay medical liens out of my settlement?

Valid liens must be paid, usually from the settlement before you receive your share. Ignoring one can leave you personally responsible and, for Medicare, can lead to penalties.

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: What a medical lien is

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: When a health plan, Medicare, Medicaid or a hospital pays for treatment of an injury someone else caused, it can claim repayment from your settlement. That claim is a lien or a right of reimbursement (subrogation). It must be resolved before the settlement money is paid out.

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: Medicare’s procurement-cost reduction

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: Medicare reduces its claim by its share of what it cost to get the recovery: the attorney fee and case costs. The formula is in the federal regulations (42 C.F.R. § 411.37). On a $100,000 settlement with a one-third fee and $3,000 of costs, procurement costs are about 36%, so a $20,000 Medicare claim drops to about $12,700.

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: Other lien holders

blocks.name: core/list
blocks.html:
• Medicaid can recover only from the part of a settlement that pays medical costs, and most states also reduce for procurement costs.
  • Self-funded employer plans (ERISA) follow the plan document, which often demands full repayment. Reductions are possible but depend on negotiation and the plan terms.
  • Private insurers are often subject to the common fund doctrine and state anti-subrogation rules, which can cut their share.
  • Hospital liens are governed by state lien laws, which can cap the amount or require reasonable charges.

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: Why reductions matter

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: When insurance limits keep a settlement below the full value of the claim, lien holders are often asked to take less so the injured person is not left with nothing. Every dollar saved on a lien goes to you.

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: Example: a pro rata reduction

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: You settle for $75,000. Your lawyer’s fee is one-third ($25,000) plus $1,500 in costs, so procurement costs are 35.3% of the settlement. Your health plan paid $15,000 and claims a lien.

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: Many plans and state laws reduce a lien by the same share it cost to get the money: $15,000 × 35.3% = $5,300 off, leaving a lien of about $9,700. Your net rises from $33,500 to about $38,800.

blocks.html: Who can claim a lien

blocks.name: core/list
blocks.html:
• Medicare must be repaid under federal law, reduced for procurement costs, and the case can’t close until Medicare’s final demand is resolved
  • Medicaid can recover from the part of the settlement that represents medical expenses
  • Employer health plans governed by ERISA follow the plan document, and self-funded plans often claim full repayment
  • Hospitals in many states can file liens under state law
  • Your own insurer may claim MedPay or PIP reimbursement in some states

blocks.html: Reducing what you repay

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: Ask for an itemized lien and check every charge relates to the injury. Ask for a procurement cost reduction. In some states, the made-whole doctrine limits recovery when the settlement doesn’t cover all your losses. Lawyers negotiate these reductions routinely.

Often yes, if your plan has a reimbursement clause or the law gives it a lien. The amount is frequently negotiable.

posts.content:
The rule for physical injuries

Federal law excludes from income damages received “on account of personal physical injuries or physical sickness” (26 U.S.C. § 104(a)(2)). That covers medical expenses, lost wages and pain and suffering in a typical injury claim, as long as they flow from a physical injury.

What is usually taxable

Deducted medical expenses

If you deducted medical expenses in an earlier year and the settlement repays them, that part can be taxable. Keep records of what you deducted.

Wording matters

How the settlement agreement allocates the money between categories affects the tax result. Talk to a tax professional before you sign, not after.

Examples

  • Car accident: a $60,000 settlement for a broken leg covering medical bills, lost wages and pain and suffering is generally tax-free in full.
  • Employment claim: a $60,000 discrimination settlement split $40,000 back pay and $20,000 emotional distress is taxable. The back pay is wages, with payroll taxes withheld, and the distress portion is reported on a Form 1099.
  • Interest: if a court judgment adds $4,000 of interest to a tax-free injury award, the $4,000 is taxable.

Forms you may receive

Taxable settlement payments are usually reported on Form 1099-MISC or a W-2 for wages. A tax-free physical injury settlement often comes with no tax form at all. Getting a 1099 doesn’t by itself make an amount taxable, but you should be able to explain why it isn’t.

Attorney fees in taxable cases

In employment and some whistleblower cases, the IRS can treat the full settlement, including the part paid to your lawyer, as your income. Federal law allows an above-the-line deduction for those fees in discrimination and certain other claims. Ask a tax professional how this applies before the settlement is final.

Questions people ask

Are car accident settlements taxable?

Usually not, because they compensate a physical injury. Interest and any punitive damages are taxable.

Do I pay tax on a wrongful death settlement?

Compensatory damages for a death caused by physical injury are generally not taxable. Punitive damages are.

Is a slip and fall settlement taxable?

Usually not, because it compensates a physical injury. Punitive damages or interest included in the payment would be taxable.

Do I report a tax-free injury settlement on my return?

Generally no, if it is entirely for a physical injury and you didn’t deduct the medical costs in an earlier year. Keep the settlement agreement with your tax records.

seo.title: Structured Settlement Calculator: Lump Sum vs Payments
seo.description: Compare a lump sum with structured settlement payments. See the present value of a payment stream and how much a buyer’s discount rate would cost you.
seo.focus: structured settlement calculator,structured settlement present value,lump sum vs structured settlement

posts.content:
What a structured settlement is

Instead of one lump sum, part or all of a settlement is paid over time, usually through an annuity bought from a life insurer. Payments can be monthly or yearly, fixed or rising, for a set period or for life. They are common in large claims and claims for minors.

Present value in plain terms

A dollar paid in 10 years is worth less than a dollar today, because today’s dollar could be invested. Present value converts a stream of future payments into what it is worth now, using a discount rate. The higher the rate, the lower the present value.

Comparing with a lump sum

If a lump sum offer is higher than the present value of the payments at a reasonable rate, the lump sum is worth more. If it is lower, the payments are. Structured payments also offer tax-free growth for injury settlements and protection against spending the money too quickly.

Selling payments later

Companies buy structured settlement payments for cash, but they use high discount rates, so their offers are far below the payments’ value. State laws require a court to approve the sale. Run their offer through this calculator before you agree.

Example: lump sum versus payments

Say your settlement offers either $200,000 now or $1,500 a month for 15 years, a total of $270,000. At a 4% discount rate, the payments are worth about $202,000 today, close to the lump sum. At a 6% rate they are worth about $178,000, so the lump sum looks better if you could reliably earn 6%. The right rate is what you could actually earn on the money after fees and taxes.

Why people choose structured payments

  • Guaranteed income that can’t be spent all at once
  • Payments for a physical injury are generally tax-free, including the growth built into them
  • Useful for minors, people with ongoing care needs and people receiving needs-based benefits

Selling payments later is expensive

Companies that buy structured settlement payments apply steep discount rates, so you get far less than the payments are worth. Sales need court approval under state structured settlement protection laws, and a federal excise tax applies to sales that aren’t approved. Use the calculator to see what a buyer’s rate would cost before you sign.

Questions people ask

What discount rate should I use?

A rate close to what you could safely earn on a lump sum, often 4% to 5% in recent years. Buyers of structured settlements use 9% or more.

Are structured settlement payments taxable?

For physical injury settlements, payments are generally tax-free, including the growth built into the annuity.

Can I change a structured settlement after it is set up?

Usually not. The payment schedule is fixed by an annuity contract. The main way to get cash early is to sell payments, which needs court approval.

posts.content:
What lost wages include

Lost wages cover the pay you missed because of the injury: days off work, reduced hours, lost overtime and tips, missed bonuses, and paid leave you had to use. If the injury limits what you can earn in the future, that loss of earning capacity is claimed separately.

How to document them

  • Pay stubs from before and after the injury
  • A letter from your employer showing dates missed and your rate of pay
  • Doctor’s notes taking you off work or limiting duties
  • For the self-employed: tax returns, invoices, bank statements and lost contracts

Self-employed claims

Without a paycheck, the loss is shown by comparing earnings before and after the injury. Net profit from tax returns is the usual starting point. Lost clients or contracts, and the cost of hiring help to cover your work, can be claimed too.

Future earnings

When an injury is permanent, an economist or vocational expert may project the difference between what you would have earned and what you can earn now, over the rest of your working life. The calculator multiplies a yearly loss by the number of years for a quick figure; experts discount it to present value.

Example

You earn $26 an hour, work 40 hours a week and usually get 5 hours of overtime at time-and-a-half. You miss six weeks of work:

  • Regular pay: $26 × 40 × 6 = $6,240
  • Overtime: $39 × 5 × 6 = $1,170
  • Lost wages: $7,410, plus any PTO you used, which counts because you had to spend it

Proving lost wages

  • Employees: a wage verification letter from your employer listing your pay rate, usual hours and the dates you missed, plus pay stubs from before and after
  • Self-employed: tax returns for the last two or three years, invoices, canceled contracts and a statement of how the injury stopped your work
  • Gig workers: platform earnings statements showing average weekly earnings before the injury

A doctor’s note that you couldn’t work, and for how long, ties the lost time to the injury.

Lost earning capacity

If the injury permanently reduces what you can earn, the claim includes future losses: the gap between what you would have earned and what you can earn now, over your working life. These claims usually need a vocational expert and an economist, and they can be the largest part of a serious injury claim.

Questions people ask

Can I claim lost wages if I used sick days?

Yes. Paid leave you were forced to use is a real loss, because you no longer have it for later.

Are lost wages in an injury settlement taxable?

Not when they are part of a physical injury settlement. Back pay in an employment claim is taxable.

Can I claim lost wages if I used sick days or PTO?

Yes, in most states. You lost paid time you would otherwise have kept, so its value is part of your damages.

Are lost wages in an injury settlement taxable?

Usually not when they are part of a settlement for a physical injury. Lost wages from an employment claim are taxed as wages.

posts.content:
How to judge an offer

An offer is fair if it sits within the range a jury in your state would likely award, adjusted for the risks of trial and limited by the insurance available. The calculator builds that range from your medical bills, lost income and injury severity, applies your state’s fault rule and caps, then shows where the offer lands.

Why first offers run low

Adjusters expect to negotiate. A first offer often covers medical bills and little more, especially before your treatment ends. Insurers also count on people needing money quickly. A low first offer is not a final answer.

Before you accept

  • Make sure treatment is finished or your doctor has estimated future care
  • Add up every bill, including those paid by health insurance, which may need repaying
  • Check the filing deadline so you do not lose leverage while negotiating
  • Read the release: once signed, the claim is closed for good

How to respond

Reply in writing with a counteroffer and the reasons for it: the bills, the treatment, the effect on your life and the evidence of fault. Then use the counteroffer calculator to plan each step down, or start with a demand letter if you have not sent one.

Questions people ask

Should I accept the first settlement offer?

Rarely. First offers are usually opening positions. Compare the offer with your estimated range and counter in writing.

Can I reopen a claim after accepting a settlement?

Almost never. A signed release ends the claim, even if your injury later turns out to be worse.

How long do insurers take to respond to a counteroffer?

Usually days to a few weeks. Many states require insurers to respond within set times under fair claims practices rules.

posts.content:
How settlement negotiation moves

Most injury claims settle after a few rounds. You open with a demand above your target, the adjuster offers well below it, and each side moves toward the middle. The size of each step sends a signal: big drops suggest your number was inflated, small ones suggest you are near your limit.

Set your floor before you start

Decide the lowest amount you would accept, based on your estimated range, the insurance available and your appetite for a lawsuit. Write it down. Do not reveal it.

Explain every move

A counteroffer is stronger with a reason attached: a new bill, a doctor’s opinion on future care, a photo, a witness statement. Moving without a reason invites the adjuster to keep pushing.

When to stop negotiating

If the insurer will not come near your floor and your filing deadline is getting close, it is time to talk to a lawyer about filing suit. A lawsuit often brings a better offer, but it also adds cost and time.

A sample negotiation

Here is how a claim with an estimated value of $40,000 to $55,000 might move:

Each of your counters gave up less ground than the round before, which tells the adjuster you are nearing your floor. Each came with a reason: a therapy bill, a doctor’s note on future care, the photos of the scene.

Mistakes that cost money

  • Negotiating against yourself: don’t lower your number twice without a new offer in between
  • Moving by round numbers: $44,000 reads as a calculation; $45,000 reads as a guess
  • Talking only on the phone: confirm every offer and counter in writing
  • Ignoring the deadline: if the statute of limitations is close, the insurer knows your leverage is shrinking

How much should my first counteroffer drop?

Often 10% to 25% of the gap between your demand and their offer. Smaller steps show you are confident in your number.

How many rounds does negotiation take?

Three to five rounds is common for a claim that settles without a lawsuit.

Should I counter in writing?

Yes. A short letter or email with your number and the reason for it creates a record, keeps the negotiation focused and avoids misunderstandings about what was offered.

posts.content:
What a demand letter does

A demand letter tells the insurer what happened, why its insured is at fault, how you were hurt, what it cost you and how much you want to settle. A clear, documented letter often brings a better first offer than a phone call.

What to include

  • The claim number, date and place of the accident
  • A short, factual description of how it happened
  • Your diagnosed injuries and the treatment you received
  • An itemized list of medical bills and lost income, with copies attached
  • How the injury affected daily life, work and sleep
  • A specific demand and a date to respond

What to leave out

Do not admit fault, guess at medical issues your doctors have not confirmed, or send records you have not read. Keep emotion out and facts in. Do not include your full medical history; send records related to this injury.

When to send it

After you finish treatment or reach maximum medical improvement, so you know the full cost, and well before the filing deadline.

Questions people ask

How much should I demand?

Usually the high end of a reasonable range, so you have room to negotiate. The generator suggests economic damages plus a pain and suffering multiplier.

Should I send a demand letter myself or hire a lawyer?

For small, clear claims many people negotiate themselves. For serious injuries or disputed fault, a lawyer’s demand usually recovers more.

posts.content:
What a statute of limitations is

A statute of limitations is the deadline to file a lawsuit. Miss it and the court will almost always dismiss the case, no matter how strong it is. Insurers know the date too: once it passes, they have no reason to settle.

Deadlines range from one to six years

Personal injury deadlines run from one year in Kentucky, Louisiana (for older claims) and Tennessee to six years in Maine, Minnesota and North Dakota. Most states use two or three years. Some set a different deadline for vehicle crashes or wrongful death. Compare all states in the statute of limitations by state table.

When the clock starts

Usually on the date of the injury. Exceptions can delay or pause it:

  • Discovery rule: when an injury could not reasonably be discovered at once
  • Minors: many states pause the deadline until the injured child turns 18
  • Absence or incapacity: some states pause it while the defendant is out of state or the injured person is incapacitated

Claims against the government

A claim against a city, county, state or federal agency usually needs a written notice of claim within a much shorter time, sometimes 30 to 180 days. Missing that notice can bar the claim even if the lawsuit deadline is years away.

Questions people ask

Does filing an insurance claim stop the statute of limitations?

No. Only filing a lawsuit in court does, unless the parties sign a written agreement to extend it.

What if I miss the deadline?

The claim is almost always lost. Talk to a lawyer at once in case an exception applies.

posts.content:
Five rules for shared fault

When both sides share the blame for an accident, each state applies one of five rules:

Every point of fault has a price

On a $100,000 claim, each percentage point of fault costs $1,000. That is why adjusters argue about whether you were speeding, distracted or should have seen the hazard. In a bar state, the argument can be worth everything.

Michigan’s hybrid

Michigan cuts awards by the plaintiff’s share of fault, and above 50% bars pain and suffering damages while still allowing reduced economic damages.

See every state’s rule in comparative negligence by state.

Questions people ask

What is the difference between the 50% and 51% bar?

Under the 51% bar you can recover at exactly 50% fault; under the 50% bar you cannot. An even split matters.

Which states use contributory negligence?

Alabama, Maryland, North Carolina, Virginia and the District of Columbia.

posts.content:
Policy limits set the real ceiling

Liability policies are written as three numbers, such as 30/60/25: $30,000 per injured person, $60,000 per crash and $25,000 for property damage. The insurer will rarely pay more than the limit, however serious your injuries. If several people are hurt, they share the per-crash limit.

Underinsured motorist coverage

Your own underinsured motorist (UIM) coverage pays when the at-fault driver’s limit is too low. It comes in two kinds, set by your state and policy:

  • Excess (add-on): pays on top of the at-fault driver’s limit, up to your UIM limit
  • Reducing (offset): pays your UIM limit minus what the at-fault policy paid, so it adds nothing if your limit is not higher than theirs

Uninsured motorist (UM) coverage pays when the driver has no insurance or flees.

Collecting beyond the policy

Lawsuits against an individual for more than their policy rarely produce money, because most drivers with minimum coverage have few assets. Other sources may exist: an employer if the driver was working, a vehicle owner, or a bar that over-served the driver.

Check your declarations page

Your auto policy’s declarations page lists your UM and UIM limits. Many people carry less than they think. Raising UM/UIM is one of the cheapest ways to protect yourself.

Questions people ask

What happens if my damages exceed the policy limits?

Your UIM coverage can pay the difference up to its limit. Beyond that, recovery depends on other insurance or the driver’s assets.

Will my rates go up if I use UIM coverage?

In most states insurers cannot raise rates for a UIM claim when you were not at fault.
