posts.content:
How no-fault insurance works

In a no-fault state, your own personal injury protection (PIP) pays your medical bills and part of your lost income after a crash, whoever caused it. In exchange, you can sue the at-fault driver for pain and suffering only if your injury passes the state’s threshold.

Thresholds to sue

States use one of two kinds:

  • Monetary threshold: medical bills above a set amount, such as $2,000 in Massachusetts or $4,000 in Minnesota
  • Verbal threshold: a serious injury as defined by law, such as a fracture, permanent injury or significant disfigurement, used in Florida, Michigan, New Jersey, New York and Pennsylvania

Kentucky, New Jersey and Pennsylvania let drivers choose between no-fault and traditional tort rules.

What PIP pays

PIP typically pays reasonable medical expenses and a share of lost wages, often 60% to 85%, up to the policy limit. Some states add replacement services and funeral benefits. Florida pays 80% of medical bills and 60% of lost income up to $10,000.

When PIP runs out

Once PIP is exhausted, health insurance usually pays medical bills. If your injury meets the threshold, the claim against the at-fault driver covers what PIP did not, plus pain and suffering. See every state’s threshold in no-fault states.

The 12 no-fault states

Florida, Hawaii, Kansas, Kentucky, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, New York, North Dakota, Pennsylvania and Utah use no-fault auto insurance. Kentucky, New Jersey and Pennsylvania are “choice” states, where drivers can choose a policy that keeps their right to sue. See every state’s PIP minimum and threshold in the no-fault states table.

Example

You live in a no-fault state with $10,000 of PIP. A crash leaves you with $14,000 in medical bills and $4,000 in lost income. In Florida, for example, PIP pays 80% of reasonable medical bills and 60% of lost income, up to the limit, so the $10,000 goes quickly. The remaining $8,000 or more of losses, plus pain and suffering, can be claimed from the at-fault driver only if your injury meets the state’s threshold.

Verbal and monetary thresholds

  • Verbal threshold: you must have a serious injury defined by statute, such as a fracture, permanent injury, significant disfigurement or death
  • Monetary threshold: your medical expenses must exceed a set dollar amount

Medical records that clearly document the injury, imaging and lasting limits are how you meet a verbal threshold. Read no-fault states and pain and suffering for more.

Questions people ask

Which states are no-fault?

Florida, Hawaii, Kansas, Kentucky, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, New York, North Dakota, Pennsylvania and Utah.

Do I have to use PIP first?

In no-fault states, yes. PIP is the primary coverage for your medical bills after a crash.

Does PIP cover passengers and pedestrians?

Usually yes. Passengers are generally covered by the PIP of the car they were in or by their own policy, and pedestrians by their own auto policy or the car that hit them, depending on the state.

Can I sue for pain and suffering in a no-fault state?

Yes, if your injury meets the state’s threshold. Below it, PIP is usually your only recovery for your injuries.

posts.content:
What MedPay is

Medical payments coverage is optional auto coverage in most at-fault states. It pays medical bills for you and your passengers after a crash, regardless of fault, up to a limit such as $1,000, $5,000 or $10,000. It can also pay health insurance deductibles and copays.

MedPay and your settlement

Some states and policies let your insurer recover MedPay from your settlement with the at-fault driver (subrogation). Others do not. The calculator flags the issue when you expect a settlement; your policy and state law decide the answer.

MedPay or PIP?

PIP, used in no-fault states, covers medical bills and lost income. MedPay covers medical bills only. A few at-fault states offer both.

How a MedPay claim works

  1. Tell your own insurer about the crash and ask to open a medical payments claim.
  2. Send itemized bills from each provider, or have the providers bill the insurer directly.
  3. The insurer pays reasonable medical costs up to your MedPay limit, usually without a deductible.
  4. If you also have a liability claim against the other driver, keep copies of everything MedPay paid. Those bills still count toward your damages.

Example

Say you carry $5,000 of MedPay and your health plan has a $2,000 deductible. After a crash, you have $7,500 in medical bills. MedPay pays $5,000. Your health plan covers the rest after your deductible, and MedPay can usually be used for that deductible if it hasn’t been exhausted. If you settle with the at-fault driver for $30,000, your insurer may ask to be repaid the $5,000 from that settlement, depending on your state and policy.

Choosing a MedPay limit

Common limits run from $1,000 to $10,000, and some insurers offer more. MedPay is inexpensive compared with liability coverage, and it helps most when you have a high health insurance deductible, no health insurance, or regular passengers who may not be insured.

MedPay and the rest of your claim

MedPay is usually the fastest money after a crash, but it is small. For anything beyond basic treatment, the at-fault driver’s bodily injury coverage and your own underinsured motorist coverage matter more. In no-fault states, PIP takes MedPay’s place as the first source of payment.

Questions people ask

Does MedPay pay if the crash was my fault?

Yes. MedPay pays regardless of fault.

Is MedPay worth having if I have health insurance?

It can be, because it pays deductibles and copays and covers passengers who may not have insurance.

Does MedPay cover lost wages?

No. MedPay pays medical and funeral expenses only. Lost income is covered by PIP in no-fault states, or claimed from the at-fault driver.

Does MedPay cover passengers?

Yes. MedPay usually covers everyone in your car, and it covers you as a pedestrian or passenger in someone else’s car.

Will a MedPay claim raise my premium?

Not usually when another driver was at fault, but rating rules vary by insurer and state. Ask your insurer how it treats medical payments claims.

blocks.html: What MedPay is

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: Medical payments coverage is optional auto coverage in most at-fault states. It pays medical bills for you and your passengers after a crash, regardless of fault, up to a limit such as $1,000, $5,000 or $10,000. It can also pay health insurance deductibles and copays.

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: MedPay and your settlement

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: Some states and policies let your insurer recover MedPay from your settlement with the at-fault driver (subrogation). Others do not. The calculator flags the issue when you expect a settlement; your policy and state law decide the answer.

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: MedPay or PIP?

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: PIP, used in no-fault states, covers medical bills and lost income. MedPay covers medical bills only. A few at-fault states offer both.

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: How a MedPay claim works

blocks.name: core/list
blocks.html:
1. Tell your own insurer about the crash and ask to open a medical payments claim.
  2. Send itemized bills from each provider, or have the providers bill the insurer directly.
  3. The insurer pays reasonable medical costs up to your MedPay limit, usually without a deductible.
  4. If you also have a liability claim against the other driver, keep copies of everything MedPay paid. Those bills still count toward your damages.

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: Example

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: Say you carry $5,000 of MedPay and your health plan has a $2,000 deductible. After a crash, you have $7,500 in medical bills. MedPay pays $5,000. Your health plan covers the rest after your deductible, and MedPay can usually be used for that deductible if it hasn’t been exhausted. If you settle with the at-fault driver for $30,000, your insurer may ask to be repaid the $5,000 from that settlement, depending on your state and policy.

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: Choosing a MedPay limit

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: Common limits run from $1,000 to $10,000, and some insurers offer more. MedPay is inexpensive compared with liability coverage, and it helps most when you have a high health insurance deductible, no health insurance, or regular passengers who may not be insured.

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: MedPay and the rest of your claim

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: MedPay is usually the fastest money after a crash, but it is small. For anything beyond basic treatment, the at-fault driver’s bodily injury coverage and your own underinsured motorist coverage matter more. In no-fault states, PIP takes MedPay’s place as the first source of payment.

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: Questions people ask

blocks.name: core/details
blocks.html:
Does MedPay pay if the crash was my fault?

Yes. MedPay pays regardless of fault.

blocks.name: core/details
blocks.html:
Is MedPay worth having if I have health insurance?

It can be, because it pays deductibles and copays and covers passengers who may not have insurance.

blocks.name: core/details
blocks.html:
Does MedPay cover lost wages?

No. MedPay pays medical and funeral expenses only. Lost income is covered by PIP in no-fault states, or claimed from the at-fault driver.

blocks.name: core/details
blocks.html:
Does MedPay cover passengers?

Yes. MedPay usually covers everyone in your car, and it covers you as a pedestrian or passenger in someone else’s car.

blocks.name: core/details
blocks.html:
Will a MedPay claim raise my premium?

Not usually when another driver was at fault, but rating rules vary by insurer and state. Ask your insurer how it treats medical payments claims.

seo.description: Estimate your total loss payout: actual cash value plus sales tax and title fees, minus your deductible, and whether it pays off your car loan or needs gap.
seo.focus: total loss calculator,total loss car value,actual cash value car,total loss payout

posts.content:
When a car is a total loss

An insurer declares a car a total loss when repairs would cost more than its value, or more than a percentage of its value set by state law, commonly 70% to 80%. You are then paid the car’s actual cash value (ACV) instead of repairs.

What the payment should include

  • Actual cash value: what a comparable car, same model, trim, mileage and condition, sold for locally just before the crash
  • Sales tax on that value, required in many states
  • Title and registration fees, required in many states
  • Minus your deductible if you claim through your own collision coverage

Challenging a low valuation

Ask for the valuation report and the comparable vehicles used. Check the trim, options and mileage, and look up local listings for the same model. Many policies include an appraisal clause that lets you hire an independent appraiser if you disagree.

When you owe more than the car is worth

If your loan balance is higher than the settlement, you still owe the difference. Gap insurance covers it if you have it.

Example

Your car is totaled with an actual cash value of $18,000. Your state requires the insurer to pay sales tax at 6% ($1,080) and title and registration fees ($150). You claim through your own collision coverage with a $500 deductible:

$18,000 + $1,080 + $150 − $500 = $18,730

If you still owe $21,000 on the loan, the payout leaves you $2,270 short. Gap insurance would cover that difference. If the other driver caused the crash and you claim against their insurer, there is no deductible.

Total loss thresholds

Each state sets when a car must be totaled. Some use a fixed percentage of the car’s value, often 70% to 80%. Others use a total loss formula: the car is totaled when repair cost plus salvage value exceeds its actual cash value. Insurers can also total a car below the threshold if repairs aren’t economical.

Getting a better offer

The insurer’s valuation is a starting point. Comparable cars should match your model, trim, options, mileage and condition, and be for sale near you. Point out missing options, recent major repairs or new tires with receipts. If you and the insurer still disagree, check your policy for an appraisal clause.

Questions people ask

Can I keep my totaled car?

Usually yes, for the settlement minus its salvage value, but it will get a salvage title.

Does the insurer have to pay sales tax on a total loss?

In many states, yes. Check your state insurance department’s rules.

How long does a total loss settlement take?

Often two to four weeks after the car is declared a total loss, longer if you dispute the value or a lender needs to release the title.

Is the total loss payout taxable?

Generally no. It replaces the value of property you lost rather than giving you income, unless it exceeds what you paid for the car.

posts.excerpt: Estimate diminished value, the resale value a car loses after accident repairs, using the 17c formula many insurers start from.

meta.rank_math_description: Estimate your car’s diminished value after an accident with the 17c formula, using pre-accident value, damage severity and mileage, before you file a claim.
meta.rank_math_focus_keyword: diminished value calculator,diminished value claim,17c formula
meta.rank_math_title: Diminished Value Calculator (17c Formula & Market Method)

seo.title: Diminished Value Calculator (17c Formula & Market Method)
seo.description: Estimate your car’s diminished value after an accident with the 17c formula, using pre-accident value, damage severity and mileage, before you file a claim.
seo.focus: diminished value calculator,diminished value claim,17c formula

posts.content:
What diminished value is

A repaired car with an accident on its history report is worth less than the same car without one. That difference is diminished value. In most states you can claim it from the at-fault driver’s insurer.

The 17c formula

The formula comes from a Georgia class action and is used by many insurers:

  1. Start with 10% of the car’s pre-accident value (the cap)
  2. Multiply by a damage factor from 1.00 (severe structural damage) to 0.00 (no structural damage)
  3. Multiply by a mileage factor from 1.0 (under 20,000 miles) to 0 (100,000 miles or more)

It tends to undervalue newer, low-mileage and luxury cars. An independent appraisal based on market data often comes in higher.

Who can claim it

Claims against the at-fault driver’s insurer are allowed in most states. Claims against your own insurer for diminished value are allowed in only a few.

Worked example of the 17c formula

Take a car worth $30,000 before the crash with 35,000 miles and moderate structural damage:

  1. Base loss cap: 10% of $30,000 = $3,000
  2. Damage factor for moderate structural damage, 0.50: $3,000 × 0.50 = $1,500
  3. Mileage factor for 20,000 to 39,999 miles, 0.80: $1,500 × 0.80 = $1,200

The 17c result is $1,200. A dealer appraisal based on what similar cars with an accident history actually sell for might show a larger loss, especially for a newer or luxury car.

How to make the claim

  1. Finish repairs and get the final repair invoice.
  2. Get an independent diminished value appraisal, or collect dealer trade-in offers that note the accident history.
  3. Send a written demand to the at-fault driver’s insurer with the appraisal and the repair invoice.
  4. Negotiate. If the insurer won’t move, small claims court is often a practical option for diminished value claims.

When diminished value is worth pursuing

The claim is strongest for cars that are newer, low-mileage or high-value, with structural or frame damage that shows on a vehicle history report. Older, high-mileage cars often have little diminished value left to claim. Georgia is the best-known state that also lets you claim diminished value from your own insurer.

Questions people ask

How do I prove diminished value?

With an independent appraisal comparing the market value of your repaired car with similar cars without accident history.

Is there a deadline for a diminished value claim?

Yes, the property damage statute of limitations in your state, often two to three years.

Can I claim diminished value if my car was totaled?

No. A total loss is paid at the car’s pre-crash value, so there is no repaired car left to lose value.

Should I claim diminished value if I was partly at fault?

You can, but your state’s comparative fault rule reduces the claim by your share, the same as other damages.

posts.excerpt: Estimate rental car reimbursement or loss-of-use damages while your car is being repaired or replaced after a crash.

meta.rank_math_description: Estimate how much rental car reimbursement or loss-of-use pay you can claim after an accident, based on daily rates, repair time and your policy limits.
meta.rank_math_focus_keyword: rental car reimbursement calculator,rental reimbursement coverage,loss of use claim
meta.rank_math_title: Rental Car Reimbursement & Loss of Use Calculator

seo.title: Rental Car Reimbursement & Loss of Use Calculator
seo.description: Estimate how much rental car reimbursement or loss-of-use pay you can claim after an accident, based on daily rates, repair time and your policy limits.
seo.focus: rental car reimbursement calculator,rental reimbursement coverage,loss of use claim

posts.content:
What you can claim

When another driver caused the crash, their insurer owes you the reasonable cost of a comparable rental car while yours is repaired, or until a total loss is paid. If you did not rent a car, many states let you claim loss of use: the value of going without, usually measured by a comparable rental rate.

Reasonable time

The insurer pays for a reasonable repair time. Delays caused by the insurer, such as a slow inspection, should not shorten your rental. Ask for extensions in writing.

Your own policy

Rental reimbursement on your own policy usually has a daily and total limit, such as $40 a day for 30 days. The calculator applies a daily limit if you enter one.

Example

Your car needs 12 days in the shop after a crash another driver caused. A comparable midsize rental costs $52 a day, so a fair claim is 12 × $52 = $624. If the shop waited four extra days for parts the insurer was slow to approve, those days should be covered too, bringing the claim to $832. If you claim under your own policy instead, a $40-a-day, 30-day limit would pay $480 for the original 12 days and leave you to cover the difference.

Total losses end the rental sooner

When your car is declared a total loss, the at-fault insurer usually pays rental until a few days after it makes a reasonable settlement offer on the car. Start shopping for a replacement as soon as the total loss is confirmed, and use the total loss calculator to check the offer.

Keep these records

  • The rental agreement and receipts, or quotes for a comparable car if you didn’t rent
  • The repair shop’s dates: drop-off, estimate, parts delay, pickup
  • Emails or letters with the adjuster about how long they will pay

Which insurer to use

You can claim from the at-fault driver’s insurer once it accepts liability. If it hasn’t, use your own rental coverage and let your insurer recover the cost later. Using your own coverage first usually gets you a car faster.

Questions people ask

Can I get loss-of-use money without renting a car?

In many states, yes, for the time you were without a car.

Do I get a car the same size as mine?

The at-fault insurer owes a comparable vehicle, not a basic economy car if you drive a truck or minivan.

Does the other driver’s insurer have to pay for a rental while it investigates?

Usually not until it accepts liability. Use your own rental coverage in the meantime if you have it; your insurer can recover the cost later.

How long can I keep the rental?

For the reasonable time needed to repair the car, or until a few days after a fair total loss offer. Delays you cause can shorten it.

seo.title: Workers’ Comp Settlement Calculator ()
seo.description: Estimate a workers’ compensation settlement from your weekly benefit rate, impairment rating and future medical costs, using your state’s formula.
seo.focus: workers comp settlement calculator,workers compensation settlement amounts,average workers comp settlement

posts.content:
What a workers’ comp settlement covers

Workers’ compensation pays medical care and part of your wages after a work injury, without proving the employer was at fault. A settlement closes some or all of those benefits in exchange for a lump sum. It usually reflects:

  • Permanent partial disability (PPD): your impairment rating applied to a number of weeks set by your state for the body part or the whole person
  • Temporary disability still owed: weekly benefits you would otherwise receive
  • Future medical care: treatment your doctors expect, if the settlement closes medical benefits

How the weekly rate is set

Most states pay about two-thirds of your average weekly wage, up to a state maximum that changes each year. The rate drives every part of the settlement, so check your state agency’s current maximum and enter it.

Why settlements come in below full value

Insurers discount for disputes about the rating, the chance a judge awards less, and the time value of paying now. The calculator shows the full value and a 70% to 100% range. Your bargaining position depends on the evidence and your state’s rules.

Medicare and future medical money

If you receive Medicare or expect to soon, a settlement that closes future medical care may need a Medicare set-aside so Medicare does not pay costs the settlement covered.

Workers’ comp and an injury lawsuit

You generally cannot sue your employer, but you can bring an injury claim against a third party who caused the injury, such as a negligent driver or equipment maker. Read workers’ comp or a personal injury claim.

Average workers’ comp claim costs

The average workers’ compensation claim cost $47,316 for injuries in 2022–2023, combining medical and wage-loss benefits, according to National Safety Council analysis of NCCI data. Motor vehicle crashes were the costliest cause at $91,433 per claim. Those are total claim costs, not settlement checks: a settlement usually buys out the remaining value of a claim after some benefits have been paid. Read average workers’ comp settlements for how lump sums are figured.

Example

You reach maximum medical improvement (MMI) with a 10% impairment rating to the whole body. Your weekly benefit rate is $620. If your state pays permanent partial disability at 3 weeks per impairment point for a whole-body rating, the benefit is 10 × 3 × $620 = $18,600. Add an estimate of future medical care, say $12,000 for injections and medication, and a negotiated lump sum might fall around $25,000 to $30,000, discounted for paying it all now. State formulas vary widely, so check the multiplier your state uses.

Medicare and settlements

If you are on Medicare, or reasonably expect to be within 30 months, a settlement that closes future medical care may need a Medicare set-aside. CMS reviews proposed set-asides for Medicare beneficiaries when the total settlement is more than $25,000, and for others when it is more than $250,000.

Things to settle carefully

Closing future medical care is the biggest decision in a workers’ comp settlement. Get an estimate of what treatment will cost before you agree, and remember that a settlement usually needs approval from your state’s workers’ compensation board or judge.

Questions people ask

How is a workers’ comp settlement calculated?

Usually from your weekly benefit rate, your impairment rating and your state’s schedule of weeks, plus remaining disability pay and future medical costs, then negotiated down for risk.

Is a workers’ comp settlement taxable?

Workers’ compensation benefits are generally not taxable under federal law.

Should I accept a workers’ comp settlement?

Compare it with the full value of your benefits, especially future medical care. Once medical benefits are closed, you pay for later treatment yourself.

When should I settle a workers’ comp claim?

Usually after you reach maximum medical improvement and have an impairment rating, so the value of your permanent injury and future care is known.

Is a workers’ comp settlement taxable?

Generally no. Workers’ compensation benefits paid under a workers’ comp act are excluded from federal income tax.

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: The average workers’ compensation claim cost $47,316 for injuries in 2022–2023, combining medical and wage-loss benefits, according to National Safety Council analysis of NCCI data. Motor vehicle crashes were the costliest cause at $91,433 per claim. Those are total claim costs, not settlement checks: a settlement usually buys out the remaining value of a claim after some benefits have been paid. Read average workers’ comp settlements for how lump sums are figured.

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: Example

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: You reach maximum medical improvement (MMI) with a 10% impairment rating to the whole body. Your weekly benefit rate is $620. If your state pays permanent partial disability at 3 weeks per impairment point for a whole-body rating, the benefit is 10 × 3 × $620 = $18,600. Add an estimate of future medical care, say $12,000 for injections and medication, and a negotiated lump sum might fall around $25,000 to $30,000, discounted for paying it all now. State formulas vary widely, so check the multiplier your state uses.

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: Medicare and settlements

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: If you are on Medicare, or reasonably expect to be within 30 months, a settlement that closes future medical care may need a Medicare set-aside. CMS reviews proposed set-asides for Medicare beneficiaries when the total settlement is more than $25,000, and for others when it is more than $250,000.

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: Things to settle carefully

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: Closing future medical care is the biggest decision in a workers’ comp settlement. Get an estimate of what treatment will cost before you agree, and remember that a settlement usually needs approval from your state’s workers’ compensation board or judge.

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: Questions people ask

blocks.name: core/details
blocks.html:
How is a workers’ comp settlement calculated?

Usually from your weekly benefit rate, your impairment rating and your state’s schedule of weeks, plus remaining disability pay and future medical costs, then negotiated down for risk.

blocks.name: core/details
blocks.html:
Is a workers’ comp settlement taxable?

Workers’ compensation benefits are generally not taxable under federal law.

blocks.name: core/details
blocks.html:
Should I accept a workers’ comp settlement?

Compare it with the full value of your benefits, especially future medical care. Once medical benefits are closed, you pay for later treatment yourself.

blocks.name: core/details
blocks.html:
When should I settle a workers’ comp claim?

Usually after you reach maximum medical improvement and have an impairment rating, so the value of your permanent injury and future care is known.

blocks.name: core/details
blocks.html:
Is a workers’ comp settlement taxable?

Generally no. Workers’ compensation benefits paid under a workers’ comp act are excluded from federal income tax.

posts.content:
Temporary total disability benefits

When a work injury keeps you off the job, workers’ comp pays weekly temporary total disability (TTD) benefits. Most states pay 66⅔% of your average weekly wage, a few pay more, and every state caps the benefit at a maximum that is usually updated each year.

Your average weekly wage

The average weekly wage is usually your gross pay over a period before the injury, often 13 or 52 weeks, divided by the number of weeks. Overtime and second jobs may count, depending on the state.

The waiting period

Most states do not pay for the first three to seven days off work unless you are out longer than a set period, often 14 to 21 days, when those days are paid back. Enter your state’s numbers to see the effect.

Benefits are not taxed

Workers’ comp benefits are generally not taxable income, so two-thirds of gross pay often comes closer to your normal take-home pay than it sounds.

Example

Your gross pay over the 52 weeks before the injury was $46,800, so your average weekly wage is $900. At 66⅔%, your weekly benefit is $600. If your state’s maximum weekly benefit is $1,200, you receive the full $600. If you earned $2,100 a week, two-thirds would be $1,400, but the cap would hold you to $1,200.

Types of weekly benefits

  • Temporary total disability (TTD): you can’t work at all while recovering
  • Temporary partial disability (TPD): you work reduced hours or light duty, and the benefit is usually two-thirds of the difference between your old and new earnings
  • Permanent partial disability (PPD): paid after you reach maximum medical improvement, based on an impairment rating
  • Permanent total disability (PTD): you can’t return to any work

Check your rate

Errors in the average weekly wage are common, especially when overtime, a second job or a recent raise is left out. Ask the insurer how it calculated your rate and compare it with your pay stubs.

Questions people ask

How much does workers’ comp pay per week?

Usually two-thirds of your average weekly wage, up to your state’s maximum weekly benefit.

How long do workers’ comp weekly benefits last?

Until you return to work or reach maximum medical improvement, subject to state limits on the number of weeks.

Can I work while getting workers’ comp?

You can sometimes work light duty and receive temporary partial disability benefits that make up part of the lost pay. Report all earnings to the insurer.

posts.content:
How SSDI back pay works

Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) pays benefits from your established onset date, after a five-month waiting period. Because approval can take a year or more, most people receive a lump sum of back pay covering the months between when benefits should have started and when they were approved.

The rules the calculator applies

  • Five-month waiting period: benefits start with the sixth full month of disability
  • Retroactive limit: SSDI pays no more than 12 months before the month you applied
  • Representative fee: if you had a lawyer or representative, the fee is usually 25% of back pay, capped at $9,200

SSI is different

Supplemental Security Income (SSI) has no five-month waiting period and no retroactive benefits before the application month. It is needs-based and paid at a federal rate. This calculator covers SSDI.

Check your numbers

Your Social Security statement at ssa.gov shows your estimated monthly disability benefit. The onset date that Social Security accepts can differ from the date you claim, which changes the back pay.

Example

Your disability began on January 10, 2025, you applied in March 2025, and you were approved in February 2026 with a monthly benefit of $1,650.

  • The five-month waiting period covers February through June 2025, the first five full months
  • Benefits start with July 2025
  • Back pay runs from July 2025 through January 2026: 7 months × $1,650 = $11,550
  • A representative’s fee of 25% would be $2,887.50, under the $9,200 cap

Offsets that reduce SSDI

SSDI can be reduced if you also receive workers’ compensation or certain public disability benefits, when the combined total is more than 80% of your average current earnings before you became disabled. Private long-term disability usually doesn’t reduce SSDI, but your LTD benefit is often reduced by SSDI instead.

Medicare after SSDI

SSDI recipients usually become eligible for Medicare 24 months after their first month of entitlement to benefits, which can be a key part of planning a disability or workers’ comp settlement.

Questions people ask

How long does it take to get SSDI back pay?

Often one to three months after approval, paid as a lump sum to your bank account.

Is SSDI back pay taxable?

Part of SSDI can be taxable depending on your total income. A lump sum can be spread over the years it covers for tax purposes.

Is SSDI back pay paid in one lump sum?

Usually yes for SSDI. SSI back pay above a set amount is paid in installments.

Can I get SSDI back pay for more than 12 months before I applied?

No. SSDI retroactive benefits are limited to 12 months before the month you applied, after the waiting period.

posts.content:
Why VA ratings do not add up

The VA combines ratings using the combined ratings table in 38 C.F.R. § 4.25. Each rating applies to the “efficiency” left after the higher ratings. A 50% rating leaves 50% efficiency; a 30% rating applied to that takes 15 more, for a combined 65%, not 80%.

Rounding

After combining, the VA rounds the result to the nearest 10. Values ending in 5 round up, so 65% becomes 70% and 64% becomes 60%.

The bilateral factor

When you have ratings on both arms or both legs, the VA combines those first, then adds 10% of that value before combining with your other ratings (38 C.F.R. § 4.26). Tick “Bilateral” for those ratings.

Monthly payment

Your monthly compensation depends on your combined rating and dependents. The VA publishes the current rate tables each December at va.gov.

VA math, worked through

The VA doesn’t add ratings together. Each rating applies to the part of you that remains “unimpaired” after the higher ratings:

  1. Start with your highest rating, say 50%. You are 50% disabled and 50% efficient.
  2. Apply the next rating, 30%, to the remaining 50%: 30% of 50 = 15. Combined value: 65.
  3. Apply a 10% rating to the remaining 35: 10% of 35 = 3.5. Combined value: 68.5.
  4. Round to the nearest 10: 70%.

The bilateral factor

When disabilities affect both arms, both legs or paired muscles, the VA combines those ratings first and adds 10% of that combined value before combining with your other ratings. That small addition can push a rating over a rounding line.

Why the rounding matters

Monthly compensation rises at each 10% step, and payments for dependents start at 30%. A combined value of 64.9 rounds down to 60%; 65 rounds up to 70%. If you are close to a line, check whether any condition is under-rated or missing.

Questions people ask

How do I get to a 100% VA rating?

Through combined ratings that round to 100%, a single 100% rating, or Total Disability Individual Unemployability (TDIU) when service-connected conditions prevent work.

Does the VA round 95% up to 100%?

Yes. Combined values from 95% round up to 100%.

Why is my VA rating lower than my ratings added together?

Because the VA combines ratings with “VA math”, applying each rating to the remaining efficiency rather than adding them, then rounds to the nearest 10%.

posts.content:
How LTD benefits are figured

Most group long-term disability policies pay 50% to 70% of your pre-disability monthly earnings, up to a monthly maximum. The benefit is then reduced by “other income”, usually Social Security disability, workers’ comp and state disability benefits. A minimum benefit, often $100, applies even after offsets.

Taxes depend on who paid the premiums

If your employer paid the premiums, benefits are generally taxable. If you paid them with after-tax dollars, benefits are generally tax-free.

Own occupation and any occupation

Many policies pay for an initial period, often 24 months, if you cannot do your own job, then only if you cannot do any job suited to your training. Benefits often stop at that change.

Denials

Employer LTD plans are usually governed by ERISA, which requires an internal appeal before a lawsuit and limits what a court will consider. Build the record during the appeal.

Example

You earned $6,000 a month. Your policy pays 60%, so the gross benefit is $3,600, up to a $10,000 monthly maximum. You are later approved for SSDI at $1,900 a month, which the policy offsets: $3,600 − $1,900 = $1,700 a month from the LTD insurer. If the policy has a $100 minimum benefit, that floor only matters when offsets reduce the benefit close to zero.

If the insurer paid the full $3,600 while your SSDI claim was pending, it will usually ask you to repay the overpayment from your SSDI back pay.

The elimination period

Most policies have an elimination period, commonly 90 or 180 days, that you must be disabled before benefits start. Short-term disability or sick pay often covers that gap.

Appealing a denial

For employer plans covered by ERISA, you usually have at least 180 days to file an internal appeal. Use it to add medical records, doctors’ opinions and vocational evidence, because a court reviewing the denial is often limited to the record from the appeal.

Questions people ask

Does LTD reduce my benefit if I get SSDI?

Usually yes. Most policies subtract SSDI and many require you to apply for it.

How long do LTD benefits last?

Often until age 65 or Social Security retirement age, if you remain disabled under the policy’s definition.

Do I have to apply for SSDI if I get LTD?

Most group policies require it, because they offset SSDI. The insurer may even help with the application.

posts.content:
What a discrimination claim can recover

Under Title VII, the ADA and related federal laws, a worker who proves discrimination or retaliation can recover:

  • Back pay: lost wages and benefits from the job loss to the resolution, minus earnings from new work
  • Front pay: future lost pay when reinstatement is not practical
  • Compensatory damages: emotional distress and other non-wage losses
  • Punitive damages: for malice or reckless indifference (not available against government employers)

Federal damage caps

Compensatory and punitive damages combined are capped by employer size (42 U.S.C. § 1981a(b)(3)):

Back pay and front pay are not capped. Many state laws allow uncapped damages, and claims under 42 U.S.C. § 1981 for race discrimination are not capped.

Short deadlines

A charge must usually be filed with the EEOC within 180 days, or 300 days where a state agency also enforces a discrimination law. Back pay is limited to two years before the charge.

Example

You earned $70,000 a year and were fired 18 months before your case settles. You found a new job after 10 months paying $60,000.

  • Back pay: 18 months of lost salary ($105,000) minus earnings at the new job (8 months × $5,000 = $40,000) = $65,000
  • Front pay for the remaining $10,000 annual gap, for two years: $20,000
  • Compensatory and punitive damages, capped at $100,000 for an employer with 101 to 200 employees

Settlements usually come in below a full trial award because both sides discount for the risk of losing.

How the process works

Most federal claims start with a charge filed with the EEOC or a state agency. The agency may offer mediation, investigate, or issue a right-to-sue notice. Many claims settle in mediation or soon after a lawsuit is filed. Read what back pay includes for the wage side of the claim.

Questions people ask

What is the average employment discrimination settlement?

It varies widely. Many settle for less than a year’s pay, while strong cases with large employers reach far higher.

Are discrimination settlements taxable?

Back pay is taxable as wages, and emotional distress damages are generally taxable unless tied to a physical injury.

How long does an employment discrimination case take?

An EEOC charge can take several months to over a year. If a lawsuit follows, resolution often takes another one to two years, though many cases settle earlier.

blocks.html: What a discrimination claim can recover

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: Under Title VII, the ADA and related federal laws, a worker who proves discrimination or retaliation can recover:

blocks.name: core/list
blocks.html:
• Back pay: lost wages and benefits from the job loss to the resolution, minus earnings from new work
  • Front pay: future lost pay when reinstatement is not practical
  • Compensatory damages: emotional distress and other non-wage losses
  • Punitive damages: for malice or reckless indifference (not available against government employers)

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: Federal damage caps

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: Compensatory and punitive damages combined are capped by employer size (42 U.S.C. § 1981a(b)(3)):

blocks.name: core/table
core/paragraph
blocks.html: Back pay and front pay are not capped. Many state laws allow uncapped damages, and claims under 42 U.S.C. § 1981 for race discrimination are not capped.

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: Short deadlines

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: A charge must usually be filed with the EEOC within 180 days, or 300 days where a state agency also enforces a discrimination law. Back pay is limited to two years before the charge.

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: Example

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: You earned $70,000 a year and were fired 18 months before your case settles. You found a new job after 10 months paying $60,000.

blocks.name: core/list
blocks.html:
• Back pay: 18 months of lost salary ($105,000) minus earnings at the new job (8 months × $5,000 = $40,000) = $65,000
  • Front pay for the remaining $10,000 annual gap, for two years: $20,000
  • Compensatory and punitive damages, capped at $100,000 for an employer with 101 to 200 employees

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: Settlements usually come in below a full trial award because both sides discount for the risk of losing.

blocks.html: How the process works

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: Most federal claims start with a charge filed with the EEOC or a state agency. The agency may offer mediation, investigate, or issue a right-to-sue notice. Many claims settle in mediation or soon after a lawsuit is filed. Read what back pay includes for the wage side of the claim.

What is the average employment discrimination settlement?

It varies widely. Many settle for less than a year’s pay, while strong cases with large employers reach far higher.

Are discrimination settlements taxable?

Back pay is taxable as wages, and emotional distress damages are generally taxable unless tied to a physical injury.

seo.title: Wrongful Termination Back Pay Calculator

posts.content:
What back pay is

Back pay is the wages and benefits you would have earned from the day you were fired to the day the case is resolved, minus what you earned elsewhere in the meantime. It is the core of most wrongful termination and discrimination awards.

Benefits count too

Lost health insurance, retirement contributions, bonuses and paid time off add to back pay. Employer benefits commonly equal 20% to 30% of salary.

The duty to mitigate

You must make reasonable efforts to find comparable work. Keep a record of applications and interviews. If you stop looking, back pay can be cut off.

Is it wrongful termination?

Most US employment is at will, so being fired unfairly is not always illegal. A firing is wrongful when it breaks a law or contract: discrimination, retaliation for reporting wrongdoing, taking protected leave, or breaching an employment agreement.

Example

You earned $1,250 a week with benefits worth 25% of salary. You were fired 40 weeks ago and earned $18,000 at a temporary job since then.

  • Lost pay: 40 × $1,250 = $50,000
  • Lost benefits: 25% × $50,000 = $12,500
  • Minus interim earnings: −$18,000
  • Back pay: $44,500

Courts often add prejudgment interest to back pay, and in some federal claims a jury can award an equal amount as liquidated damages for willful violations.

Front pay

When going back to the old job isn’t realistic, front pay covers the gap between your old pay and your expected future pay for a reasonable period. It depends on your age, field and how long it should take to find comparable work.

Taxes

Back pay and front pay are taxed as wages. Plan for withholding when you compare settlement offers. Use the settlement tax calculator to see how a settlement might be split.

Questions people ask

Is unemployment deducted from back pay?

It depends on the law and the state. Federal courts are split, and some states deduct it.

How far back does back pay go?

From the termination date, though some claims limit the period, such as two years before an EEOC charge.

Does severance pay reduce back pay?

Often yes, because it replaces lost wages. How it is treated depends on the claim and the severance agreement, which may also require you to give up claims.

seo.description: Calculate unpaid overtime and wages under the FLSA: time-and-a-half over 40 hours, liquidated damages that can double the award, and the lookback period.

posts.content:
The federal overtime rule

Under the Fair Labor Standards Act, non-exempt employees must be paid at least 1.5 times their regular rate for hours over 40 in a workweek (29 U.S.C. § 207). The regular rate includes most bonuses and commissions, not just the hourly wage.

What you can recover

  • Unpaid overtime for up to two years before you file, or three years if the violation was willful
  • Liquidated damages equal to the unpaid amount, doubling the recovery, unless the employer proves good faith
  • Attorney fees and costs, paid by the employer if you win

Straight time for overtime

If you were paid your regular rate for overtime hours, you are owed the missing half-time. If those hours were not paid at all, you are owed the full time and a half. Pick the option that fits.

State law can add more

Some states require daily overtime (California, Alaska, Nevada and Colorado in some cases), set higher minimum wages, or allow longer lookbacks. Your state’s labor department can confirm.

Example

You were paid $20 an hour and regularly worked 48 hours a week without overtime pay for 70 weeks.

  • Overtime owed: 8 hours × $10 (the half-time premium on top of straight pay already received) × 70 weeks = $5,600
  • If you were paid nothing for the extra hours: 8 × $30 × 70 = $16,800
  • Liquidated damages under the FLSA can double either amount

Who is owed overtime

The FLSA requires time-and-a-half for hours over 40 in a workweek for non-exempt employees. Being paid a salary doesn’t make you exempt by itself. Exemption also depends on your duties and on a minimum salary level. A job title such as “manager” doesn’t settle it.

Deadlines and state law

FLSA claims must be filed within two years, or three for willful violations, and each paycheck starts its own clock, so older weeks drop off over time. Some states, such as California, require daily overtime and give you longer to sue. Keep your own record of hours worked: texts, emails, badge logs and a simple calendar all help.

Questions people ask

Am I exempt from overtime?

Exemption depends on your salary and actual duties, not your job title. Many workers called “managers” are not exempt.

Can my employer retaliate if I claim overtime?

Retaliation for an FLSA complaint is illegal and can lead to additional damages.

Can my employer give comp time instead of overtime pay?

Private employers generally can’t replace overtime pay with comp time under the FLSA. Public employers can in some situations.

posts.content:
How to read this table

When an injured person is partly to blame for an accident, the fault rule decides whether they can recover and how much. The rule that applies is usually the one where the accident happened, not where you live.

The five rules, with the same example

Take a $100,000 claim where the injured person is found 30% at fault, then 50%.

Recent changes

Florida moved from pure comparative fault to a 51% bar for negligence claims filed after March 24, 2023. Louisiana moved to a 51% bar for injuries on or after January 1, 2026. Earlier claims keep the old rules.

Fault is a negotiation, then a verdict

Insurers assign a fault percentage when they evaluate a claim, and juries decide it at trial. Evidence such as police reports, video, photos and witness statements moves the number. See what your share costs with the comparative fault calculator.

posts.content:
What these deadlines mean

The statute of limitations is the last day to file a lawsuit in court. It is not a deadline to settle, and talking to an insurer does not pause it. If the date passes, the court will almost always dismiss the case.

Exceptions that change the date

  • Discovery rule: some injuries are not known at once, and the clock may start when they are discovered
  • Minors: many states pause the deadline until an injured child turns 18
  • Government claims: a written notice of claim is usually due within months
  • Medical malpractice: often has its own shorter deadline and an outer limit (statute of repose)

Recent changes

Florida cut its negligence deadline from four years to two for claims arising after March 24, 2023. Louisiana raised its deadline from one year to two for injuries on or after July 1, 2024.

Find your exact date with the statute of limitations calculator.

posts.content:
What no-fault means

In a no-fault state, your own personal injury protection (PIP) pays your medical bills and part of your lost income after a crash, whoever caused it. You can step outside the system and sue the at-fault driver only when your injury meets the state’s threshold.

Monetary and verbal thresholds

A monetary threshold is met when reasonable medical bills pass a set amount. A verbal threshold requires a serious injury as the law defines it, such as a fracture, permanent injury or significant disfigurement.

Choice states

In Kentucky, New Jersey and Pennsylvania, drivers can choose a policy that keeps their full right to sue, usually for a higher premium. Your choice is on your policy’s declarations page.

Property damage is not no-fault

No-fault rules cover injuries only. Vehicle damage is still claimed against the at-fault driver’s property damage liability coverage, except in Michigan, where limited property protection applies.

Estimate benefits with the no-fault and PIP calculator.

Most states do not cap ordinary injury damages

Caps on pain and suffering are most common in medical malpractice cases. Only a handful of states cap non-economic damages in ordinary injury claims, such as car crashes and falls. Several states have struck caps down as unconstitutional.

Medical bills and lost income are almost never capped. Caps apply to pain and suffering, emotional distress and loss of enjoyment of life, and separately to punitive damages in many states.

How to read 30/60/25

Liability limits are written as three numbers in thousands of dollars: bodily injury per person, bodily injury per crash and property damage per crash. 30/60/25 means $30,000, $60,000 and $25,000.

Why minimums matter for your claim

The at-fault driver’s limit is usually the most their insurer will pay. A serious injury can exceed a state minimum many times over, which is why your own uninsured and underinsured motorist coverage matters.

Recent increases

California raised its minimums to 30/60/15 in 2025, the first change since 1967. North Carolina (50/100/50), Virginia (50/100/25), Utah (30/65/25) and Massachusetts (25/50/30) also raised theirs in 2025. Hawaii (40/80/20) and New Jersey (35/70/25 for standard policies) followed in 2026.

posts.content:
Strict liability

In strict liability states, a statute makes the owner responsible for bite injuries even if the dog had never bitten before. Defenses such as trespassing or provoking the dog usually still apply.

The one-bite rule and negligence

Where there is no statute, the owner is liable if they knew or should have known the dog was dangerous, or were careless, for example by breaking a leash law. A prior bite or aggressive behavior is the usual proof.

Limited statutes

posts.content:
This calculator estimates what a truck accident injury claim could be worth under Pennsylvania law. It applies Pennsylvania’s 51% bar rule, the two-year deadline to file suit and the insurance that usually pays, then shows the math line by line, including what you might take home after a lawyer’s fee.

Because Pennsylvania is a no-fault state, the calculator first subtracts what your own PIP coverage pays, then asks whether your injury meets the threshold to claim pain and suffering from the at-fault driver.

Truck claims differ from car claims in three ways: there can be several defendants (the driver, the motor carrier, a broker or the company that loaded the trailer), federal safety rules on driver hours and maintenance apply, and evidence such as electronic logging device data needs to be preserved quickly.

posts.content:
Enter the date of the injury and this calculator works out the last day to file an injury lawsuit in Washington. It uses Washington’s general three-year deadline and the three-year wrongful death deadline.

The date it gives is the general rule. Exceptions can pause or shorten the clock, and claims against government agencies need notice far sooner. If your date is close, call a lawyer this week.

A statute of limitations is the deadline to file a lawsuit, not to settle. Most injury claims settle without one, but once the deadline passes the insurer has no reason to pay, so the date still controls your negotiation.

posts.title: How Injury Settlements Are Calculated
posts.excerpt: The formula insurers start from, what moves the multiplier, how fault and policy limits cut the number, and what you keep after fees.

meta.rank_math_description: The formula insurers use to value injury claims: economic damages times a multiplier, cut by fault and policy limits, minus fees and liens. With examples.
meta.rank_math_focus_keyword: how are personal injury settlements calculated,settlement formula,how insurance companies calculate settlements
meta.rank_math_title: How Are Personal Injury Settlements Calculated? (Formula)

seo.title: How Are Personal Injury Settlements Calculated? (Formula)
seo.description: The formula insurers use to value injury claims: economic damages times a multiplier, cut by fault and policy limits, minus fees and liens. With examples.
seo.focus: how are personal injury settlements calculated,settlement formula,how insurance companies calculate settlements

posts.content:
Key points

  • Most settlements start from economic damages plus a pain-and-suffering multiplier of about 1.5× to 5×.
  • Your share of fault reduces the total, and in some states it can bar the claim.
  • The at-fault party’s policy limit often caps what can actually be collected.
  • Attorney fees, case costs and medical bills come out before you are paid.

There is no official formula for an injury settlement. Adjusters and lawyers still start from the same rough math, then argue over each input. Here is that math in the order it is applied.

1. Add up your economic damages

Economic damages are the losses with a receipt: medical bills already paid or owed, care your doctors expect you to need, and income you lost while recovering. Damage to your car is usually handled as a separate property claim.

Count every bill, including the ones health insurance paid. The insurer of the at-fault party owes the full reasonable cost of your care, and your health plan may need repaying from the settlement anyway.

2. Price the pain and suffering

Most adjusters value pain and suffering as a multiple of economic damages. The multiple rises with how serious and how lasting the injury is, and with how well your records prove it.

Some claims use a per-diem rate instead: a daily amount times the days you were in pain. At $150 a day for 120 days, that is $18,000. Compare both with the pain and suffering calculator.

3. Apply your state’s fault rule

If you share the blame, most states cut your award by your percentage of fault. On a $100,000 claim at 20% fault, you would recover $80,000. States differ on where recovery stops: some bar it at 50% or 51% fault, and a few can bar it for almost any fault. See comparative negligence by state.

4. Check the insurance that can pay

A claim is worth what can be collected. If the other driver carries the Texas minimum of $30,000 per person, that is usually the most their insurer pays for your injuries. Your own underinsured motorist coverage can pay the difference up to its limit.

5. Subtract fees, costs and medical bills

The settlement is not what you take home. Here is the Texas example from our calculator, at its midpoint value.

Lien reductions and a lower fee can raise that figure. Run your own numbers with the attorney fee and net payout calculator.

What no formula captures

Adjusters also weigh how believable you are, whether treatment was consistent, the quality of the medical records, local jury attitudes and how strong the proof of fault is. Two claims with the same bills can settle far apart. The formula gives you a range to judge offers against, not a promise.

Sources

  • Tex. Civ. Prac. & Rem. Code § 33.001, proportionate responsibility
  • Tex. Transp. Code § 601.072, minimum liability coverage
  • ClaimValuator methodology, how our calculators apply these rules

posts.title: The Pain and Suffering Multiplier, Explained
posts.excerpt: Why one claim gets 1.5× and another gets 4×, and the records that move the multiplier.

meta.rank_math_description: Why one claim gets a 1.5x pain and suffering multiplier and another gets 4x or 5x, and the medical records and facts that move the multiplier up.
meta.rank_math_focus_keyword: pain and suffering multiplier,multiplier method,pain and suffering settlement
meta.rank_math_title: Pain and Suffering Multiplier: How 1.5x to 5x Is Chosen

seo.title: Pain and Suffering Multiplier: How 1.5x to 5x Is Chosen
seo.description: Why one claim gets a 1.5x pain and suffering multiplier and another gets 4x or 5x, and the medical records and facts that move the multiplier up.
seo.focus: pain and suffering multiplier,multiplier method,pain and suffering settlement

posts.content:
Key points

  • The multiplier is a shorthand for valuing pain, distress and lost enjoyment of life.
  • Severity, permanence, treatment and proof move it more than anything else.
  • Gaps in treatment and weak records push it toward the bottom of the range.

Pain and suffering has no receipt. To put a number on it, adjusters often multiply your economic damages, mainly medical bills and lost income, by a figure between about 1.5 and 5. The multiplier is not a law; it is a habit of the claims industry that roughly tracks what juries award.

What the multiplier is trying to measure

Non-economic damages compensate physical pain, emotional distress, sleep loss, anxiety, scarring and the loss of things you used to do. A claim where you were sore for six weeks and fully recovered is worth less than one where you had surgery and still cannot lift your child.

What pushes it up

  • Objective proof: fractures on X-ray, a disc herniation on MRI, surgery
  • Permanence: an impairment rating, scarring or a lasting limitation
  • Consistent treatment: regular visits without long gaps
  • Clear fault: a citation, video or admission by the other driver
  • A sympathetic story told with detail: a journal, photos and statements from people who saw the change in your life

What pulls it down

  • Waiting weeks before seeing a doctor
  • Gaps in treatment, or stopping physical therapy early
  • A pre-existing condition in the same part of the body
  • Treatment that looks excessive for the injury
  • Social media posts that contradict the claim

The multiplier in numbers

On $20,000 of medical bills and lost income:

The per-diem alternative

Some lawyers argue a daily rate instead, often a day’s take-home pay, times the days of pain or recovery. It works best when recovery has a clear end date and can produce a higher figure for long recoveries with modest bills.

Do insurers really use it?

Many large insurers use claims software that scores injuries, treatments and recovery time rather than a single multiplier. The result usually lands in a similar range, so the multiplier remains a good way to sanity-check an offer. Try both methods in the pain and suffering calculator.

posts.title: Should You Accept the First Settlement Offer?
posts.excerpt: How to read a first offer, what a release gives up, and when to counter.

meta.rank_math_description: Why first settlement offers are usually low, what signing a release gives up, and how to decide whether to accept, counter or have a lawyer review it.
meta.rank_math_focus_keyword: should i accept the first settlement offer,first settlement offer,low settlement offer
meta.rank_math_title: Should You Accept the First Settlement Offer? How to Decide

seo.title: Should You Accept the First Settlement Offer? How to Decide
seo.description: Why first settlement offers are usually low, what signing a release gives up, and how to decide whether to accept, counter or have a lawyer review it.
seo.focus: should i accept the first settlement offer,first settlement offer,low settlement offer

posts.content:
Key points

  • First offers are usually opening positions, often near the low end of a fair range.
  • Signing a release ends the claim for good, even if your injury gets worse.
  • Counter in writing, with the bills and records that support your number.

An adjuster calls with a number. It may arrive quickly, sometimes before you have finished treatment. Here is how to decide what to do with it.

Why first offers run low

Insurers expect to negotiate, and a first offer leaves room to move. Some offers come early because the insurer knows medical costs are still rising. Others count on people needing money for rent and bills. None of that means the offer reflects what the claim is worth.

Questions to ask before you answer

  1. Is treatment finished? If not, you do not know the claim’s full cost. Ask your doctor whether more care is expected.
  2. Does the offer cover every bill? Add up all medical bills, including those your health plan paid, plus lost income.
  3. What is left for pain and suffering? Subtract economic damages from the offer. If little is left, the offer is low.
  4. What is the policy limit? If the offer equals the limit, it may be the most this insurer can pay.
  5. How close is the filing deadline? Negotiating past it destroys your leverage.

What signing the release means

To get paid you will sign a release. It usually waives every claim arising from the accident, known or unknown. If you later need surgery, you cannot go back. Read it before signing, and do not sign while treatment is ongoing unless you have good reason.

When accepting makes sense

  • The offer covers your bills, lost income and a fair amount for pain and suffering
  • It equals the at-fault party’s policy limit and there is no other coverage
  • Fault is disputed and the offer reflects that risk fairly
  • The amount is small and your time matters more than a modest increase

How to counter

Reply in writing. State your counteroffer and the reasons: the treatment, the bills, how the injury affected your work and life, and the evidence of fault. Then plan each move with the counteroffer calculator. To see where the offer sits in your state’s range first, use Is my settlement offer fair?

posts.title: Policy Limits and UM/UIM Coverage: Who Pays When the Other Driver Is Underinsured
posts.excerpt: How liability limits cap a claim and how your own coverage fills the gap.

meta.rank_math_description: How the at-fault driver’s policy limits cap your claim, and how uninsured and underinsured motorist (UM/UIM) coverage on your own policy fills the gap.
meta.rank_math_focus_keyword: underinsured motorist coverage,policy limits settlement,uim claim
meta.rank_math_title: Policy Limits and UM/UIM: When the Driver Is Underinsured

seo.title: Policy Limits and UM/UIM: When the Driver Is Underinsured
seo.description: How the at-fault driver’s policy limits cap your claim, and how uninsured and underinsured motorist (UM/UIM) coverage on your own policy fills the gap.
seo.focus: underinsured motorist coverage,policy limits settlement,uim claim

posts.content:
Key points

  • The at-fault driver’s bodily injury limit is usually the most their insurer will pay.
  • Several injured people share the per-crash limit.
  • Your own UM/UIM coverage is often the only other source of money.

Most injury claims after a car crash are paid by the at-fault driver’s liability insurance. That insurance has limits, and the limits often decide what a claim is worth in practice.

Reading 25/50/25

Policies are written as three numbers in thousands of dollars. 25/50/25 means up to $25,000 for one injured person, $50,000 for everyone hurt in the crash and $25,000 for property damage. If your injuries are worth $80,000 and the driver has a $25,000 per-person limit, their insurer will almost always pay no more than $25,000.

When several people are hurt

The per-crash limit is shared. With a 25/50 policy and three injured people, $50,000 is split among all three, so each may receive well under $25,000.

Underinsured motorist coverage fills the gap

Underinsured motorist (UIM) coverage on your own policy pays when the at-fault driver’s limit is too low. There are two types:

  • Excess (add-on): pays on top of the other driver’s limit. With their $25,000 and your $100,000 UIM, up to $125,000 is available.
  • Reducing (offset): pays your UIM limit minus what their policy paid. With the same numbers, up to $100,000 is available in total.

Uninsured motorist (UM) coverage pays when the driver has no insurance or flees the scene.

Steps to take

  1. Get the at-fault driver’s policy limit in writing. Many states require insurers to disclose it on request.
  2. Notify your own insurer of a possible UIM claim early. Many policies require consent before you settle with the other driver.
  3. Check for other coverage: the driver’s employer, the vehicle owner, an umbrella policy.

See what your coverage adds in the policy limits and UM/UIM gap calculator, and compare limits in minimum car insurance by state.

seo.title: Comparative Negligence Explained: How Fault Cuts Payouts
seo.description: How pure comparative, 50% bar, 51% bar and contributory negligence rules reduce an injury settlement, with worked examples for each type of state.
seo.focus: comparative negligence,comparative negligence example,modified comparative negligence

posts.content:
Key points

  • Every state reduces or bars recovery when the injured person shares the fault.
  • The difference between a 50% and a 51% bar decides cases split down the middle.
  • Five jurisdictions still use contributory negligence, which can bar a claim for any fault.

Accidents are rarely one-sided. A driver may have run a red light while you were a few miles over the limit. A store may have left a spill while you were looking at your phone. Your state’s fault rule decides what that shared blame costs.

The rules, from most to least forgiving

Pure comparative fault. Your award is reduced by your share of fault, at any level. At 70% fault you still recover 30%. Used in 10 states, including California, New York and Washington.

Modified comparative fault with a 51% bar. Your award is reduced by your share, and you recover nothing at 51% or more. Used in 24 states, including Texas, Florida and Pennsylvania.

Modified comparative fault with a 50% bar. Your award is reduced by your share, and you recover nothing at 50% or more. Used in 11 states, including Georgia, Colorado and Tennessee.

Contributory negligence. Any fault on your side can bar recovery. Used in Alabama, Maryland, North Carolina, Virginia and DC.

Slight/gross negligence. South Dakota lets you recover only if your fault was slight compared with the other party’s.

Worked example

A $100,000 claim:

Rules change

Florida moved from pure comparative fault to a 51% bar in 2023. Louisiana did the same for injuries on or after January 1, 2026. The rule in force when the injury happened usually applies.

What it means for your claim

Expect the insurer to argue your share up, because each point is worth money. Evidence that pins fault on the other side, such as photos, video, the police report and witnesses, is worth gathering early. posts.title: No-Fault States: When You Can Sue for Pain and Suffering
posts.excerpt: How PIP pays first and what it takes to step outside the no-fault system.

meta.rank_math_description: How PIP pays first in no-fault states, and the verbal and monetary thresholds you must meet to step outside the system and sue for pain and suffering.
meta.rank_math_focus_keyword: pain and suffering in a no-fault state,no-fault threshold,can you sue in a no-fault state
meta.rank_math_title: Can You Sue for Pain and Suffering in a No-Fault State?

seo.title: Can You Sue for Pain and Suffering in a No-Fault State?
seo.description: How PIP pays first in no-fault states, and the verbal and monetary thresholds you must meet to step outside the system and sue for pain and suffering.
seo.focus: pain and suffering in a no-fault state,no-fault threshold,can you sue in a no-fault state

posts.content:
Key points

  • In 12 states your own PIP pays medical bills and lost income first, whoever caused the crash.
  • You can sue for pain and suffering only if your injury meets the state’s threshold.
  • Thresholds are either a dollar amount of medical bills or a serious-injury definition.

No-fault insurance was designed to pay injured people quickly without fights over who caused the crash. The trade-off is a limit on lawsuits for pain and suffering.

The 12 no-fault states

Florida, Hawaii, Kansas, Kentucky, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, New York, North Dakota, Pennsylvania and Utah. In Kentucky, New Jersey and Pennsylvania, drivers choose between no-fault and traditional tort coverage.

What PIP pays

Personal injury protection pays reasonable medical expenses and part of your lost wages, often 60% to 85%, up to your policy limit. Minimums range from $3,000 in Utah to $50,000 in New York, and Michigan drivers choose levels up to unlimited medical coverage.

Monetary thresholds

In some states you can sue once your medical bills pass a set amount: $1,000 in Kentucky, $2,000 in Kansas and Massachusetts, $2,500 in North Dakota, $3,000 in Utah, $4,000 in Minnesota and $5,000 in Hawaii. Most also allow a suit for certain serious injuries regardless of bills.

Verbal thresholds

Florida, Michigan, New Jersey, New York and Pennsylvania require a serious injury as the law defines it. New York, for example, lists fractures, significant disfigurement, permanent limitations and injuries that keep you from your usual activities for 90 of the first 180 days.

If you meet the threshold

You can claim pain and suffering, and economic losses PIP did not pay, from the at-fault driver’s liability insurance. If you do not, PIP and your health insurance are usually your main recovery.

See each state’s threshold in no-fault states and estimate benefits with the no-fault and PIP calculator.

posts.title: How Medical Liens Shrink a Settlement, and How They Get Reduced
posts.excerpt: Hospital, health-plan and Medicare liens, and the steps that lower them.

meta.rank_math_description: How hospital, health plan and Medicare liens are paid from a personal injury settlement, and the steps that can negotiate them down before you sign.
meta.rank_math_focus_keyword: medical liens on settlement,how to reduce medical liens,medicare lien settlement
meta.rank_math_title: Medical Liens on Settlements: How to Reduce Them

seo.title: Medical Liens on Settlements: How to Reduce Them
seo.description: How hospital, health plan and Medicare liens are paid from a personal injury settlement, and the steps that can negotiate them down before you sign.
seo.focus: medical liens on settlement,how to reduce medical liens,medicare lien settlement

posts.content:
Key points

  • Whoever paid for your treatment may have a right to be repaid from the settlement.
  • Medicare reduces its claim by its share of your attorney fee and costs.
  • Many liens are negotiable, and every dollar saved goes to you.

You settle for $100,000 and then learn your health plan wants $20,000 of it back. Medical liens surprise many people, but they follow predictable rules.

Who can claim part of a settlement

  • Health insurers and employer plans, under reimbursement clauses in the plan
  • Medicare, by federal law, for any injury-related care it paid
  • Medicaid, by federal and state law
  • Hospitals and providers, under state hospital lien laws or letters of protection
  • Your own auto insurer, for MedPay or PIP in some states

How Medicare’s reduction works

Medicare shares the cost of getting the recovery. Its claim is reduced by the ratio of procurement costs, the attorney fee and case costs, to the total settlement.

Other ways liens get reduced

  • Common fund doctrine: many states make private insurers share the fee
  • Made-whole rules: some states bar repayment until you are fully compensated
  • Hospital lien caps: many state laws limit hospital liens to reasonable charges or a share of the recovery
  • Negotiation: when insurance limits keep the settlement low, lien holders often agree to take less

Self-funded employer plans governed by ERISA are the hardest, because the plan document usually controls, but reductions are still common in practice.

Estimate your payoff with the medical lien calculator.

posts.title: How to Write a Demand Letter to an Insurance Adjuster
posts.excerpt: What to include, what to leave out, and how to set your opening number.

meta.rank_math_description: What to include in a personal injury demand letter, what to leave out, and how to set an opening demand that leaves room to negotiate with the adjuster.
meta.rank_math_focus_keyword: how to write a demand letter,personal injury demand letter,demand letter to insurance company
meta.rank_math_title: How to Write a Demand Letter to an Insurance Adjuster

seo.title: How to Write a Demand Letter to an Insurance Adjuster
seo.description: What to include in a personal injury demand letter, what to leave out, and how to set an opening demand that leaves room to negotiate with the adjuster.
seo.focus: how to write a demand letter,personal injury demand letter,demand letter to insurance company

posts.content:
Key points

  • A demand letter sets the frame for the whole negotiation.
  • Lead with facts and documents, not emotion.
  • Open above your target so you have room to move.

A demand letter is your written case for settlement. Done well, it tells the adjuster you understand your claim and have the records to prove it.

When to send it

After you finish treatment or reach maximum medical improvement, so you know the full cost, and well before your filing deadline. Sending it too early can leave money on the table.

What to include

  1. Header: your name, the adjuster, the claim number, the insured’s name and the accident date
  2. What happened: two or three factual sentences showing why their insured was at fault
  3. Injuries: the diagnoses from your medical records
  4. Treatment: providers, procedures and the length of care
  5. Damages: an itemized list of medical bills and lost income, with copies attached
  6. Impact: how the injury affected work, sleep, family life and activities
  7. Demand: a specific amount and a date to respond, often 30 days

Setting the number

Start from economic damages, add pain and suffering using a multiplier that fits your injury, and open toward the high end of the range. Insurers rarely pay more than the demand, so an opening number that is too modest caps the outcome.

What to leave out

  • Any admission of fault or apology for the accident
  • Medical history unrelated to this injury
  • Guesses about diagnoses your doctors have not made
  • Threats or anger

Send it so you can prove it

Email it and send a copy by certified mail. Keep copies of everything you attach.

posts.title: What to Do in the First 72 Hours After a Car Accident
posts.excerpt: The records and decisions that protect a claim before you talk to an adjuster.

meta.rank_math_description: What to do after a car accident to protect your injury claim: medical care, photos, the police report, insurance calls and what not to tell the adjuster.
meta.rank_math_focus_keyword: what to do after a car accident,after a car accident checklist,car accident claim steps
meta.rank_math_title: What to Do After a Car Accident: The First 72 Hours

seo.title: What to Do After a Car Accident: The First 72 Hours
seo.description: What to do after a car accident to protect your injury claim: medical care, photos, the police report, insurance calls and what not to tell the adjuster.
seo.focus: what to do after a car accident,after a car accident checklist,car accident claim steps

posts.content:
Key points

  • Get medical care quickly, even if you feel fine.
  • Document the scene, the cars and your injuries with photos.
  • Report the crash to your own insurer, but be careful what you say to theirs.

What you do in the first three days after a crash shapes the claim for months. Most of it is simple.

At the scene

  • Call 911 if anyone is hurt, and ask for a police report
  • Photograph the vehicles, plates, the road, signals, skid marks and injuries
  • Exchange names, phone numbers, license and insurance details
  • Get names and phone numbers of witnesses
  • Do not argue about fault or apologize

Within 24 hours

See a doctor. Adrenaline hides pain, and many injuries, such as whiplash and concussions, show up later. A same-day or next-day visit links the injury to the crash. Insurers use delays to argue you were not hurt.

Report the crash to your insurer. Policies require prompt notice. Stick to the facts.

Within 72 hours

  • Get the police report number and request a copy
  • Start a folder for bills, receipts, mileage and time off work
  • Write down what happened while it is fresh
  • Photograph your injuries as they change

Talking to the other driver’s insurer

Their adjuster may call quickly and ask for a recorded statement. You do not have to give one. If you do, keep to the facts, do not guess about speed or distance, and do not describe your injuries as minor before a doctor has examined you.

Do not sign anything yet

Early offers often come before the extent of your injury is known. Do not sign a release until treatment ends.

Know your deadline
