posts.title: Workers’ Comp or a Personal Injury Claim: Can You File Both?
posts.excerpt: When a third party caused a work injury, and how the two claims interact.

meta.rank_math_description: When a third party causes a work injury, you may have a workers’ comp claim and a personal injury lawsuit. How the two claims interact and who gets repaid.
meta.rank_math_focus_keyword: workers comp vs personal injury,third party claim workers comp,can you sue and get workers comp
meta.rank_math_title: Workers’ Comp vs Personal Injury: Can You File Both?

seo.title: Workers’ Comp vs Personal Injury: Can You File Both?
seo.description: When a third party causes a work injury, you may have a workers’ comp claim and a personal injury lawsuit. How the two claims interact and who gets repaid.
seo.focus: workers comp vs personal injury,third party claim workers comp,can you sue and get workers comp

posts.content:
Key points

  • Workers’ comp pays without proving fault, but usually bars a lawsuit against your employer.
  • If someone other than your employer caused the injury, you can often bring a separate injury claim.
  • The comp insurer usually gets repaid from the injury settlement.

A delivery driver is rear-ended on the job. A warehouse worker is hurt by a defective machine. Both can claim workers’ compensation, and both may also have a personal injury claim against someone else.

Workers’ comp in brief

Workers’ compensation pays medical care and part of lost wages for work injuries, regardless of fault. In exchange, it is usually the only remedy against your employer: you cannot sue your employer for pain and suffering.

Third-party claims

When someone other than your employer or a co-worker caused the injury, you can usually sue them too. Common examples:

  • A driver who hit you while you were working
  • The maker of a defective tool or machine
  • A property owner where you were working, other than your employer
  • A subcontractor on a construction site

How the two fit together

Repaying the comp insurer

The workers’ comp insurer usually has a lien on the third-party recovery for what it paid. State law decides how much, and many states reduce it for the fee and costs of getting the recovery.

Estimate both sides with the workers’ comp settlement calculator and the personal injury settlement calculator.

posts.title: Average Car Accident Settlement Amounts: What the Data Shows
posts.excerpt: Insurers paid an average of $28,278 per bodily injury claim in 2024. Here is what that number includes, why your claim may be far above or below it, and how to estimate your own.

meta.rank_math_description: Insurers paid an average of $28,278 per bodily injury claim in 2024. See what that includes, why your claim may differ and how to estimate your own.
meta.rank_math_focus_keyword: average car accident settlement,car accident settlement amounts,average settlement for car accident with injury
meta.rank_math_title: Average Car Accident Settlement Amounts (%currentyear% Data)

seo.title: Average Car Accident Settlement Amounts ( Data)
seo.description: Insurers paid an average of $28,278 per bodily injury claim in 2024. See what that includes, why your claim may differ and how to estimate your own.
seo.focus: average car accident settlement,car accident settlement amounts,average settlement for car accident with injury

posts.content:
Key points

  • The best national benchmark is claim severity: auto insurers paid an average of $28,278 per bodily injury liability claim in 2024.
  • That average mixes minor soft-tissue claims with surgical and catastrophic ones, so most claims settle for less and serious ones for much more.
  • Your own value depends on medical bills, lost income, how lasting the injury is, your share of fault and the insurance available.
  • The fastest way to a realistic number is to run your own figures, then compare offers against that range.

People search for an average car accident settlement because they want to know whether an offer is fair. The honest answer is that a single average says very little about one claim. It is still useful to know what the data shows, and why your number may land far from it.

The national numbers

Insurers don’t publish settlement amounts, but the insurance industry tracks claim severity, the average amount paid per claim. According to ISO data published by the Insurance Information Institute, private passenger auto insurers paid:

Bodily injury claim severity rose about 36% from 2020 to 2024, driven by higher medical costs, more litigation and larger awards. Those figures include loss adjustment expenses and cover paid claims only.

Why the average misleads

An average is pulled up by a small number of very large claims. A few six- and seven-figure claims for spinal injuries or brain damage raise the mean far above what a typical whiplash claim settles for. The median claim, the one in the middle, is lower than $28,278.

The average also hides what the claim was for. Two people with the same $28,000 settlement may have had very different injuries: one with $9,000 in bills and an easy fault case, the other with $40,000 in bills, 30% of the blame and a driver who carried only $25,000 of coverage.

What actually sets the value of your claim

Medical bills and lost income

Economic damages are the base of every estimate. They include past and future medical care and income you lost while recovering. Keep every bill and pay stub.

How serious and lasting the injury is

Pain and suffering is usually valued as a multiple of economic damages, from about 1.5× for an injury that heals fully in a few months to 4× or 5× for a permanent one. Read the pain and suffering multiplier, explained.

Your share of fault

Most states cut your award by your percentage of fault, and some bar recovery entirely past 50% or 51%. Four states and DC still use contributory negligence, where even slight fault can end a claim. Check your state on the comparative negligence by state chart.

The insurance available

A claim is worth what can be collected. If the at-fault driver carries only their state’s minimum, often $25,000 or $30,000 per person, that is usually the most their insurer pays, whatever the injury is worth. Your own underinsured motorist coverage can add to it. See minimum car insurance by state.

No-fault rules

In the 12 no-fault states, your own PIP pays first, and you can claim pain and suffering only if the injury meets a threshold. Read no-fault states and pain and suffering.

Settlement examples by injury type

These examples use the same formula as our calculator. They are illustrations, not reported settlements.

Read our guides to whiplash, herniated discs, concussions and broken bones for what moves each one.

From settlement to take-home

A settlement is a gross figure. If you hire a lawyer on a one-third contingency fee, the fee, case costs and any medical liens come out first. On a $45,000 settlement with a $15,000 fee, $1,000 in costs and a $7,000 health plan lien, you would keep $22,000. Lawyers often negotiate liens down, which raises the net. Compare any offer with your own estimate, not the national average. posts.title: Whiplash Settlement Amounts: How Neck Injury Claims Are Valued
posts.excerpt: Why whiplash claims are often valued low, what evidence raises them, and worked examples using the same math adjusters start from.

meta.rank_math_description: How insurers value whiplash and neck injury claims, the evidence that raises them, and worked examples using 1.5× to 3× multipliers.
meta.rank_math_focus_keyword: whiplash settlement amounts,average whiplash settlement,whiplash injury claim
meta.rank_math_title: Whiplash Settlement Amounts: How Claims Are Valued

seo.title: Whiplash Settlement Amounts: How Claims Are Valued
seo.description: How insurers value whiplash and neck injury claims, the evidence that raises them, and worked examples using 1.5× to 3× multipliers.
seo.focus: whiplash settlement amounts,average whiplash settlement,whiplash injury claim

posts.content:
Key points

  • Whiplash is a soft-tissue neck injury, and insurers usually value it at the low end of the multiplier range, around 1.5× to 2×.
  • Claims settle higher when imaging, consistent treatment and lasting symptoms back them up.
  • Gaps in care and delays in seeing a doctor are the most common reasons offers come in low.
  • Many whiplash claims settle without a lawsuit, so the strength of your records does most of the work.

Whiplash is the most common injury in rear-end crashes. The head snaps forward and back, straining the muscles and ligaments of the neck. Most people improve within weeks to a few months, which is why insurers treat it as a minor injury. Some people have pain, stiffness, headaches or numbness that last much longer, and those claims are worth more.

How insurers value whiplash

Adjusters start with economic damages, mainly medical bills and lost income, and add pain and suffering as a multiple of them. Because whiplash rarely shows on an X-ray, insurers tend to use a low multiplier unless there is other objective evidence.

Worked examples

Recovered in ten weeks. Urgent care, a primary care visit and 12 physical therapy sessions total $5,400, and you missed $1,200 of work. Economic damages: $6,600. At 1.5× to 2×, pain and suffering is $9,900 to $13,200, for a total of $16,500 to $19,800 before any fault reduction.

Symptoms for eight months. Add an MRI, pain management injections and longer therapy, for $18,000 in medical bills and $4,000 in lost income. At 2× to 3×, the total is $66,000 to $88,000 before fault.

Run your own figures in the calculator below. In a no-fault state, your PIP pays the medical bills first, and whiplash often doesn’t meet the threshold to sue for pain and suffering unless the injury is serious or permanent.

Evidence that raises a whiplash claim

  • Prompt care: seeing a doctor within a day or two of the crash links the injury to it
  • Consistent treatment: following through on physical therapy without long gaps
  • Imaging when symptoms persist: an MRI can show disc or nerve involvement that an X-ray misses
  • A treating doctor’s opinion on how long symptoms will last and what care you may need
  • A pain journal recording what you couldn’t do: sleep, work, lift, drive, play with your kids
  • Photos of the vehicles: a heavily damaged rear end makes the injury easier to believe

What insurers argue

Expect the adjuster to point to low vehicle damage, a gap in treatment, chiropractic care they consider excessive, or an earlier neck problem. None of these ends a claim. Low damage doesn’t rule out injury, and a pre-existing condition that the crash made worse is still compensable. But each argument needs an answer in your records.

Should you hire a lawyer for whiplash?

Many people handle short, fully healed whiplash claims themselves. A lawyer makes more sense when symptoms last, imaging shows a disc injury, the insurer disputes fault, or the at-fault driver’s policy limit looks too small. Compare your likely net both ways with the attorney fee calculator, and use the demand letter generator if you negotiate yourself.

  • Herniated disc settlement value

posts.title: Herniated Disc Settlement Value: With and Without Surgery
posts.excerpt: How a herniated or bulging disc changes an injury claim, why surgery moves the value so much, and how insurers argue pre-existing degeneration.

meta.rank_math_description: How a herniated disc changes an injury settlement, why surgery moves the value so much, and how to answer the pre-existing degeneration argument.
meta.rank_math_focus_keyword: herniated disc settlement,herniated disc settlement amounts,bulging disc settlement
meta.rank_math_title: Herniated Disc Settlement Value: With and Without Surgery

seo.title: Herniated Disc Settlement Value: With and Without Surgery
seo.description: How a herniated disc changes an injury settlement, why surgery moves the value so much, and how to answer the pre-existing degeneration argument.
seo.focus: herniated disc settlement,herniated disc settlement amounts,bulging disc settlement

posts.content:
Key points

  • A herniated disc shown on MRI is objective evidence, which usually moves a claim above soft-tissue values.
  • Surgery is the biggest single driver of value: it adds large medical bills, time off work and a higher multiplier.
  • Insurers commonly argue the disc was already degenerating, so a doctor’s opinion linking the herniation to the crash matters.
  • Future care, such as more injections or a later surgery, belongs in the claim and is often the largest part of it.

Spinal discs cushion the vertebrae. A herniation happens when the soft center pushes through the outer ring and can press on nearby nerves, causing back or neck pain, numbness, tingling or weakness in an arm or leg. Crashes and falls are common causes.

Why a herniated disc is worth more than a sprain

Unlike whiplash, a disc herniation can be seen on an MRI. Imaging, nerve symptoms that match the level of the herniation and a specialist’s diagnosis give an adjuster less room to call the injury minor. Treatment also tends to be longer and more expensive.

Treatment paths and their effect on value

Worked examples

No surgery. MRI, physical therapy, medication and two injections cost $24,000, and you missed $6,000 of work. Economic damages: $30,000. At 2× to 3×, the claim is worth $90,000 to $120,000 before fault.

With surgery. A discectomy and rehab bring medical bills to $85,000, plus $15,000 in lost income. At 3× to 4×, the claim is worth $400,000 to $500,000 before fault, and future care can add to it.

Those are formula examples, not reported settlements. At these values, the at-fault party’s insurance limit often matters more than the formula. Check it with the policy limits calculator.

The pre-existing condition argument

Disc degeneration is common with age, and many adults have bulging discs on an MRI without symptoms. Insurers use this to argue the crash didn’t cause your herniation. Your answer is evidence that the crash made things worse:

  • No back or neck complaints, or only occasional ones, in your records before the crash
  • Symptoms that began right after the crash
  • A treating doctor’s written opinion that the crash caused or aggravated the herniation

The law in every state allows recovery when an accident aggravates a pre-existing condition, although damages are limited to the worsening.

Future medical care and lost earning capacity

If your doctor expects more injections, a future surgery or lifelong pain management, those costs belong in the claim. So does lost earning capacity if you can’t return to physical work. Get these opinions in writing before you settle, because a settlement is final. The lost wages calculator covers the income side.

Related

  • Whiplash settlement amounts
  • Medical liens on a settlement
  • How long a settlement takes

posts.title: Concussion and Brain Injury Settlements: What Drives the Value
posts.excerpt: Concussion claims range from a few weeks of symptoms to lifelong disability. Here is how insurers value them and the evidence that proves an injury that rarely shows on a scan.

meta.rank_math_description: How concussion and brain injury claims are valued, the evidence that proves an injury that rarely shows on a scan, and why settling early is risky.
meta.rank_math_focus_keyword: concussion settlement,traumatic brain injury settlement,tbi settlement amounts
meta.rank_math_title: Concussion and TBI Settlements: What Drives the Value

seo.title: Concussion and TBI Settlements: What Drives the Value
seo.description: How concussion and brain injury claims are valued, the evidence that proves an injury that rarely shows on a scan, and why settling early is risky.
seo.focus: concussion settlement,traumatic brain injury settlement,tbi settlement amounts

posts.content:
Key points

  • A concussion is a mild traumatic brain injury (TBI), but symptoms and claim values vary enormously.
  • Most concussions don’t show on a CT or MRI, so proof comes from symptoms, testing and treating doctors.
  • Lasting symptoms, such as memory problems, headaches or trouble working, push a claim into much higher value.
  • Moderate and severe TBIs are among the largest injury claims, where the insurance limit often sets the ceiling.

A traumatic brain injury happens when a blow or jolt to the head disrupts how the brain works. Car crashes and falls are among the most common causes. A concussion is the mildest form, and many people recover within weeks. Others develop persistent symptoms that last months or longer.

Common symptoms worth documenting

  • Headaches, dizziness and sensitivity to light or noise
  • Trouble concentrating, remembering or finding words
  • Fatigue and sleep changes
  • Irritability, anxiety or depression
  • Slower reaction time or difficulty with work tasks

Many of these are invisible to others. Write them down as they happen and tell your doctor at every visit.

How concussion claims are valued

Worked example

An ER visit, CT scan, neurology follow-ups and six weeks of vestibular therapy cost $11,000, and you miss $5,000 of work. With symptoms lasting four months, a 2× to 3× multiplier puts the claim at $48,000 to $64,000 before fault. If testing later shows lasting cognitive deficits that limit your work, lost earning capacity can become the largest part of the claim.

Proving an injury that doesn’t show on a scan

Insurers often argue that a normal CT means no injury. A normal scan is common with concussions and doesn’t rule one out. Strong evidence includes:

  • Records of confusion, memory loss or loss of consciousness at the scene or in the ER
  • A neurologist’s diagnosis and treatment notes
  • Neuropsychological testing that measures memory, attention and processing speed
  • Statements from family, friends and coworkers about changes in you
  • Work records showing missed time or reduced performance

Brain injuries and insurance limits

Serious brain injuries can be worth far more than a typical auto policy covers. If the at-fault driver carries $25,000 or $50,000 per person, look at every source: your own underinsured motorist coverage, a commercial policy if the driver was working, and other responsible parties. The policy limits calculator shows the gap.

Don’t settle too early

Concussion symptoms can evolve over the first months. Settling before you know whether symptoms will last can leave you without money for future care. Most lawyers advise waiting until your doctors can say whether you have reached maximum medical improvement, while keeping an eye on your filing deadline.

Related

  • The pain and suffering multiplier, explained
  • Average car accident settlement amounts
  • Policy limits and UIM coverage

posts.excerpt: Fractures are easy to prove, which helps a claim. How the type of break, surgery and lasting effects change the value, with worked examples.

meta.rank_math_description: How fracture type, surgery, hardware and lasting effects change a broken bone settlement, with worked examples for a wrist and an ankle fracture.

seo.title: Broken Bone Settlement Amounts: Fractures and Surgery
seo.description: How fracture type, surgery, hardware and lasting effects change a broken bone settlement, with worked examples for a wrist and an ankle fracture.
seo.focus: broken bone settlement,fracture settlement amounts,broken bone injury claim

posts.content:
Key points

  • A fracture shows on an X-ray, so insurers rarely dispute the injury itself; fault and value are the fights.
  • Value rises with the type of break, the need for surgery or hardware, recovery time and lasting limits.
  • Simple fractures that heal fully often settle in the moderate range; surgical fractures with permanent effects can be worth several times more.
  • Arthritis risk and future hardware removal are future costs that belong in the claim.

Broken bones are among the most common injuries in car crashes, falls and pedestrian accidents. Because a fracture is objective, these claims avoid the arguments that dog soft-tissue claims. The value then depends on how bad the break was and how well you recovered.

Fracture types and their effect on value

Worked examples

Broken wrist, cast only. ER care, a cast, follow-ups and therapy cost $9,500, and you miss $3,500 of work. At 2× to 3×, the claim is worth $39,000 to $52,000 before fault.

Ankle fracture with surgery. Surgery with plates and screws, a hospital stay and four months of therapy cost $46,000, plus $12,000 in lost income. At 3× to 4×, the claim is worth $232,000 to $290,000 before fault.

These are formula illustrations, not reported settlements. Slip and fall fractures follow the same math; see the slip and fall settlement calculator.

What raises a fracture claim

  • Surgery, hardware or a second surgery to remove it
  • A long recovery, especially for manual workers
  • Loss of motion, a limp or chronic pain after healing
  • A doctor’s opinion on future arthritis or joint replacement
  • Effects on daily life: sports, caring for children, driving

What can lower it

Fault arguments matter more than injury arguments in fracture cases. In a fall, the property owner may claim the hazard was obvious. In a crash, the other driver may argue you were speeding. Your state’s fault rule decides how much those arguments cost you; see comparative negligence by state.

Future costs to include

Ask your surgeon about the likely course: hardware removal, physical therapy flare-ups, arthritis and possible joint replacement years later. Those future costs and any reduced ability to work belong in your demand. Once you settle, you can’t reopen the claim.

posts.title: How Long Does a Personal Injury Settlement Take?
posts.excerpt: A stage-by-stage timeline from the accident to the check, why waiting until treatment ends usually pays, and what speeds a claim up or slows it down.

meta.rank_math_description: A stage-by-stage personal injury settlement timeline, from the accident to the check, plus what speeds a claim up or slows it down.
meta.rank_math_focus_keyword: how long does a personal injury settlement take,settlement timeline,how long does a car accident settlement take
meta.rank_math_title: How Long Does a Personal Injury Settlement Take? (Timeline)

seo.title: How Long Does a Personal Injury Settlement Take? (Timeline)
seo.description: A stage-by-stage personal injury settlement timeline, from the accident to the check, plus what speeds a claim up or slows it down.
seo.focus: how long does a personal injury settlement take,settlement timeline,how long does a car accident settlement take

posts.content:
Key points

  • Simple claims often settle within three to nine months after treatment ends; claims that go to a lawsuit commonly take one to three years.
  • The biggest variable is how long your medical treatment lasts, because a claim is hard to value before you know the full injury.
  • After you sign a release, payment usually arrives within a few weeks, but liens can delay your share.
  • Your filing deadline keeps running the whole time, so track it from day one.

The timeline, stage by stage

Why waiting for treatment to end usually pays

A settlement is final. If you settle while still treating, you are guessing at future costs and at whether symptoms will last. Most lawyers wait until you have recovered or your doctor says you have reached maximum medical improvement, so the full value of the injury is known.

The exception is a small claim where the insurer’s limit is already lower than your damages. Then there may be little reason to wait, because more treatment won’t raise the amount that can be paid. Check that with the policy limits calculator.

What speeds a claim up

  • Clear fault, such as a rear-end crash or a police citation
  • Complete records sent with the demand, so the adjuster has nothing to request
  • A demand that explains the number; use the demand letter generator
  • Responding quickly to the adjuster’s questions

What slows it down

  • Disputed fault or multiple vehicles
  • Long or ongoing treatment
  • Large damages that need supervisor approval or exceed policy limits
  • Medicare or other liens that must be resolved before you are paid
  • A lawsuit, which adds discovery, depositions and court schedules

After you accept an offer

You will sign a release giving up further claims. The insurer usually sends payment to your lawyer’s trust account, or to you if you have no lawyer, within a few weeks. The lawyer pays the fee, costs and liens and sends you the rest. Medicare liens in particular can take time to finalize.

Watch the deadline

Negotiating doesn’t stop the statute of limitations. If talks drag on, you must file suit before the deadline or lose the claim. Find yours with the statute of limitations calculator, and see every state in the statute of limitations by state table.

Related

  • Should you accept the first settlement offer?
  • How to write a demand letter
  • Medical liens on a settlement

posts.title: Rear-End Collision Settlements: Fault, Injuries and Value
posts.excerpt: The driver in back is usually at fault in a rear-end crash, but not always. How fault, common injuries and insurance limits shape a rear-end settlement.

meta.rank_math_description: Who is at fault in a rear-end collision, the injuries these crashes cause, and how fault and insurance limits shape a rear-end accident settlement.
meta.rank_math_focus_keyword: rear end collision settlement,rear end accident settlement amounts,who is at fault in a rear end collision
meta.rank_math_title: Rear-End Collision Settlements: Fault, Injuries and Value

seo.title: Rear-End Collision Settlements: Fault, Injuries and Value
seo.description: Who is at fault in a rear-end collision, the injuries these crashes cause, and how fault and insurance limits shape a rear-end accident settlement.
seo.focus: rear end collision settlement,rear end accident settlement amounts,who is at fault in a rear end collision

posts.content:
Key points

  • The rear driver is presumed at fault in most rear-end crashes, because drivers must keep a safe following distance.
  • That presumption can be challenged, for example when the front car stopped suddenly for no reason or had broken brake lights.
  • Neck and back injuries are the most common, so medical documentation often decides the value.
  • Clear fault usually means a faster settlement and little or no reduction for comparative fault.

Rear-end collisions are among the most common crashes on US roads, from low-speed fender benders in traffic to highway crashes at full speed. They are also among the most straightforward claims, because fault is usually clear.

Who is at fault in a rear-end crash?

Every state requires drivers to keep a safe distance and speed so they can stop. When one car hits another from behind, the rear driver is presumed negligent in most cases. Insurers may still try to shift some blame to the front driver when:

  • The front driver stopped suddenly without reason or cut in and braked
  • The front car’s brake lights didn’t work
  • The front driver reversed into the car behind
  • A chain-reaction crash involved several cars

Any fault assigned to you reduces your award under your state’s rule, and in contributory negligence states it can bar the claim. See how a fault share changes the value with the comparative fault calculator.

Common rear-end injuries

  • Whiplash and other neck strains
  • Back injuries, including herniated discs
  • Concussions from the head striking the headrest or steering wheel
  • Wrist and shoulder injuries from bracing against the wheel

Read our guides to whiplash settlements and herniated disc settlements.

Worked example

You are stopped at a red light when a driver hits you from behind. Medical care for a neck and back injury costs $12,400 over four months, and you miss $3,600 of work. Economic damages: $16,000. At a 2× to 3× multiplier, pain and suffering adds $32,000 to $48,000, for a total of $48,000 to $64,000. With no fault on your side, nothing is taken off.

Then check the insurance. If the driver carries only a $25,000 per-person minimum, their insurer will usually pay no more than $25,000, and your underinsured motorist coverage would have to make up the rest. Check the gap with the policy limits calculator.

Low-impact crashes

When the vehicle damage is small, insurers often argue nobody could be hurt. Injury doesn’t depend only on visible damage: modern bumpers can absorb a hit with little sign of it, and the position of your head at impact matters. Prompt medical care and consistent treatment are how you answer that argument.

Evidence to keep

  • Photos of both cars and the scene
  • The police report, and any citation issued to the rear driver
  • Dashcam or nearby security video, which is often erased within days
  • Witness names and phone numbers
  • All medical records and bills from the first visit on

posts.title: Should You Give a Recorded Statement to the Other Driver’s Insurer?
posts.excerpt: You usually don’t have to give the other driver’s insurer a recorded statement. What adjusters look for, what to say if you do talk, and how it differs from your own insurer.

meta.rank_math_description: You usually don’t have to give the other driver’s insurer a recorded statement. What adjusters look for and what to say if you do talk.
meta.rank_math_focus_keyword: recorded statement insurance adjuster,should i give a recorded statement,recorded statement car accident
meta.rank_math_title: Recorded Statement to an Insurance Adjuster: Should You?

seo.title: Recorded Statement to an Insurance Adjuster: Should You?
seo.description: You usually don’t have to give the other driver’s insurer a recorded statement. What adjusters look for and what to say if you do talk.
seo.focus: recorded statement insurance adjuster,should i give a recorded statement,recorded statement car accident

posts.content:
Key points

  • You generally have no legal duty to give a recorded statement to the other driver’s insurer.
  • Your own policy usually requires you to cooperate with your own insurer, which can include a statement.
  • Adjusters use statements to look for fault admissions, gaps in your account and early downplaying of injuries.
  • If you do talk, stick to basic facts, don’t guess, and don’t describe your injuries as minor or fully healed.

After a crash, the other driver’s insurance adjuster often calls within days, asking to record your account of what happened. The adjuster may be friendly and say it’s routine. It is routine, but the statement is evidence, and it is gathered by the company that will decide how much to pay you.

Your own insurer versus theirs

What adjusters look for

  • Fault: an “I didn’t see them” or “I was going a little fast” can shift blame to you, and under your state’s fault rule that reduces the claim or, in some states, ends it
  • Injuries: saying “I’m fine” or “just a little sore” on day two is quoted later when symptoms worsen
  • Inconsistencies between your statement, the police report and your medical records
  • Prior injuries to the same part of the body

If you choose to talk

  • Ask that the call not be recorded, or ask to answer questions in writing instead
  • Give your name, contact details, your insurer and basic facts: where, when, which vehicles
  • Don’t speculate about speed, distance or what the other driver was doing if you aren’t sure
  • Say you are still being treated and can’t yet describe your injuries fully
  • Don’t sign a medical authorization that gives access to your entire medical history
  • Don’t accept an early offer on the call

When to involve a lawyer first

If you were seriously hurt, fault is disputed, or the adjuster pushes for details about your health, a lawyer can handle communications. Most offer a free consultation. You can also prepare your own figures first with the car accident settlement calculator so you know what the claim is worth before any negotiation.

Related

  • What to do in the first 72 hours after a car accident
  • Should you accept the first settlement offer?
  • How long a settlement takes

posts.title: Hit-and-Run and Uninsured Driver Claims: How UM Coverage Pays
posts.excerpt: When the driver who hit you has no insurance or drives away, your own uninsured motorist coverage usually becomes the claim. How it works, deadlines and what to do first.

meta.rank_math_description: When the at-fault driver has no insurance or drives away, your uninsured motorist coverage pays. How UM and UIM claims work and what to do first.
meta.rank_math_focus_keyword: hit and run claim,uninsured motorist claim,uninsured motorist coverage
meta.rank_math_title: Hit-and-Run and Uninsured Driver Claims: How UM Pays

seo.title: Hit-and-Run and Uninsured Driver Claims: How UM Pays
seo.description: When the at-fault driver has no insurance or drives away, your uninsured motorist coverage pays. How UM and UIM claims work and what to do first.
seo.focus: hit and run claim,uninsured motorist claim,uninsured motorist coverage

posts.content:
Key points

  • Uninsured motorist (UM) coverage on your own policy pays for your injuries when the at-fault driver has no insurance, and in most states after a hit-and-run.
  • Underinsured motorist (UIM) coverage pays the gap when the at-fault driver’s limits are too low.
  • A UM claim is made against your own insurer, but it is valued like a claim against the other driver and can still be disputed.
  • Report a hit-and-run to police quickly; many policies require prompt reporting and may require physical contact with the other vehicle.

More than one in seven US drivers (15.4%) was uninsured in 2023, according to the Insurance Research Council, and the share is far higher in some states. A crash with one of them, or with a driver who never stops, leaves no liability policy to claim against. That is the gap uninsured motorist coverage exists to fill.

How UM and UIM coverage work

  • Uninsured motorist bodily injury (UMBI): pays your medical bills, lost income and pain and suffering when the at-fault driver has no liability insurance or can’t be identified
  • Underinsured motorist (UIM): pays when the at-fault driver’s liability limit is less than your damages, up to your UIM limit
  • Uninsured motorist property damage (UMPD): available in some states, for damage to your car

Some states require UM coverage; most others require insurers to offer it and let you reject it in writing. Check your declarations page for your limits.

Worked example

A driver runs a red light, hits you and drives off. Your injuries total $20,000 in medical bills and lost income, and with a 2× to 3× multiplier the claim is worth $60,000 to $80,000. With $100,000 of UM coverage, your insurer can pay the full value. With $25,000, it pays up to $25,000, and you may need other sources such as health insurance or MedPay.

In a no-fault state, your PIP pays first, and a UM claim covers pain and suffering only if the injury meets the threshold.

What to do after a hit-and-run

  1. Call the police from the scene and get a report number; many policies require prompt reporting.
  2. Write down everything you remember about the car: color, make, plate, direction of travel.
  3. Look for witnesses and cameras: businesses, doorbells, traffic cameras, dashcams.
  4. Get medical care, even if you feel fine.
  5. Notify your insurer quickly and ask about UM, MedPay or PIP coverage.

Some policies and states require physical contact between the vehicles for a hit-and-run UM claim, or independent witness evidence when there was no contact. Read the uninsured motorist section of your policy.

Your insurer is now on the other side

Even though you pay for UM coverage, your insurer evaluates the claim much like the at-fault driver’s insurer would. It can dispute fault, the injuries and the value. Many policies require arbitration of UM disputes, and many have their own deadlines for making a claim, which can differ from the statute of limitations.

posts.title: Dog Bite Settlement Amounts: Average Payouts and What Drives Them
posts.excerpt: Insurers paid an average of $65,450 per dog-related injury claim in 2025. What that figure includes, how state law decides liability, and how scarring changes the value.

meta.rank_math_description: Insurers paid an average of $65,450 per dog-related injury claim in 2025. How state dog bite laws, scarring and surgery drive settlement value.
meta.rank_math_focus_keyword: dog bite settlement amounts,average dog bite settlement,dog bite claim payout
meta.rank_math_title: Dog Bite Settlement Amounts: Average Payouts and Value

seo.title: Dog Bite Settlement Amounts: Average Payouts and Value
seo.description: Insurers paid an average of $65,450 per dog-related injury claim in 2025. How state dog bite laws, scarring and surgery drive settlement value.
seo.focus: dog bite settlement amounts,average dog bite settlement,dog bite claim payout

posts.content:
Key points

  • Insurers paid $1.86 billion on 28,450 dog-related injury claims in 2025, an average of $65,450 per claim.
  • The average is pulled up by severe attacks, facial injuries and claims for children, so most bite claims settle for less.
  • Your state’s dog bite law decides whether the owner is liable automatically or only if they knew the dog was dangerous.
  • Scarring, especially on the face, and the need for plastic surgery are the biggest drivers of value.

The national numbers

According to Triple-I and State Farm, dog-related injury claims in 2025 totaled $1.86 billion, up 18.6% from 2024. The number of claims rose more than 25% to 28,450. The average cost per claim was $65,450, down from $69,272 in 2024, and up 97% over the past decade. California and Florida each had more than 2,000 claims. New York had the highest average cost per claim, at $92,154.

These figures include claims for falls and other injuries caused by dogs, not only bites, and they reflect paid homeowner’s and renter’s claims.

Who is liable depends on your state

Every state’s rule is in the dog bite laws by state table, and each state page of the dog bite settlement calculator applies its own rule.

What drives the value of a dog bite claim

  • Scarring and disfigurement, especially on the face, neck or hands
  • Plastic or reconstructive surgery, now and in the future
  • Infection, nerve or tendon damage
  • Emotional harm, such as fear of dogs or anxiety after the attack, often documented by a counselor
  • The victim’s age: children are especially vulnerable to facial injuries and lasting emotional effects
  • Provocation: if the owner proves you provoked or teased the dog, the claim can be reduced or barred

Worked example

A bite to the forearm needs stitches, antibiotics and follow-up care for $6,500, and you miss $1,000 of work. The wound leaves a visible scar. At a 2× to 3× multiplier, pain and suffering is $15,000 to $22,500, for a total of $22,500 to $30,000. A facial bite needing reconstructive surgery could be worth several times more.

Who pays

Most dog bite claims are paid by the owner’s homeowner’s or renter’s insurance, which often carries $100,000 to $300,000 of liability coverage. Some policies exclude certain breeds or dogs with a bite history. If the bite happened at a rental property, the landlord may also be liable in some states if they knew the dog was dangerous.

Steps after a dog bite

  1. Get medical care; dog bites carry a high infection risk.
  2. Report the bite to animal control, which creates an official record.
  3. Get the owner’s name, address and insurance details.
  4. Photograph the wounds as they heal, and the scene.
  5. Note your filing deadline, usually your state’s personal injury deadline.

Sources

  • Triple-I, Dog-related injury claims on the rise in 2025
  • Dog bite laws by state

posts.title: Average Workers’ Comp Settlement: How Lump Sums Are Calculated
posts.excerpt: The average workers’ comp claim cost $47,316 for injuries in 2022–2023. How a settlement is built from your weekly rate, impairment rating and future medical care.

meta.rank_math_description: The average workers’ comp claim cost $47,316 for 2022–2023 injuries. How a settlement is built from your weekly rate, impairment rating and future care.
meta.rank_math_focus_keyword: average workers comp settlement,workers comp settlement amounts,workers comp lump sum
meta.rank_math_title: Average Workers’ Comp Settlement: How Lump Sums Are Figured

seo.title: Average Workers’ Comp Settlement: How Lump Sums Are Figured
seo.description: The average workers’ comp claim cost $47,316 for 2022–2023 injuries. How a settlement is built from your weekly rate, impairment rating and future care.
seo.focus: average workers comp settlement,workers comp settlement amounts,workers comp lump sum

posts.content:
Key points

  • The average workers’ comp claim cost $47,316 for injuries in 2022–2023, combining medical and wage benefits, based on NCCI data.
  • That is the total cost of claims, not the average settlement check, which buys out the remaining value of a claim.
  • Settlement value comes from your weekly benefit rate, your impairment rating, future medical care and the risk on each side.
  • Workers’ comp pays no pain and suffering, which is why it usually pays less than a personal injury claim for the same injury.

What the data shows

According to the National Safety Council, using NCCI data for injuries in 2022–2023, the average workers’ compensation claim cost $47,316. The cost varies widely by cause and type of injury:

  • Motor vehicle crashes were the costliest cause, at $91,433 per claim
  • Amputations were the costliest type of injury, at $125,058 per claim

These figures include both medical benefits and lost-wage benefits paid over the life of the claim. A settlement is usually a lump sum that closes some or all of the remaining benefits, so it can be smaller or larger than the average depending on what has already been paid and what lies ahead.

How a workers’ comp settlement is calculated

1. Your weekly benefit rate

Most states pay about two-thirds of your average weekly wage, up to a state maximum. Find yours with the weekly benefit calculator.

2. Your impairment rating

When you reach maximum medical improvement (MMI), a doctor rates your permanent impairment. States convert that rating into weeks of permanent partial disability benefits using their own schedule.

3. Future medical care

If the settlement closes future medical benefits, it must include enough to pay for the care you are likely to need: medication, injections, therapy or surgery.

4. Risk on each side

The insurer pays something extra to close the claim and avoid future costs. You may accept a discount for getting money now and ending disputes.

Worked example

Your weekly benefit is $620, and you have a 10% whole-body impairment rating. If your state pays 3 weeks of benefits per point for a whole-body rating, that is 30 weeks × $620 = $18,600. Add $12,000 of expected future medical care and the settlement might be negotiated around $25,000 to $30,000. Every state’s formula is different; this example shows the method, not your state’s numbers.

Workers’ comp versus a personal injury claim

Workers’ comp is no-fault: you don’t have to prove your employer was negligent, but you also can’t claim pain and suffering. If someone other than your employer caused the injury, such as a driver who hit your work vehicle, you may also have a third-party personal injury claim. Read workers’ comp vs. personal injury.

Settlements, Medicare and SSDI

If you receive Medicare, or expect to within 30 months, a settlement that closes future medical care may need a Medicare set-aside. Workers’ comp can also reduce SSDI benefits when the combined total is more than 80% of your average earnings before the injury. See the SSDI back pay calculator.

Sources

  • National Safety Council Injury Facts, Workers’ Compensation Costs (NCCI data)

posts.title: Injured by a City, County or State Agency? Notice of Claim Deadlines
posts.excerpt: Claims against a government agency usually need a written notice of claim within months, long before the normal filing deadline. What triggers it, what to include and how to protect yourself.

meta.rank_math_description: Claims against a city, county or state agency usually need a written notice of claim within months. What triggers it and what the notice must include.
meta.rank_math_focus_keyword: notice of claim,claim against government agency,notice of claim deadline
meta.rank_math_title: Notice of Claim Deadlines for Government Injury Claims

seo.title: Notice of Claim Deadlines for Government Injury Claims
seo.description: Claims against a city, county or state agency usually need a written notice of claim within months. What triggers it and what the notice must include.
seo.focus: notice of claim,claim against government agency,notice of claim deadline

posts.content:
Key points

  • Claims against a government body, such as a city bus, a public hospital or a pothole on a state road, usually need a formal notice of claim first.
  • The notice deadline is often measured in months, sometimes 30 to 180 days, far shorter than the normal statute of limitations.
  • Missing the notice deadline can end the claim even if the lawsuit deadline is years away.
  • Government claims can also face damage caps and immunity rules that private claims don’t.

Most injury claims follow your state’s ordinary statute of limitations, usually two or three years. Claims against government agencies are different. Governments have sovereign immunity, which they waive only on their own terms, and one of the most common terms is a short deadline to give written notice of the claim.

When a notice of claim applies

You may be dealing with a government defendant if you were hurt by:

  • A city bus, police car, garbage truck or other government vehicle
  • A dangerous condition on public property: a sidewalk, park, school or government building
  • A road defect the government was responsible for maintaining
  • Care at a public hospital or clinic
  • An employee of a public school, transit authority or other agency

Public transit authorities, school districts and some hospitals are government entities even when it isn’t obvious.

How short is the deadline?

It depends on the state and the type of government body. Notice deadlines of 30, 60, 90, 120 or 180 days are common, and some states allow a year. The federal government, under the Federal Tort Claims Act, requires an administrative claim within two years. Because deadlines vary so much, treat any injury involving a government body as urgent and confirm the rule for your state and the agency involved.

What a notice usually includes

  • Your name and address
  • The date, time and place of the injury
  • A description of what happened and how the government was responsible
  • The injuries and damages you are claiming, sometimes with a dollar amount
  • Delivery to the correct office, often by certified mail, on the agency’s form if it has one

A notice sent to the wrong office or missing required details can be rejected.

Other rules that limit government claims

  • Damage caps: many states cap what a government body can pay per person or per incident
  • Immunity: some decisions, such as how to design a road, may be immune from suit
  • No jury in some government claims
  • A waiting period after the notice before you can file a lawsuit

Protect the claim

  1. Write down exactly where and when the injury happened, and take photos.
  2. Ask who owns or maintains the property or vehicle.
  3. Find the notice deadline for that agency immediately.
  4. Talk to a lawyer quickly; many will file the notice to protect your rights.

Use the statute of limitations calculator for the general lawsuit deadline, but remember that the notice deadline comes first.

Related

  • Statute of limitations by state
  • Damage caps by state
  • How long a settlement takes

posts.title: Brian Boxer Wachler MD Malpractice Lawsuits, Controversy and the Rise of TikTok’s Eye Doctor
posts.excerpt: Court indexes list at least three lawsuits naming Beverly Hills eye surgeon Brian Boxer Wachler, MD. Here is what the records show, the criticism of his eye color procedure, and how to check any doctor.

meta.rank_math_description: Court records, criticism and credentials: what the malpractice lawsuits against Beverly Hills eye surgeon Brian Boxer Wachler, MD, do and don’t show.
meta.rank_math_focus_keyword: brian boxer wachler md malpractice,brian boxer wachler lawsuit,dr brian boxer wachler,boxer wachler vision institute,keratopigmentation
meta.rank_math_title: Brian Boxer Wachler MD Malpractice: Lawsuits & Facts (2026)

seo.title: Brian Boxer Wachler MD Malpractice: Lawsuits & Facts (2026)
seo.description: Court records, criticism and credentials: what the malpractice lawsuits against Beverly Hills eye surgeon Brian Boxer Wachler, MD, do and don’t show.
seo.focus: brian boxer wachler md malpractice,brian boxer wachler lawsuit,dr brian boxer wachler,boxer wachler vision institute,keratopigmentation

posts.content:
Key points

  • Court indexes list at least three civil lawsuits naming Brian Boxer Wachler, MD, in Los Angeles County Superior Court: BC476444, BC505018 and BC550150.
  • None of the coverage we reviewed reports a verdict or judgment against him, and a lawsuit filing is an allegation, not a finding of negligence.
  • The most public criticism today concerns cosmetic keratopigmentation, a permanent eye color procedure the American Academy of Ophthalmology has warned against.
  • You can check any doctor yourself through the Medical Board of California license search and the county court’s case records.

Dr. Brian Boxer Wachler is two things at once. To millions of TikTok followers, he is the Beverly Hills eye surgeon who fact-checks viral health claims. To anyone who searches his name with the word “malpractice,” he is also a named defendant in lawsuits filed in Los Angeles County Superior Court.

Both are true, and neither tells the whole story. A lawsuit is an allegation, not a finding. Many malpractice cases in California end in a settlement or dismissal with no ruling that the doctor did anything wrong. At the same time, a long-running surgical practice that also offers elective cosmetic eye procedures deserves closer scrutiny than most.

This article sets out what the public record shows: his training and practice, how he became one of the most-followed physicians on social media, the lawsuits that court indexes list against him, what the Medical Board of California record covers, and the criticism of his cosmetic eye color procedure. It ends with a step-by-step guide to checking any doctor’s malpractice history yourself. Every factual claim links to its source, and where the record is incomplete, we say so.

Brian Boxer Wachler, MD, at a glance

Who is Dr. Brian Boxer Wachler?

Brian Boxer Wachler, MD, is a board-certified ophthalmologist who runs the Boxer Wachler Vision Institute in Beverly Hills. His practice centers on keratoconus, a disease in which the cornea thins and bulges into a cone and distorts vision. It also offers LASIK, implantable lenses and cosmetic eye procedures.

According to his practice’s biography, his training and posts include:

  • An MD from Dartmouth Medical School
  • An ophthalmology residency at the Saint Louis University Eye Institute
  • A fellowship in refractive and corneal surgery at the University of Kansas Medical Center and Hunkeler Eye Center
  • Director of the UCLA Laser Refractive Center at the Jules Stein Eye Institute, which the practice calls the “youngest director in UCLA’s history”
  • Certification by the American Board of Ophthalmology, and a staff position at Cedars-Sinai Medical Center

The same page credits him with pioneering Intacs and Holcomb C3-R treatments for keratoconus, inventing the WhiterEyes eye-whitening procedure, publishing 74 peer-reviewed articles and book chapters, and serving as an FDA investigator in 13 clinical trials. These are the practice’s own claims.

The Steve Holcomb case that made his name

His best-known patient was Steven Holcomb, the U.S. bobsled pilot. Holcomb was diagnosed with keratoconus in 2001, according to Britannica. By 2007 his vision had fallen to 20/500 and he could not read the top line of an eye chart, Fox News reported.

Boxer Wachler treated him with a riboflavin-based procedure to strengthen the cornea, then called C3-R, followed by implanted lenses. Britannica records a 2008 surgery to place a corrective lens behind each iris, after which Holcomb’s vision eventually reached 20/20. In 2010 Holcomb drove the U.S. four-man sled to Olympic gold in Vancouver, the country’s first four-man gold since 1948. Boxer Wachler later renamed the treatment the Holcomb C3-R. Holcomb died in May 2017.

The story gave Boxer Wachler national exposure years before TikTok. It also frames what came later: his reputation was built on surgery for a serious disease, while most of today’s criticism concerns elective cosmetic work.

How he became TikTok’s eye doctor

Boxer Wachler joined TikTok in 2020 to counter medical misinformation online, Spectrum News reported. The account grew fast. In March 2022, Becker’s Hospital Review ranked him second on its list of the most-followed physician influencers, with 3.2 million TikTok followers. By December 2022 he had about 3.4 million.

His videos respond to health claims circulating online, in line with his stated aim of countering misinformation. That combination of a practicing surgeon, a Beverly Hills address and quick verdicts on viral claims is why he is so often described as a medical fact-checker.

The audience brought its own problems, and he has said so himself. In 2022 he published Influenced: The Impact of Social Media on Our Perception, a book about how social media shapes belief, especially among children and teenagers. Spectrum News reported that the thrill of viral posts had become an addiction for him, taking time away from his family and his practice.

For a prospective patient, the lesson is simple. A large following shows skill at communicating, not surgical results. Reach, court records and the license record measure different things, and anyone choosing a surgeon should look at all three.

Brian Boxer Wachler MD malpractice lawsuits: what the court records show

Court indexes list at least three civil lawsuits naming Dr. Boxer Wachler in Los Angeles County Superior Court. Press coverage citing county court records describes his practice as facing malpractice suits over more than ten years.

We have left out the plaintiffs’ names. They are private individuals, and the case numbers are enough to pull each docket through the court’s Case Access search.

What these cases do and don’t show

  • A filing is an allegation. Anyone can file a complaint. It proves only that a patient believed they were harmed and went to court, not that the doctor was negligent.
  • “Et al.” means more than one defendant. Malpractice suits usually also name the practice, its corporate entity or staff.
  • The outcome is what matters, and it isn’t public in the coverage. None of the reporting we reviewed describes a verdict or judgment against Dr. Boxer Wachler in these cases. A case can end in dismissal, settlement or trial, and the court’s own docket is the record that shows which.
  • Counts mean little alone. The number of suits says little without knowing how many procedures a surgeon performs, over how many years, and how each case ended.

How malpractice claims work in California

Two rules shape every case like these:

  • The deadline. Under Code of Civil Procedure § 340.5, a patient must sue within three years of the injury or one year after discovering it, whichever comes first. The three-year limit stretches only for fraud, intentional concealment or a foreign object left in the body. Our California statute of limitations calculator covers the deadlines for other injury claims.
  • The damages cap. California’s MICRA law capped pain-and-suffering damages in malpractice cases at $250,000 from 1975 until 2023. Under AB 35, the cap rose to $350,000 for injury cases and $500,000 for death cases in 2023, and climbs $40,000 and $50,000 a year until it reaches $750,000 and $1 million in 2033 (Milliman). For cases resolved in 2026, that works out to $470,000 and $650,000. See how caps compare in our damage caps by state table.

Caps and the cost of expert witnesses push many California malpractice cases toward settlement. A settlement typically involves no admission of fault, which is why a lawsuit history should be read alongside the license record rather than in place of it.

Brian Boxer Wachler and the Medical Board of California

The Medical Board of California licenses physicians and disciplines them. Its record answers a different question from the court record. A lawsuit is a private claim for money; board action is the state deciding whether a doctor may keep practicing, and on what terms.

In the news coverage and court indexes we reviewed, we found no report of Medical Board discipline against Dr. Boxer Wachler. That is not the same as a record confirmed at the source. The board’s License Verification tools show three things:

  • License status: whether a license is current, and whether it carries any restriction or probation
  • Public documents: accusations, decisions and other administrative actions, through the Public Document Lookup
  • Some malpractice history: limited by law, as explained below

California’s disclosure rules are narrower than most patients expect. The board can disclose civil malpractice judgments in any amount. Settlements are disclosed only in limited cases, such as three or more in ten years for doctors in lower-risk specialties, and the settlement amounts are never released (Health Information & the Law summary of Business and Professions Code § 803.1). A doctor can settle several claims and still show none of them on a board profile.

To confirm Dr. Boxer Wachler’s current status, search his name in the board’s License Verification. That record, not news coverage, is the authoritative answer.

The real controversy: permanent eye color change

The most public criticism of Dr. Boxer Wachler today is not about the lawsuits. It is about cosmetic keratopigmentation, a procedure that places pigment inside the cornea to change the apparent color of the eye for good.

Scientific American reported that he has performed hundreds of these procedures since adding it to his practice in early 2024.

Why ophthalmologists object

  • A formal warning. In January 2024, the American Academy of Ophthalmology warned that cosmetic keratopigmentation and iris implants “carry serious risks for vision loss and complications.” The Academy has stood by that warning.
  • No FDA approval. The procedure is done off-label, without explicit FDA approval or oversight. The FDA does not regulate the pigments, and no U.S. medical organization has standardized the procedure.
  • Thin long-term evidence. Studies are small, with short follow-up. Corneal specialist Roberto Pineda told Scientific American that it “currently lacks scientific rigor.”
  • Documented complications. A 2018 study of 204 people found complications in 29, most often light sensitivity that usually faded within six months, plus color fading. Later reports describe cases of ectasia, a bulging of the cornea that can distort vision.

His side

Boxer Wachler told Scientific American that few lasting adverse effects have been reported in the medical literature. He says he turns away patients with a history of LASIK, eye inflammation or autoimmune disease, and urges patients to choose experienced providers. He and other doctors wrote to the Academy asking it to withdraw its warning. He declined to name the ingredients or sources of his dyes.

His practice also credits him with inventing WhiterEyes, a cosmetic eye-whitening procedure. It belongs to the same category as keratopigmentation: surgery on a healthy eye for appearance rather than to treat disease. That is the thread running through the controversy. The surgeon whose name was made by restoring a bobsledder’s sight now draws criticism for operating on eyes that work fine.

Anyone weighing an elective eye procedure should ask the surgeon three things in writing: how many they have done, what complications their own patients have had, and what long-term data exists.

How to check any doctor’s malpractice history

The same steps work for Dr. Boxer Wachler or any other surgeon you are considering.

  1. Check the license first. Search the doctor’s name in the Medical Board of California License Verification, or the medical board in your state. Look for license status, probation and any public documents.
  2. Search the county court. Malpractice suits are filed where the treatment happened. In Los Angeles County, use the Superior Court’s Case Access search for a known case number, or its party name search (which charges a fee). Search the practice’s business name as well as the doctor’s.
  3. Read the outcome, not the headline. Open each docket and see how it ended: dismissal, settlement or judgment. A dismissed case and a jury verdict are very different records.
  4. Know what stays hidden. Settlement amounts are not released by the Medical Board, and the National Practitioner Data Bank, which tracks malpractice payments nationally, is not open to the public.
  5. Verify board certification. For eye surgeons, the American Board of Ophthalmology confirms whether a doctor is currently certified.
  6. Ask the surgeon directly. How many of this procedure have you done? What complications have your patients had? What happens, and who pays, if something goes wrong?
  7. Get a second opinion for elective surgery. For cosmetic eye procedures especially, see an ophthalmologist who does not offer the procedure.

Yes. Court indexes list at least three civil lawsuits naming him in Los Angeles County Superior Court: case numbers BC476444, BC505018 and BC550150. A lawsuit is an allegation, not a finding of negligence.

Has Brian Boxer Wachler, MD, lost a malpractice case?

We found no news report or public summary describing a verdict or judgment against him. Each case’s outcome is recorded in its docket, which you can look up by case number on the Los Angeles Superior Court website.

Is Dr. Boxer Wachler’s medical license in good standing?

We found no report of Medical Board of California discipline against him in the coverage we reviewed. For his current status, search his name in the board’s License Verification, which is the official record.

No. It is performed off-label, the FDA does not regulate the pigments, and the American Academy of Ophthalmology warned in January 2024 that it carries serious risks of vision loss and complications.

He joined TikTok in 2020 to counter medical misinformation. By March 2022 he had 3.2 million followers and ranked second among the most-followed physician influencers, and by December 2022 he had about 3.4 million.

Olympic bobsledder Steven Holcomb, whose keratoconus left him with 20/500 vision by 2007. After treatment, Holcomb won the 2010 Olympic four-man gold, the first for the U.S. since 1948.

Three years from the injury or one year from when you discovered it, whichever comes first, under Code of Civil Procedure § 340.5. Fraud, intentional concealment or a foreign object left in the body can extend the three-year limit.

posts.title: Daniel Reed Jessica Moore Lawsuit: What Really Happened, and Can a Rescuer Be Sued?
posts.excerpt: There is no Daniel Reed Jessica Moore lawsuit. The viral video is a 2020 Cincinnati rescue with invented names. Here is the real story, and what the law says about suing a rescuer.

seo.title: Daniel Reed Jessica Moore Lawsuit: Real or Fake? Fact Check
seo.description: There is no Daniel Reed Jessica Moore lawsuit. The viral video is a 2020 Cincinnati rescue with invented names. The real story, and can a rescuer be sued?
seo.focus: daniel reed jessica moore lawsuit,daniel reed jessica moore,man sued for saving woman,daniel reed jessica moore court case,can you be sued for saving someone

posts.content:
Key points

  • There is no Daniel Reed Jessica Moore lawsuit. Fact-checkers found no lawsuit, criminal charge or police report.
  • The video is real but old: a January 26, 2020 rescue in Walnut Hills, Cincinnati, where the woman thanked her rescuer.
  • AI narration, invented names and a chatbot that vouched for the story helped it spread in late October 2025.
  • Good Samaritan laws in California and Ohio protect people who help a stranger in good faith in an emergency.

There is no Daniel Reed Jessica Moore lawsuit. The viral story says a man named Daniel Reed saved a woman named Jessica Moore from a speeding car in Los Angeles, and was then charged with or sued for sexual harassment. That story is fabricated.

The video is real, but it is old and it shows something else. It is dashcam footage of a January 2020 rescue in the Walnut Hills neighborhood of Cincinnati, Ohio. The real rescuer said the woman thanked him and they went their separate ways. Fact-checkers found no lawsuit, no charge and no police report.

Below is what the viral posts claimed, what the original footage shows, how AI tools helped the hoax spread, which real court cases share the name “Reed v. Moore,” and the question the hoax raises: can you actually be sued for saving someone?

Claim vs. fact at a glance

Verdict: false. The names are invented, the location is wrong, and the lawsuit never existed.

The viral claim: what the posts said

The story took off in late October 2025. According to Lead Stories, one widely shared Instagram video posted on October 24, 2025 opened with this line:

“A man saved a woman who was on the verge of being hit by a car, but was charged with sexual harassment.”

The video named the man “Daniel Reed” and the woman “Jessica Moore” and set the story in Los Angeles. Other versions, ThatsNonsense reported, described Reed as 32 and said Moore had sued him for sexual assault. The details shifted from post to post, which is itself a warning sign.

The clips were packaged to look like a TV news segment:

  • A narrator that ThatsNonsense describes as likely AI-generated
  • The real rescue footage, spliced with unrelated clips of cars, lawyers and police officers
  • Mismatched details. Lead Stories noted a car with a long yellow European-style license plate, which U.S. cars don’t have, and a woman without the headphones visible in the original clip

The format did its job. Searches for “Daniel Reed and Jessica Moore court case” and “ruling” spread across TikTok, and people went looking for a verdict that never existed.

What really happened: the 2020 Cincinnati rescue

The footage at the center of the hoax was recorded on January 26, 2020, in Walnut Hills, a neighborhood of Cincinnati, Ohio. A neighbor’s dashcam caught Criss Allen, then 25, pulling a pedestrian back as a car bore down on her.

The clip went viral the first time in February 2020. It was posted to YouTube by the clip agency Caters, and Inside Edition aired it on February 7, 2020, with an interview with Allen. He told the program the woman thanked him after he pulled her back, and then they went their separate ways (as summarized by Lead Stories).

That is the whole story. There was no arrest, no harassment complaint and no lawsuit. Lead Stories searched Google News and Yahoo News for any report of a Daniel Reed charged in Los Angeles after a rescue and found only copies of the viral claim. The Los Angeles Police Department told Lead Stories it could not search its records without a date, and none of the viral posts gave one.

Two fact-checks spell the rescuer’s name differently: Lead Stories uses “Criss Allen” and ThatsNonsense uses “Chris Allen.” Either way, he is not named Daniel Reed, and the woman he helped is not identified in either fact-check.

How the hoax spread: AI voiceovers, invented names and Grok

Nothing in the fake story required new footage. Its makers took a real, emotional clip, gave the people new names, moved the scene to Los Angeles and added a twist designed to make viewers angry: the hero gets punished.

Three things carried it further than the original clip ever went:

  1. AI narration. A synthetic news-anchor voice gave the clip borrowed authority. Viewers hear a confident narrator and assume someone checked the facts.
  2. Influencer reposts. ThatsNonsense notes the story was boosted by social media influencers, each repost adding reach without adding a source.
  3. A chatbot that vouched for it. When users asked X’s Grok whether the story was real, it wrongly told them it was. ThatsNonsense reports that Grok first denied having done so, then conceded its information came from “viral reports lacking primary verification.”

The last point matters most. People increasingly ask AI chatbots to fact-check what they see, and a chatbot that summarizes viral posts can end up repeating the hoax back to them with an air of authority. ThatsNonsense notes this was not the first time Grok had inserted itself into a fake news story this way.

The story also fit a template that spreads well: the Good Samaritan who gets sued. Stories like it spread easily because they confirm a fear many people already have, that helping a stranger could cost you. The law, as the next sections show, mostly says otherwise.

Real cases named Reed v. Moore, and why they aren’t this one

Search court databases for “Reed v. Moore” and you will find real cases. Neither has anything to do with the viral video, but both turn up in searches and in some articles about the hoax, so it helps to know what they are.

The 1957 case is a piece of legal history in its own right. It reflects the old “zone of danger” rule, under which a bystander could recover for emotional shock only if they were in danger themselves. California rejected that rule eleven years later in Dillon v. Legg (1968), allowing a mother who watched her child killed by a negligent driver to recover even though she was outside the zone of danger.

Neither case involves a rescue, a harassment claim, a Daniel Reed or a Jessica Moore.

Could a rescuer really be sued for saving someone?

The hoax was fake, but the fear behind it is worth answering. Short version: anyone can file a lawsuit, but a person who grabs a stranger in good faith to save them from an oncoming car is well protected in both states the story touches.

Filing a lawsuit is not winning one

Courts do not screen complaints before they are filed, so in theory almost anyone can sue almost anyone. Whether the claim survives is a different question. A rescuer pulling someone out of a car’s path is touching them to prevent serious harm, in an emergency, with no time to ask. That is the situation Good Samaritan laws were written for.

California, where the fake story was set

California is where this exact question became a real legal fight. In Van Horn v. Watson (2008) 45 Cal.4th 322, a woman pulled a friend from a crashed car because she feared it would catch fire. The friend was left paralyzed and sued, alleging she had been pulled out “like a rag doll.” The California Supreme Court ruled 4–3 that the state’s Good Samaritan statute covered only medical care, so the rescuer could be sued.

The Legislature responded the next year. AB 83 (2009) made clear that anyone who, in good faith and not for pay, gives emergency medical or non-medical care or assistance at the scene of an emergency is not liable for civil damages. The protection does not cover gross negligence or willful or wanton misconduct.

Ohio, where the rescue actually happened

Ohio’s Good Samaritan law, Ohio Revised Code § 2305.23, says no person is liable in civil damages for administering emergency care or treatment at the scene of an emergency, unless the acts amount to willful or wanton misconduct. It does not cover care given for pay. Pulling a pedestrian out of a car’s path in Walnut Hills sits comfortably inside that protection.

Do you have to help at all?

In most states, a bystander has no legal duty to rescue a stranger. A few states go further. Minnesota requires a person at an emergency scene who knows someone faces grave physical harm to give reasonable assistance if they can do so safely, and failing to is a petty misdemeanor. The same law protects helpers from civil liability unless they act in a willful and wanton or reckless manner (Minn. Stat. § 604A.01).

What if the pedestrian had been hit?

Then the claim would have been against the driver, not the rescuer. The driver’s liability insurance pays a pedestrian’s medical bills, lost wages and pain and suffering, and the amount can be reduced if the pedestrian shared the blame, for example by walking into traffic while distracted. Ohio bars recovery when the injured person is more than 50% at fault. See how each state handles shared fault in our comparative negligence by state chart, or estimate a claim with the pedestrian accident settlement calculator.

How to check whether a viral lawsuit story is real

The Daniel Reed Jessica Moore hoax failed every one of these checks. Run them before you share the next one.

  1. Look for the court record. Real lawsuits leave a paper trail. Federal cases are searchable through PACER and free docket sites such as Justia Dockets; most state courts have an online case search. A “landmark case” with no case number, court or date is a red flag.
  2. Check whether real newsrooms covered it. A rescuer charged with harassment would be national news. When the only results are reposts of the same video, as Lead Stories found here, the story usually isn’t real.
  3. Reverse-search the footage. Take a screenshot of a key frame and run it through a reverse image search. Old clips like this one often surface with their original date and place within minutes.
  4. Watch for mismatched details. License plates from the wrong country, clothing that changes between shots, and a narrator who never names a source all point to spliced footage.
  5. Be wary of AI voices and AI answers. A synthetic news voice is not a newsroom, and a chatbot summarizing viral posts is not a fact-check. Grok vouched for this hoax before admitting it had no primary source.
  6. Read a fact-checker. Lead Stories and ThatsNonsense both debunked this story within three weeks. Searching the claim plus “fact check” is often the fastest test.

Frequently asked questions

Is the Daniel Reed Jessica Moore lawsuit real?

No. Fact-checkers found no lawsuit, criminal charge or police report. The story was built on a real 2020 video with invented names and a made-up harassment claim.

Who are Daniel Reed and Jessica Moore?

The names appear only in the viral posts. The man in the video is Criss Allen, who pulled a pedestrian away from a car in Cincinnati in January 2020. Nobody named Daniel Reed was involved.

Where is the video really from?

Walnut Hills, Cincinnati, Ohio, on January 26, 2020. A neighbor’s dashcam recorded it, and Inside Edition aired it in February 2020.

Was the rescuer ever sued or charged?

No record of any charge or lawsuit has been found. He told Inside Edition the woman thanked him and they went their separate ways.

Can you be sued for saving someone?

Anyone can file a lawsuit, but Good Samaritan laws protect people who help in good faith in an emergency. California covers both medical and non-medical help unless the helper is grossly negligent or acts with willful or wanton misconduct. Ohio protects emergency care unless it is willful or wanton misconduct.

Is there a real Reed v. Moore case?

Yes, two unrelated ones: a 1957 California appeals case about a bystander’s emotional distress after a car crash, and a 2026 personal injury case in federal court in Louisiana. Neither involves a rescue or a harassment claim.

Did Grok confirm the story?

Grok initially told users the story was true. It later conceded its answer came from “viral reports lacking primary verification.”

  • ThatsNonsense: Man sued for saving woman from being run over? Another fake story amplified by AI (November 3, 2025)
  • Reed v. Moore (1957) 156 Cal. App. 2d 43, via Justia
  • Dillon v. Legg (1968) 68 Cal. 2d 728, via Justia
  • Reed v. Moore, No. 2:2026cv02226 (E.D. La.), via Justia Dockets
  • FindLaw: The California Supreme Court holds that Good Samaritans providing nonmedical aid can be held liable (2009)
  • California Assembly floor analysis of AB 83 (2009)
