Home/Find a lawyer

Free directory · No paid placements

Find a personal injury lawyer

Search injury lawyers by name, firm, city or state. Every profile starts from the official bar record, then adds the firm’s website, office, the cases it handles and where to read its reviews.

  • Bar records from official state data
  • Lawyers can’t pay to rank higher
  • Free, no sign-up
Search the directory
Claim your free profile

Search the directory

Filter by state, type of case or years in practice. Results are sorted by name or admission year, never by who paid.

Browse by type of case

Start with what happened. Each link opens the directory filtered to lawyers whose firms say they handle that kind of case.

  • Car accidentsCrashes, no-fault and injury claims
  • Truck accidentsCommercial trucks and higher policy limits
  • Motorcycle accidentsRider injuries, often the most serious
  • Slip and fallInjuries on someone else’s property
  • Medical malpracticeErrors by doctors, hospitals and clinics
  • Wrongful deathClaims by a family after a fatal accident
  • Workers’ compensationInjured on the job
  • Pedestrian and bicycleHit while walking or cycling

Browse by office location

Every lawyer listed so far is admitted to the New York bar. Most practice in New York, and some also run offices in other states. More state bars are being added.

  • New York
  • Florida
  • California
  • Connecticut
  • Georgia
  • New Jersey
  • Arizona
  • Colorado
  • Iowa
  • Massachusetts
  • Pennsylvania
  • Texas
  • Alabama
  • Minnesota
  • Nevada
  • Oregon
  • Washington
  • Ontario, Canada

How every profile is built

Three sources, in this order, and nothing we can’t point you to.

Step 1

Start from the official record

Name, firm, admission year and registration status come from the state’s public attorney registration data, and each profile links to that record.

Step 2

Add the firm’s own details

The website, office address, phone and the cases the firm handles come from the firm’s own website, with the month we checked it.

Step 3

Link to reviews, never copy them

We link to the firm’s reviews on Google and other sites so you read them where they were posted. Lawyers can correct or remove a listing at any time.

A listing is not a referral, a recommendation or a rating of a lawyer’s work. Lawyers do not pay to appear. Read our editorial policy.

Before you hire a lawyer

Meet two or three lawyers before you sign. These free tools help you compare them.

  • GuideHow to choose a personal injury lawyerQuestions to ask in the free consultation, how contingency fees work and the red flags to watch for.Read the guide →
  • CalculatorAttorney fee and net payout calculatorSee what you keep after the contingency fee, case costs and medical liens.Run the numbers →
  • CalculatorPersonal injury settlement calculatorGet a rough value for your claim under your state’s fault rule before the first call.Estimate my claim →
  • GuideDo you need a car accident lawyer?When hiring one is worth the fee, and when you can settle on your own.Read the guide →

For lawyers

Is your profile here? Claim it for free

Add your practice areas, a photo and a short biography, or correct a detail. An editor checks your bar admission before anything goes live, and listing is free.

Submit your profile

Update or remove a listing

Questions about this directory

How do lawyers get into this directory?

We start from public bar registration records and list lawyers whose registered firm is an injury law firm. Lawyers can also submit a profile, which an editor checks against the bar record before it is published.

Do lawyers pay to be listed or to rank higher?

No. Listings are free, and results are sorted by name or admission year, never by payment.

Is a listing a recommendation?

No. A listing is not a referral, a recommendation or a rating of a lawyer’s work. Use a profile as a starting point, read the reviews where they were posted and meet more than one lawyer before you hire.

Why don’t all profiles show a photo or reviews?

We publish a photo only when the lawyer sends one. We link to reviews on Google and other sites rather than copy them, so you can read every review in full where it was posted.

How do I check that a lawyer is licensed?

Every profile links to the lawyer’s bar record. For New York, you can also search the courts’ official attorney directory. Check before you sign anything.

How do I fix or remove a listing?

Use the update form. Tell us what to change and how to confirm you are the lawyer, and an editor will review it.

The registry records each lawyer’s firm and admission, not their practice areas, so practice areas appear only once a lawyer adds them.

Lawyers do not pay to appear, and a listing is not a referral, a recommendation or a rating. Always confirm a lawyer’s license with the state bar before you hire them.

Are you a lawyer?

Add your profile with your practice areas and a short biography, or correct or remove an existing listing. An editor reviews every change before it goes live.

Browse by type of case

Start with what happened. Each link opens the directory filtered to lawyers whose firms say they handle that kind of case.

  • Car accidentsCrashes, no-fault and injury claims
  • Truck accidentsCommercial trucks and higher policy limits
  • Motorcycle accidentsRider injuries, often the most serious
  • Slip and fallInjuries on someone else’s property
  • Medical malpracticeErrors by doctors, hospitals and clinics
  • Wrongful deathClaims by a family after a fatal accident
  • Workers’ compensationInjured on the job

Every lawyer listed so far is admitted to the New York bar. Most practice in New York, and some also run offices in other states. More state bars are being added.

How every profile is built

Three sources, in this order, and nothing we can’t point you to.

Step 1

Start from the official record

Name, firm, admission year and registration status come from the state’s public attorney registration data, and each profile links to that record.

Step 2

Add the firm’s own details

The website, office address, phone and the cases the firm handles come from the firm’s own website, with the month we checked it.

Step 3

Link to reviews, never copy them

We link to the firm’s reviews on Google and other sites so you read them where they were posted. Lawyers can correct or remove a listing at any time.

A listing is not a referral, a recommendation or a rating of a lawyer’s work. Lawyers do not pay to appear. Read our editorial policy.

For lawyers

Is your profile here? Claim it for free

Add your practice areas, a photo and a short biography, or correct a detail. An editor checks your bar admission before anything goes live, and listing is free.

Submit your profile

Update or remove a listing

Questions about this directory

How do lawyers get into this directory?

We start from public bar registration records and list lawyers whose registered firm is an injury law firm. Lawyers can also submit a profile, which an editor checks against the bar record before it is published.

Do lawyers pay to be listed or to rank higher?

No. Listings are free, and results are sorted by name or admission year, never by payment.

Is a listing a recommendation?

No. A listing is not a referral, a recommendation or a rating of a lawyer’s work. Use a profile as a starting point, read the reviews where they were posted and meet more than one lawyer before you hire.

Why don’t all profiles show a photo or reviews?

We publish a photo only when the lawyer sends one. We link to reviews on Google and other sites rather than copy them, so you can read every review in full where it was posted.

How do I check that a lawyer is licensed?

Every profile links to the lawyer’s bar record. For New York, you can also search the courts’ official attorney directory. Check before you sign anything.

How do I fix or remove a listing?

Use the update form. Tell us what to change and how to confirm you are the lawyer, and an editor will review it.

Tom Schimmerling is the founder of Schimmerling Injury Law, a personal injury firm in New York’s Southern Tier with offices in Endicott, Binghamton and Delhi and in Montrose, Pennsylvania. Tom is also a member of the Pennsylvania and Florida bars, a founding member of the National Academy of Motorcycle Injury Lawyers and a former section chair of the American Association for Justice.

Kenneth opened the practice on August 1, 1999, and the firm’s bio lists Social Security disability, veterans disability, VA malpractice, workers’ compensation and consumer protection cases as Kenneth’s focus.

John H. Fisher is the founder of The New York Injury & Malpractice Law Firm, with offices in Kingston and Riverdale in the Bronx. The firm’s bio says John’s practice has been limited to catastrophic injury cases for injury victims in New York State for the last 20 years, with a focus on medical malpractice, including birth injuries, delayed cancer diagnosis and surgical errors.

John earned a J.D. from Notre Dame Law School in 1991 and a B.A. in government from the University of Notre Dame, and is admitted in Connecticut (1991), New York (1992) and Illinois (1993) and in the Northern, Southern and Western Districts of New York. Slavko Ristich is the managing partner of Ristich Law, a personal injury firm in Toronto’s Etobicoke area. The firm’s bio says Slavko began practising in 2001 as a trial lawyer in New York City, tried many jury cases there and argued appeals on New York’s threshold law, wrongful imprisonment and constitutional torts.

Why lawyers write for ClaimValuator

ClaimValuator is a free legal resource for people working through injury claims, insurance disputes and court deadlines. We publish settlement calculators for all 50 states and DC, state-by-state law tables and plain-English guides. A guest post puts your expertise, and your firm, in front of readers who are researching a legal problem right now.

posts.title: Hegseth Impeachment: Massie’s 8 Articles, the Delayed House Vote and What Happens Next
posts.excerpt: Rep. Thomas Massie filed eight articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Sept. 15, 2026. Here is what each article alleges, why the House vote was put off until after the election, and what can happen next.
posts.content:
Key points

  • On Sept. 15, 2026, Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) read a 34-page resolution with eight articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on the House floor.
  • Three articles accuse Hegseth of breaking the War Powers Resolution in the Iran war. The others cite civilian deaths, the boat strikes, the Sen. Mark Kelly case, the capture of Nicolás Maduro and the 2025 Yemen strikes.
  • The House left town on Sept. 16 before the required vote. Speaker Mike Johnson says the resolution “will immediately be tabled” when members return on Nov. 9.
  • Impeachment takes a simple House majority. Removal takes a two-thirds vote in the Senate. Only two cabinet secretaries have ever been impeached, and neither was removed.
  • The articles are Massie’s allegations, not findings. The Pentagon calls Hegseth “a transformative leader.”

Rep. Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican, has filed articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. He read all 34 pages on the House floor on Sept. 15, 2026, in a speech that ran more than 67 minutes, according to ABC News. The resolution charges Hegseth with “high crimes and misdemeanors” in eight articles, most of them tied to the war with Iran.

Massie filed it as a privileged resolution, which normally forces a House vote within two legislative days. That vote never happened. The next day, House leaders canceled the rest of the pre-election session, and the House is not due back until Nov. 9.

This guide explains what each article alleges, the law behind the charges, how impeachment of a cabinet secretary works, what history says about the odds, and the four ways this can end. It is current as of Oct. 22, 2026.

What happened: the filing and the delayed vote

Massie took the floor on Sept. 15 and read the full resolution aloud. Asked why he was doing it, he said “there needs to be a marker in history.” He also explained the timing: “Speaker Johnson has basically canceled the rest of Congress until the elections,” he said, according to ABC News.

Because the resolution was privileged, House rules required leaders to bring it up within two legislative days, by Thursday, Sept. 17. Instead, House leaders canceled that Thursday’s votes and sent members home for the campaign. Stars and Stripes reported that the House is scheduled to return on Nov. 9.

Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) called the effort a “publicity stunt by someone who wants attention.” He said: “It will immediately be tabled, of course. But we probably won’t do that today. We will do it when we come back.” He added that “Secretary Hegseth has done an extraordinary job at the Department of War.”

Massie said a vote would have been “real easy.” He argued that a vote to table would “insulate the members of this body from any accountability.”

The Pentagon defended Hegseth. Press secretary Kingsley Wilson said “Secretary Hegseth has been a transformative leader for the Department of War” and that the “entire Department is unified behind the Secretary’s vision.”

What has happened since

  • Sept. 17: Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), who voted to confirm Hegseth in 2025, said, “I’ll let the House do what the House is gonna do,” but added that Hegseth “needs to go, whether it’s impeachment or the most expedient route — just the president to replace him,” Mediaite reported.
  • Oct. 15: Massie posted that “Trump should fire Hegseth to avoid Hegseth’s impeachment. It’s the honorable thing to do,” and said he will bring the articles back in the lame-duck session after the election, The Hill reported.
  • Oct. 20: Punchbowl News reported that a growing number of House members are ready to move forward with impeachment, and that House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has made “accountability for Hegseth” part of the Democrats’ post-election agenda, according to Raw Story.

Two facts shape the politics. Massie lost his May 2026 primary to Trump-backed challenger Ed Gallrein, Spectrum News reported, so his term ends in January. And on the same day he filed the articles, the House passed an Iran war powers resolution with seven Republican votes, Colorado Politics reported. Massie is the only Republican publicly backing impeachment so far.

The eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth

The table below summarizes each article as the resolution states it. These are allegations. None has been tested in a hearing or a trial, and the administration disputes the premise that the operations were unlawful.

News outlets summarized the same list. ABC News described articles on ignoring civilian-casualty laws, an “unlawful war” in Yemen, extrajudicial killings, suppressing free speech and “kidnapping a sovereign leader.” TIME and Stars and Stripes reported the same core charges.

posts.excerpt: Rep. Thomas Massie filed eight articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over the Iran war and more. What they allege, what his defenders say, and what happens when the House returns.

seo.description: Rep. Massie filed 8 articles of impeachment against Pete Hegseth over the Iran war and boat strikes. What they allege, both sides, and the vote ahead.
seo.focus: hegseth impeachment,massie hegseth impeachment,articles of impeachment against hegseth,hegseth impeachment vote,war powers resolution

posts.content:
Key points

  • On September 15, 2026, Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) filed eight articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and read them aloud on the House floor.
  • Three articles accuse Hegseth of breaking the War Powers Resolution in the Iran war. The others cover civilian casualties, the Caribbean boat strikes, Sen. Mark Kelly, the Maduro raid and strikes in Yemen.
  • Massie filed the resolution as privileged, which normally forces action within two legislative days, but the House left early for the midterm recess. It returns November 9.
  • Speaker Mike Johnson calls the effort “a stunt” and says it will be tabled. The Pentagon and the White House say Hegseth has done “a phenomenal job.”

Republican Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky has moved to impeach a Cabinet secretary serving a president of his own party. His target is Pete Hegseth, who has led the Pentagon through the 2026 war with Iran. The resolution charges Hegseth with “high crimes and misdemeanors” on eight counts, most of them built on the 1973 War Powers Resolution.

A vote was supposed to come within days. Instead, House leaders sent members home early to campaign, and the fight now lands in the lame-duck session that begins after the November 3 election. This guide explains what each article alleges, the law behind it, what Hegseth’s defenders say, how impeaching a Cabinet officer actually works, and what can happen next. It is current as of October 22, 2026.

Hegseth impeachment at a glance

What the eight articles of impeachment allege

Massie’s office published the full 34-page text and a summary of each article. The table below follows that official summary; the full resolution adds the detailed findings.

“Secretary Hegseth is breaking the law and must be held accountable,” Massie said when he filed. On the floor he said Hegseth “has demonstrated that he will remain a threat to the Constitution, if allowed to remain in office,” and that the conduct warrants “impeachment and trial, removal from office and disqualification.”

The Iran war and the War Powers Resolution (Articles I to III)

The heart of the case is the Iran war. U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran began on February 28, 2026, under the U.S. name Operation Epic Fury, without a vote in Congress. A ceasefire began in early April, a memorandum to end the war was signed on June 17, and the truce collapsed on July 8 after Iranian attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, according to Wikipedia’s timeline of the war.

The War Powers Resolution, passed over President Nixon’s veto in 1973, sets the rules Massie says were broken. The Congressional Research Service summarizes its three key parts:

  • Section 2(c) lists when the president may send forces into hostilities: a declaration of war, specific statutory authorization, or a national emergency created by an attack on the United States.
  • Section 4 requires the president to report to Congress within 48 hours of introducing forces into hostilities.
  • Section 5(b) requires the president to end the use of forces after 60 days unless Congress authorizes it, with up to 30 more days to withdraw safely (50 U.S.C. § 1544).
  • Section 5(c) lets Congress direct the removal of forces by concurrent resolution.

The 60-day clock ran out on May 1. That day the White House told Congress that “the hostilities that began on February 28, 2026, have terminated,” arguing the April ceasefire stopped the clock. Hegseth said, “We are in a ceasefire right now, which our understanding means, the 60-day clock pauses or stops.” President Trump added that “every other president considered it totally unconstitutional, and we agree with that,” PBS NewsHour reported. Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) answered that “there’s no pause button in the Constitution, or the War Powers Act.”

In June, Congress passed H. Con. Res. 86 directing the president to remove forces from hostilities with Iran. The Senate vote on June 23 was 50 to 48, with Republicans Bill Cassidy, Susan Collins, Rand Paul and Lisa Murkowski joining Democrats. Because it was a concurrent resolution, it was never sent to the president and is not legally binding, NPR reported. The Supreme Court’s 1983 decision in INS v. Chadha cast doubt on such “legislative vetoes,” which is why Congress now usually uses joint resolutions instead. On the day Massie filed, the House also passed a separate Iran war powers resolution, 220 to 204, with seven Republicans, Massie among them, voting yes.

Articles I to III turn that record into charges: the war lacked authority from the start, it continued after Congress directed withdrawal, and it ran past the statutory deadline. Hegseth’s defenders answer that presidents of both parties have treated the War Powers Resolution as unconstitutional, that the ceasefire ended the hostilities that started the clock, and that a concurrent resolution cannot bind the executive.

Civilian casualties and the Minab school strike (Article IV)

Article IV accuses Hegseth of disregarding laws meant to minimize civilian casualties. The incident most often cited by critics is the strike on the Shajareh Tayyebeh Elementary School in Minab, in southern Iran, on the first day of the war. Iranian officials put the death toll at 156, most of them children. Independent investigators identified a U.S. Tomahawk missile, and a UN fact-finding mission said in September that it had reasonable grounds to believe the United States carried out the strike, according to Wikipedia’s summary of the investigations and NBC News reporting on the strike.

In March, Hegseth said the United States was investigating and would “never target civilian targets.” President Trump first blamed Iran and later said “mistakes are made” and “nobody did that on purpose.” As of late September, the Pentagon’s internal investigation had not been released.

The Caribbean boat strikes (Article V)

Since September 2025, U.S. forces have struck vessels the administration says were smuggling drugs. Article V says those strikes replaced maritime law enforcement with “unauthorized lethal targeting,” killed at least 221 people, and included strikes on survivors and a failure to rescue the shipwrecked.

The most disputed strike came on September 2, 2025, when a follow-on attack killed two men clinging to the wreckage of a burning boat. The Washington Post reported that Hegseth had given a verbal directive to “kill everybody.” Hegseth called that report “fabricated” and said he was “not in the room” when the follow-on strike was launched; the White House confirmed he authorized Adm. Frank “Mitch” Bradley to conduct the strikes, States Newsroom reported.

The administration’s legal position is that the United States is in a “non-international armed conflict” with drug cartels it has designated as terrorist organizations, and that the people killed are “unlawful combatants.” Hegseth said the military has “the absolute and complete authority to conduct that.” Critics, including former State Department lawyer Brian Finucane, said the theory is “not supported by the facts,” CBS News reported.

Sen. Mark Kelly, Venezuela and Yemen (Articles VI to VIII)

Sen. Mark Kelly. In November 2025, Kelly and five other Democratic lawmakers released a video urging troops to refuse unlawful orders. Hegseth issued Kelly, a retired Navy captain, a censure letter on January 5, 2026, as a step toward possibly reducing his retired rank and pay. On February 12, U.S. District Judge Richard Leon temporarily blocked the Pentagon, finding it had violated Kelly’s First Amendment rights. Responding to the government’s argument, he wrote: “Horsefeathers!” (PBS NewsHour). Article VI calls the censure retaliation for protected speech.

Venezuela. On January 3, 2026, U.S. forces captured Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, in Caracas in Operation Absolute Resolve, involving about 150 aircraft. They were flown to New York to face narco-terrorism and cocaine importation charges. The administration framed the raid as support for a law enforcement arrest, and Sen. Mike Lee said it “likely falls within” the president’s Article II power. Massie criticized it at the time, USNI News reported. Article VII calls it the “kidnapping of a sovereign foreign leader.”

Yemen. Article VIII charges that Operation Rough Rider, the U.S. air campaign against Houthi forces in Yemen, began without congressional authorization or an imminent threat, broke war powers reporting rules and caused civilian deaths.

What Hegseth’s defenders say

House Republican leaders oppose the resolution, and the administration has defended Hegseth:

  • Speaker Mike Johnson called the resolution “a publicity stunt by someone who wants attention,” said it “will immediately be tabled,” and warned, “We should not be playing games with national security” (NBC). He called Massie’s effort “a stunt” and said Hegseth “has done an extraordinary job” (Newsweek).
  • Attorney General Todd Blanche said at a White House briefing that “Secretary Hegseth is doing a phenomenal job, and the secretary of war doesn’t just go off and do things,” adding that “he follows the law” (WJLA, Scripps News).
  • The Pentagon, through press secretary Kingsley Wilson, called Hegseth a “transformative leader” who “has slashed bureaucracy, unleashed innovation, and delivered for our warfighters every step of the way” (Semafor).
  • On the law, across these episodes the administration and its allies have argued that the president has inherent Article II power to use force, that the War Powers Resolution’s deadlines are unconstitutional, that the April ceasefire ended the hostilities at issue, that the boat strikes are lawful acts in an armed conflict with designated terrorist cartels, and that the Maduro operation supported a lawful arrest.

Blanche’s remark points to a structural defense: most of the conduct in the articles carried out decisions made by the president, and defenders say a Cabinet secretary should not be impeached for executing the commander in chief’s policies. Supporters of impeachment answer that war powers limits and the law of armed conflict bind every official in the chain of command, not only the president.

How impeaching a Cabinet secretary works

The Constitution says “all civil Officers of the United States” can be removed on impeachment for, and conviction of, “Treason, Bribery, or other high Crimes and Misdemeanors” (Article II, Section 4). A Cabinet secretary is a civil officer. The process has three stages:

  1. The House impeaches. Any member can offer an impeachment resolution as a question of privilege under House Rule IX. Leadership must then schedule it within two legislative days. The House can adopt it, refer it to the Judiciary Committee, or kill it with a motion to table. Each takes a simple majority.
  2. The Senate tries the case. Conviction requires “the Concurrence of two thirds of the Members present” (Article I, Section 3). With all 100 senators present, that is 67 votes.
  3. The penalty is limited. Judgment “shall not extend further than to removal from Office, and disqualification” from future federal office. By Senate practice, disqualification takes a separate majority vote. Criminal prosecution is a separate matter for the courts.

Only two Cabinet secretaries have ever been impeached. War Secretary William Belknap was impeached in 1876 after he had already resigned, and the Senate acquitted him. Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas was impeached on February 13, 2024, by a vote of 214 to 213 (Axios), and the Senate dismissed both articles without a trial on April 17, 2024 (Boston Globe). No Cabinet secretary has ever been convicted.

What makes Massie’s move unusual is party. Republicans did not want him to become the first member of Congress to try to impeach a Cabinet member of his own party, Scripps News reported.

Why the House vote was delayed

The timing was a surprise. Massie told reporters, “I didn’t give anybody heads-up.” He filed on the same day the House voted to table a separate resolution from Rep. Al Green (D-Texas) to impeach President Trump. Because Massie’s resolution was privileged, it set up a vote by Thursday, September 17. Instead, House leaders canceled Thursday’s votes and sent members home on September 16 for a seven-week campaign recess, pushing the vote past Election Day (NBC).

Johnson denied any link, saying, “It’s time for our members to go home to their districts and make the case to the American people.” Reporting at the time said leaders wanted to spare vulnerable Republicans a hard vote during an unpopular war. Massie, who lost his May primary to Trump-backed challenger Ed Gallrein, will serve the rest of his term as a lame duck.

On October 15, Massie raised the pressure again on X: “Trump should fire Hegseth to avoid Hegseth’s impeachment. It’s the honorable thing to do,” Benzinga reported. He has said he will press the impeachment when the House returns, whatever the election results. Democrats have moved closer to the effort: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries says Hegseth should be fired, and Rep. Adam Smith (D-Wash.), the top Democrat on the Armed Services Committee, has signaled he could back Massie’s measure, while some Democrats are wary of voting on articles drafted by a Republican before any investigation, Semafor reported.

What happens next

The House is scheduled to return on November 9. From there, there are four realistic paths:

  • A motion to table passes. This is Johnson’s stated plan. It ends this resolution with a simple majority, though Massie or another member could file again.
  • The resolution is referred to the Judiciary Committee. Referral avoids a direct vote. The committee need not act, and unfinished resolutions expire when the 119th Congress ends on January 3, 2027.
  • The House impeaches. That needs a majority. The case would then go to the Senate, where conviction needs two-thirds, a bar no Cabinet impeachment has ever cleared.
  • Hegseth leaves office. A resignation or firing would likely end the push, although the Belknap case shows the House can impeach an official who has already resigned, mainly to seek disqualification.

Watch three things in the lame-duck session: whether Republicans who voted for the Iran war powers resolution also vote against tabling, how many Democrats vote yes on a Republican-written resolution, and whether the Pentagon releases its Minab investigation before the vote.

Earlier impeachment resolutions against Hegseth

Massie’s is the third attempt in the 119th Congress. Rep. Shri Thanedar (D-Mich.) introduced H. Res. 935 on December 9, 2025, after the boat strike reports, and Rep. Yassamin Ansari (D-Ariz.) introduced H. Res. 1177 on April 15, 2026, during the Iran war. Both were referred to the Judiciary Committee and never reached a floor vote. Some coverage has attached the number H. Res. 1177 to Massie’s filing, but that number belongs to Ansari’s April resolution.

Frequently asked questions

What are the articles of impeachment against Hegseth?

Massie’s eight articles accuse Hegseth of waging the Iran war without legal authority, continuing it after Congress directed withdrawal and past the 60-day War Powers deadline, disregarding civilian-harm laws, ordering unlawful lethal strikes on drug boats, retaliating against Sen. Mark Kelly, seizing Nicolás Maduro without authority, and launching strikes in Yemen without authorization.

Did the House vote on Hegseth’s impeachment?

Not yet. Massie filed on September 15, 2026, but House leaders recessed the next day, before the vote the privileged resolution would have required. The House returns on November 9.

Yes. The Constitution allows the impeachment of “all civil Officers of the United States,” which includes Cabinet secretaries. The House impeaches by majority vote and the Senate convicts by a two-thirds vote.

Massie, a longtime critic of unauthorized wars, says Hegseth broke the War Powers Resolution and other laws. He voted for the Iran war powers resolution and says Congress “must not turn a blind eye” to what he calls unconstitutional actions.

What happens if the House impeaches Hegseth?

The Senate would hold a trial. Removal requires two-thirds of senators present. If convicted, the Senate could also vote by majority to bar him from future federal office.

Has a Cabinet secretary ever been removed by impeachment?

No. William Belknap was acquitted in 1876, and the Senate dismissed the articles against Alejandro Mayorkas in 2024. No Cabinet secretary has been convicted.

H. Res. 1177 is Rep. Yassamin Ansari’s April 2026 impeachment resolution against Hegseth, not Massie’s September resolution.

posts.content:
Key points

  • Judge Christopher Cooper has twice blocked efforts to put President Trump’s name on the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts: the December 2025 renaming (ruling of May 29, 2026) and the August 2026 inscriptions and “Trump Plaza” plan (ruling of September 15, 2026).
  • Both rulings rest on the Center’s founding law, which makes it “a living memorial to John Fitzgerald Kennedy” and bars new memorials in its public areas without Congress.
  • Hours after the September ruling, the board voted to close the main building. Trump said repairs would not happen without his name and that the building could be “ripped down.”
  • The court now requires 30 days’ notice before any major physical change, including demolition. The main building remains closed, and appeals are pending.

The Kennedy Center has become the setting for one of the strangest legal fights of 2026. A board appointed by President Trump renamed the national performing arts center after him, a federal judge ordered the name removed, the board tried again with inscriptions and a “President Donald J. Trump Plaza,” the judge blocked that too, and the building is now closed while lawyers argue over whether it could be torn down.

This guide sets out what the court decided, the 1964 law that decides most of the questions, what each side argues, how the demolition threat arose, and what to watch next. It is current as of October 22, 2026.

The Kennedy Center case at a glance

How the fight unfolded: a timeline

What the law says about the Kennedy Center’s name

Most of the case turns on a short federal statute. In 1964, two months after President Kennedy’s assassination, Congress renamed the planned National Cultural Center the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts (Public Law 88-260). The building opened in 1971. Four provisions of that law matter here:

  • It is a memorial by law. The board must maintain and administer the Center “as the National Center for the Performing Arts, a living memorial to John Fitzgerald Kennedy” (20 U.S.C. § 76h(a)(1)).
  • Congress set the name. Section 76i designates the institution as the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, and lets the board acknowledge private contributions only “in the interior” of the project, Beatty’s lawyers point out (Beatty’s August 2026 brief).
  • No new memorials. The board must ensure that “no additional memorials or plaques in the nature of memorials shall be designated or installed in the public areas” of the Center (20 U.S.C. § 76j(b)(1)).
  • Narrow exceptions. The ban does not cover plaques for gifts from foreign countries, plaques on donated theater chairs or boxes, or certain gallery inscriptions acknowledging a major contribution, as long as board policy permitted them on December 2, 1983.

The statute also makes the House and Senate leaders and several other members of Congress members of the board. That is why Beatty, a Democratic House member, sits on it and could bring the suit.

Ruling one: the Trump name has to come off (May 29, 2026)

In a 94-page decision, Judge Cooper held that the Center’s founding statute makes its name “crystal clear” and that the board cannot add another formal name or memorial on its own. Congress gave the Center its name, he wrote, and only Congress can change it. He gave the Center 14 days to stop using “Trump Kennedy Center” and similar names on signs and online, restored Beatty’s voting rights on the board, and temporarily blocked the two-year closure, calling the plan “murky” and finding the board had too little information when it voted (NPR).

The Kennedy Center’s spokesperson said it would appeal, noting that the building needs major restoration and that $257 million secured by Trump and approved by Congress was in place. Trump attacked the judge on Truth Social. Beatty said the Center “belongs to the American people, not to Donald Trump.”

On July 8, a D.C. Circuit panel of Judges Gregory Katsas, Patricia Millett and Robert Wilkins refused to pause the ruling while the appeal goes forward. The administration had argued that removing the name would hurt fundraising, but the court said it “failed to support this assertion with any specific facts or evidence” (Denver Gazette).

Ruling two: no inscriptions and no “Trump Plaza” (September 15, 2026)

In August, the board tried a different route. Its “recognition resolution” would have added three things:

  • An inscription beneath the Center’s name: “Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump”
  • A second line, “Endowed by The Trump Kennedy Center Fund,” once the fund reached $100 million
  • A new name for the surrounding grounds: “President Donald J. Trump Plaza”

Beatty asked for emergency relief, arguing that the plan was a renaming in another form and an unlawful memorial under section 76j, that exterior donor recognition is barred, and that the trustees were breaching their fiduciary duties (Beatty’s brief). The Justice Department answered that “an order blocking the Board from appropriately recognizing President Trump will cause donors to flee.”

Cooper sided with Beatty. The board “cannot install memorials for President Donald J. Trump, or anyone else who is not former President John F. Kennedy,” without Congress (JURIST). He also required notice before any future Trump-related inscription or acknowledgment.

The closure and the demolition threat

The idea of tearing the building down first appeared in court papers. In an August 25 filing, Justice Department lawyer Brantley Mayers called the Center “decrepit” and in an imminent “death spiral,” and said that without the administration’s plan it “will be required to be taken down.” The filing floated a cheaper replacement, an outdoor amphitheater overlooking the Potomac, while conceding it would “fail to adequately honor” Kennedy (ABC News, The Star).

The threat grew after the September ruling. The board voted on September 15 to close the main building, and Trump said repairs would happen only if the board could add his name. The next day, executive director Matt Floca shut the building without notice, citing “acute risks to public safety resulting from continued structural deterioration.” Trump said that without his plan, “it’s going to close. It’ll end up being ripped down,” adding, “It’s in very, very bad shape, very dangerous shape” (AP).

Beatty’s lawyers called the closure a “plain pretext to justify shutting down the Center permanently.” Cooper did not hold an emergency hearing, but on September 17 he ordered the Center to give 30 days’ notice before any major physical change, including demolition, to “avoid any confusion on that score given more recent events” (AP). Protesters formed a human chain around the building the next day.

The building’s problems are real. Engineers from Walter P Moore found significant corrosion and water damage on most of the exterior soffit panels, each weighing more than 2,000 pounds and hanging 60 feet above areas the public uses, and called for “immediate” repairs because of a falling object hazard (NBC Washington). In an interview with TIME, Trump declined to promise he would not demolish the building without Congress: “I’m not committing to anything” (ABC News).

Can a president tear down the Kennedy Center?

No court has ruled on whether demolition would be lawful, and no formal demolition plan has been filed. The legal framework looks like this:

  • The statute assigns a duty to maintain. The board must maintain and administer the Center as a living memorial to Kennedy. Critics argue demolition cannot be squared with that duty without new legislation. The administration argues the building’s condition leaves no responsible alternative if its plan is blocked.
  • Congress holds the money. The roughly $257 million for repairs came from Congress, and Congress controls any future appropriation for a replacement.
  • The court has set a tripwire. The 30-day notice order gives Beatty time to seek emergency relief before any major physical work begins.
  • Congress can change the rules. Lawmakers could rename the Center, authorize the Trump recognition, or pass the Kennedy Center Protection Act. None of those has happened.

What each side argues

The administration and the board say the building is in crisis and only this administration can save it. Its filings call the Center “structurally unsound, fundamentally unsafe, and embarrassing to the nation’s capital” and say “the crisis is so acute that, without the Trump Administration, its people, and President Trump, the Center cannot survive.” They say donors expect recognition, that the plaintiff herself acknowledges the building needs major restoration, and that the closure is about safety, not the naming fight.

Beatty and her allies say Congress named the Center for Kennedy alone and barred new memorials, that the inscriptions are a renaming by another route, and that the closure is a pressure tactic. They point to the construction documents the board relied on: a five-slide presentation that, her lawyers say, did not “identify even a single benefit to remaining partially open while renovating,” and a 163-page plan with no cost-benefit analysis of closure (Newsweek). Sen. Mark Warner and Rep. Chellie Pingree have criticized the closure; Pingree said, “Closing the Kennedy Center was never about renovation.”

What happens next

  • Appeals. The D.C. Circuit will decide the administration’s appeal. Until an appeals court says otherwise, the district court’s orders stand.
  • Weekly updates. Cooper has asked for weekly reports on repairs and the closure. Floca says the closure is reconsidered week by week.
  • Document fights. Cooper ordered the board’s construction presentation released and the larger plan made public with narrow redactions. A separate dispute over the administration’s executive privilege claim continues.
  • Programming. No shows are scheduled in the main building’s theaters. The Kennedy Center Honors moved to Capital One Arena on October 2.
  • Congress. After the November 3 election, the lame-duck Congress and then the new Congress in January could legislate on the name or the building.

Frequently asked questions

Is the Kennedy Center closed?

Yes. The main building has been closed since mid-September 2026, while engineers assess safety. There is no reopening date. Free events continue in The REACH, a separate building on the campus.

Did a judge block Trump’s name on the Kennedy Center?

Yes, twice. On May 29, 2026, Judge Christopher Cooper ordered the “Trump Kennedy Center” name removed. On September 15, 2026, he blocked new inscriptions honoring Trump and the renaming of the grounds as “President Donald J. Trump Plaza.”

Can the Kennedy Center be renamed?

Only by Congress, according to the court. The 1964 law that named the Center for Kennedy also makes it a living memorial to him and bars new memorials in its public areas.

Is Trump going to demolish the Kennedy Center?

No demolition has been proposed in court. A Justice Department filing said the building may have to be taken down if the administration’s plan is blocked, and Trump said it could be “ripped down.” The court requires 30 days’ notice before any major physical change.

Who sued over the Kennedy Center name?

Rep. Joyce Beatty (D-Ohio), who sits on the Kennedy Center board because of her seat in Congress. The case is Beatty v. Trump, No. 25-cv-4480, in federal court in Washington.

How much will the Kennedy Center renovation cost?

Congress provided about $257 million for repairs. The board’s plan would close the main building for about two years.

Where were the 2026 Kennedy Center Honors held?

At Capital One Arena in Washington on October 2, 2026, because of the dispute and the closure.

posts.content:
Key points

  • On March 29, 2025, a Frederick County, Maryland sheriff’s deputy arrested YouTube journalist Levi Trumbull on suspicion of impaired driving after he declined field sobriety tests. A breath test at the station read 0.00.
  • No DUI charge was filed. Two traffic citations, for an alleged red light and not having his license with him, were dismissed on May 8, 2025, when the deputy did not appear in court.
  • We found no court filing for a Levi Trumbull lawsuit in news coverage or public reporting. Video descriptions say he filed a notice of intent to sue for $1 million, which is not the same thing.
  • In Maryland, sheriff’s deputies count as state personnel, so a state-law claim generally needs written notice to the State Treasurer within one year. A federal civil rights claim has a longer clock.

Search for “Levi Trumbull lawsuit” and you will find dozens of pages announcing a $1 million case, a settlement, or a deputy who “fabricated the law.” Most of them cite each other, not records. The story underneath is real, and it raises useful questions about DUI arrests, field sobriety tests and public records. But several of the viral claims do not hold up.

This guide separates what the records show from what has been claimed, explains the Maryland law behind each step, and sets out what a claim like this would actually involve. It is current as of October 22, 2026.

Viral claims vs. the record

Who is Levi Trumbull?

Levi Trumbull is a Maryland YouTube journalist who records his interactions with police and government officials, part of the “First Amendment auditor” community. Radio Free Hub City, a local Maryland news outlet, described him as a journalist and shared body camera footage of the arrest in April 2025, along with an opinion piece by its president arguing that the arrest was unjustified (Radio Free Hub City). Compilation channels later reposted the footage under titles like “Cop Falsely Arrests Sober YouTuber,” and the story spread again in 2026.

What happened on March 29, 2025

The account below comes from the Sheriff’s Office incident report, which Radio Free Hub City published, and from reporting on the body camera footage (LegalClarity summary, MotorBiscuit).

  • The stop. At about 9:40 p.m., Deputy First Class Christian Roush reported that a car slowed and then went through a solid red light on Route 355 at Lowes Lane in Frederick. The car pulled into a car dealership lot about a quarter mile later.
  • The deputy’s observations. The report says Trumbull’s hands and body were shaking, his eyes were bloodshot, he clenched his jaw and looked left and right without apparent reason. Trumbull told the deputy he was “stone cold sober” and had nothing to drink.
  • No license on hand. Trumbull gave his registration and confirmed his identity but did not have his physical driver’s license.
  • Field sobriety tests refused. Trumbull stepped out of the car but declined standardized field sobriety tests. “Why would I give you probable cause to take me in?” he asked, according to the footage.
  • The arrest. The report says Trumbull “again refused SFSTs and was placed under arrest.” MotorBiscuit quotes the deputy on the footage: “Even if you blow zeros, it doesn’t matter; your refusal for the test gives me probable cause.”
  • The breath test. At the station, after being advised of his rights, Trumbull agreed to a breath test, which read 0.00.
  • The drug evaluation. A drug recognition expert was called. The report says the expert could not make a determination after a brief encounter; Trumbull had invoked his right to remain silent.
  • Release. The deputy issued electronic citations for the traffic violations and released Trumbull. His car was towed because it was blocking the dealership’s driveway. A YouTube description says he paid more than $367 to get it back.

One detail stands out: the report’s header classifies the incident as “police information” and “closed, no arrest,” while its narrative describes an arrest. That kind of inconsistency is exactly what a civil claim or a records request would probe.

What happened in court

No DUI or drug-impaired driving charge was ever filed. Trumbull contested the two traffic citations, one for the red light and one for failing to have his license, at a hearing on May 8, 2025. The deputy did not appear, and the judge dismissed both citations, according to Radio Free Hub City’s report of the hearing as summarized by LegalClarity and MotorBiscuit. Reports did not say why the deputy was absent.

A dismissal for a missing witness is not a finding that the stop was unlawful. It means the state could not prove the citations that day. That distinction matters for any later civil claim, which would have to prove the arrest itself lacked probable cause.

Is there a Levi Trumbull lawsuit?

As of October 22, 2026, we found no news report, court record or docket number showing a filed civil lawsuit. Here is how the claim has evolved:

  • As late as mid-2026, several sites covering the case said no lawsuit had been filed.
  • A February 24, 2026 compilation video, “$1 MILLION Lawsuit: YouTuber Arrested After 0.00 Breathalyzer,” says in its description that Trumbull “has officially filed an intent to sue” the Frederick County Sheriff’s Office for $1 million, alleging wrongful arrest and Fourth Amendment violations (YouTube).
  • A September 2026 MotorBiscuit article, syndicated by Yahoo, described both an “intent to sue” and a “pending $1 million civil lawsuit,” without citing a court filing (MotorBiscuit).

An intent to sue is usually a written notice of claim, a required first step under Maryland law before suing the state. It is not a lawsuit, and a dollar figure in a notice is a demand, not a valuation. If a suit is filed, it will appear in the Maryland Judiciary Case Search (for state court) or on PACER (for federal court). Until then, any page announcing a verdict or settlement is guessing.

How a claim like this would work in Maryland

Someone in Trumbull’s position has two main routes, and they run on different clocks.

A state-law claim under the Maryland Tort Claims Act

Maryland treats county sheriffs and their deputies as state personnel for tort purposes, so claims over their official conduct generally fall under the Maryland Tort Claims Act rather than the county’s tort law (overview of the MTCA, overview of the local government act). Its key rules:

  • Notice first. A written claim must reach the State Treasurer within one year of the injury. For a March 29, 2025 arrest, that deadline was March 29, 2026.
  • A damages cap. The State’s liability is capped at $400,000 per claimant.
  • Individual immunity. State personnel acting within the scope of their jobs are generally immune from personal liability unless they acted with malice or gross negligence, which is where intentional-wrong claims like false imprisonment come in.

For a plain-English walkthrough of notice deadlines for claims against government bodies, see our guide to the notice of claim.

A federal civil rights claim under Section 1983

The federal civil rights statute, 42 U.S.C. § 1983, lets people sue state officers who violate their constitutional rights. A false arrest claim under the Fourth Amendment turns on one question: did the officer have probable cause to believe a crime was being committed when he made the arrest? Federal courts borrow the state’s personal injury limitations period, which in Maryland is three years, so the window for a March 2025 arrest generally runs into 2028. No notice of claim is required. The officer can raise qualified immunity, which shields officials unless they violated clearly established law. Check Maryland’s deadlines with our Maryland statute of limitations calculator.

Can you be arrested for DUI with a 0.00 BAC?

Yes. A 0.00 breath result rules out alcohol, but Maryland’s impaired driving law, Transportation Article § 21-902, also covers driving while impaired by drugs, including legal medications, or by a combination of drugs and alcohol (Maryland People’s Law Library). Breath machines do not detect drugs, which is why officers call in drug recognition experts. A sober driver can lawfully be arrested if the officer has probable cause at the moment of arrest, even if later tests come back clean.

What an officer cannot do is arrest without probable cause. Courts look at the totality of the circumstances: the driving, the driver’s appearance and speech, admissions, and test results available at the time. Here the deputy relied on an alleged red light, a delayed turn, physical signs like shaking and bloodshot eyes, and the refusal of field tests. Trumbull’s supporters argue that those signs are weak, that the cruiser’s flashing lights could explain red eyes, and that the footage shows no obvious intoxication. Whether that added up to probable cause is exactly what a court would decide.

Are field sobriety tests mandatory in Maryland?

No. Maryland’s implied consent law defines the “test” a driver is deemed to have consented to as a breath test or one blood specimen to measure alcohol, or a blood test for drugs (Transportation § 16-205.1). Roadside exercises like walking a line are not part of it, and declining them carries no automatic license penalty (Maryland DUI defense overview). That is why critics of the arrest focused on the deputy’s reported statement that refusing the test “gives me probable cause.” Refusal of field exercises can be part of the overall picture, but it is not a statutory test refusal.

Refusing the chemical test is different. A driver detained on suspicion of impaired driving who refuses a breath or blood test faces a license suspension of 270 days for a first refusal and two years for a second (§ 16-205.1). Trumbull took the breath test, so this rule did not come into play.

How to get police records in Maryland

Records are the backbone of any claim like this. Maryland’s Public Information Act gives anyone the right to request public records, including many police reports and body camera footage, subject to exceptions. The basics:

  • Ask in writing. Send a request to the agency’s records custodian describing the records, such as the incident report, citations, body and dash camera footage, and tow records, with the date, time and case number.
  • Know the deadline. The custodian must grant or deny the request promptly and within 30 days, and must tell you within 10 working days if production will take longer (General Provisions § 4-203).
  • Expect limited fees. Agencies may charge reasonable costs, but the first two hours of search and preparation are free, and fee waivers are available.
  • Appeal a denial. You can go to the Public Access Ombudsman for mediation, then the Public Information Act Compliance Board, or file in circuit court.
  • Misconduct records. Records of investigations into police misconduct can be requested, though the agency may redact or deny parts of them under § 4-351.

If you are arrested for DUI while sober: a checklist

  1. Stay calm and do not resist, even if you believe the arrest is wrong. Challenge it later, on paper.
  2. You may politely decline roadside exercises in Maryland, but do not refuse a breath or blood test you are lawfully asked to take at the station unless you accept the license consequences.
  3. Write down everything as soon as you can: times, locations, what was said and the names and badge numbers of officers.
  4. Request the records quickly, before retention periods run out: incident report, citations, body and dash camera video, test results and tow records.
  5. Attend every court date. A missing officer can mean a dismissal, but you must be there to get it.
  6. Track the deadlines: in Maryland, one year for a notice of claim against state personnel and generally three years for a lawsuit.
  7. Talk to a civil rights lawyer before sending any demand. You can search our lawyer directory to find attorneys by state.

Frequently asked questions

Is there a Levi Trumbull lawsuit?

Not one we could find. As of October 22, 2026, no news report or public court record we reviewed shows a filed lawsuit. Video descriptions say he filed a notice of intent to sue for $1 million, which is a pre-suit step, not a lawsuit.

Did Levi Trumbull win his case?

He won dismissal of two traffic citations on May 8, 2025, after the deputy failed to appear. No DUI charge was ever filed. There is no known civil judgment or settlement.

What was Levi Trumbull’s BAC?

His breath test at the station read 0.00, and a drug recognition expert could not determine impairment.

Who arrested Levi Trumbull?

Deputy First Class Christian Roush of the Frederick County Sheriff’s Office, according to the incident report.

Can you be arrested for DUI with a 0.00 BAC in Maryland?

Yes, if the officer has probable cause to believe you are impaired by drugs or a combination of substances. A clean breath test does not rule out drug impairment, but every arrest still needs probable cause.

Do you have to do field sobriety tests in Maryland?

No. They are voluntary and refusing them carries no automatic license penalty. Refusing a breath or blood test under the implied consent law does carry a suspension.

How long do you have to sue for false arrest in Maryland?

Generally three years for a federal civil rights claim and a state lawsuit, but a state-law claim against state personnel, including sheriff’s deputies, requires written notice to the State Treasurer within one year.

  • LegalClarity: the 0.00 BAC arrest and dismissed citations, summarizing Radio Free Hub City’s reports (July 2026)
  • MotorBiscuit: body camera account and $1 million claim (Sept. 8, 2026)
  • YouTube: “$1 MILLION Lawsuit: YouTuber Arrested After 0.00 Breathalyzer” (Feb. 24, 2026)
  • Maryland Transportation Article § 16-205.1 (implied consent)

• The stop. At about 9:40 p.m., Deputy First Class Christian Roush reported that a car slowed and then went through a solid red light on Route 355 at Lowes Lane in Frederick. The car pulled into a car dealership lot about a quarter mile later.

seo.title: How to Choose the Best Personal Injury Lawyer in 2026
seo.description: How to pick a personal injury lawyer: when you need one, contingency fees and costs explained, questions to ask, red flags, and how to switch lawyers.
seo.focus: personal injury lawyer,best personal injury lawyer,how to choose a personal injury lawyer,best personal injury law firm,contingency personal injury lawyer

posts.content:
Key points

  • Most personal injury lawyers work on contingency: no fee unless they recover money, usually about one-third of a settlement and often 40% once a lawsuit is filed.
  • The fee agreement must be in writing and signed by you, and it must say whether case costs come out before or after the lawyer’s percentage (ABA Model Rule 1.5(c)).
  • Pick a lawyer who handles your type of injury, has trial experience, and will personally work on your file. Check their license and discipline history with the state bar.
  • You can fire your lawyer and hire another. You normally do not pay two full fees; the first lawyer is paid from the second lawyer’s fee or for the work already done.
  • A lawyer is worth the most when injuries are serious, fault is disputed, or the at-fault party’s insurance may not cover your losses.

Choosing a personal injury lawyer is one of the few decisions in an injury claim that is fully in your control. The right lawyer can change how an insurer values your claim. The wrong one can leave you waiting months for calls to be returned. Ads with phrases like “best personal injury lawyer” tell you very little, because almost every firm uses them.

This guide explains when you actually need an injury lawyer, how contingency fees work, what to check before you sign, the questions to ask in a free consultation, the red flags to walk away from, and what happens if you want to switch lawyers later.

Do you need a personal injury lawyer?

Not every injury claim needs a lawyer. A minor injury with clear fault, short treatment and small medical bills can often be settled directly with the insurer. You can test a first offer with our settlement offer calculator before deciding.

A lawyer usually adds the most value when:

  • Your injuries are serious or long-lasting, such as fractures, surgery, a brain injury or permanent scarring.
  • The other side disputes fault, or you may share some of the blame (see our comparative fault calculator).
  • The at-fault party’s policy limits may be too low to cover your losses.
  • The defendant is a business, a trucking company, a property owner or a government agency, which often brings shorter notice deadlines.
  • You missed work for a long time, or your future earnings are affected.
  • An adjuster is pushing for a recorded statement, a quick release or access to your full medical history.

Representation is now common. The Insurance Research Council, an insurer-funded research group, found that the share of auto injury claimants with a lawyer rose from 40% in 2017 to nearly 50% in 2022 (IRC, July 2026). The same study found that represented bodily injury claims took a median of nearly 440 days to close, more than double the time for unrepresented claims. After medical bills and legal fees, represented claimants kept $1.40 per dollar of medical bills, compared with $1.80 for people without a lawyer.

Read those numbers with care. Represented claims tend to involve more serious injuries, disputed fault and litigation, so the two groups are not directly comparable. The fair takeaway is that a lawyer is not automatically worth it for a small, simple claim, and is usually worth it when the stakes and the obstacles are high.

How personal injury lawyers get paid

Almost all injury lawyers work on a contingency fee. You pay nothing up front. The lawyer takes an agreed percentage of whatever is recovered, and nothing if there is no recovery. A common structure is about 33% if the case settles before a lawsuit is filed and 40% if it goes into litigation, but percentages are negotiable and vary by state and firm.

What the written fee agreement must say

Under ABA Model Rule 1.5(c), which most states follow in some form, a contingent fee agreement must:

  • Be in writing and signed by the client.
  • State the percentage or percentages the lawyer gets if the case settles, goes to trial or is appealed.
  • List the litigation expenses that will be deducted, and say whether they are deducted before or after the percentage is calculated.
  • Disclose any expenses you must pay even if you win.

At the end of the case, the lawyer must give you a written closing statement showing the recovery, the fee, the expenses and how your share was calculated.

Costs before or after the fee: a worked example

Case costs, such as filing fees, medical records, expert witnesses and depositions, are separate from the fee. Whether they come off before or after the lawyer’s percentage changes what you take home. Here is a $90,000 settlement with $5,000 in costs and a one-third fee:

Your share can drop further if health insurers, Medicare or hospitals have liens on the settlement. Our attorney fee and net payout calculator runs these numbers for you, and our guide to medical liens explains how they are reduced.

Some states and claims cap the fee

A few rules limit how much an injury lawyer may charge:

  • Federal claims. For claims against the U.S. government under the Federal Tort Claims Act, fees are capped at 20% of an administrative settlement and 25% of a judgment or settlement after suit (28 U.S.C. § 2678).
  • Florida. The Florida Bar’s Rule 4-1.5(f)(4)(B) presumes a fee is excessive above 33⅓% of the first $1 million if the case resolves before the defendant answers, and above 40% of the first $1 million after that, with lower percentages for larger recoveries. Florida clients must also receive a signed statement of client’s rights (Rules Regulating The Florida Bar).
  • Medical malpractice. Several states use sliding scales for malpractice fees. Ask any lawyer which limits apply to your case.

How to choose a personal injury lawyer: 9 things to check

  • Focus. Look for a lawyer who handles your type of case every week: car crashes, trucking, medical malpractice, product liability or premises cases are different specialties.
  • Trial experience. Very few injury cases reach a verdict. Federal data on state courts found that only about 3% of tort cases were resolved by trial (Bureau of Justice Statistics). Insurers still track which lawyers will go to trial, and they price settlements accordingly. Ask how many cases the lawyer has tried.
  • A clean license. Search the lawyer on your state bar’s website to confirm they are licensed and to see any public discipline.
  • Who does the work. At high-volume firms, the lawyer you meet may hand your file to a case manager. Ask who will negotiate with the adjuster and who will appear in court.
  • Communication. Ask how often you will get updates and how quickly calls are returned. Slow communication is the most common complaint clients have about their lawyers.
  • Clear fees. Get the percentage, the cost policy and any referral arrangement in writing before you sign.
  • Resources. Serious cases need experts and medical testimony. Ask whether the firm can fund those costs while the case is pending.
  • Local knowledge. A lawyer who regularly appears in the county where your case would be filed knows the judges, juries and local defense firms.
  • Certification (optional). Some lawyers are board certified in civil trial advocacy by organizations such as the National Board of Trial Advocacy. It is a useful signal, not a requirement.

You can find candidates through your state bar’s lawyer referral service, recommendations from people you trust, and our Find an Expert directory. Meet two or three lawyers before you decide. Consultations are almost always free.

Questions to ask in the free consultation

  1. How many cases like mine have you handled in the past two years?
  2. What do you think my case is worth, and what could make it worth more or less?
  3. Who will handle my case day to day?
  4. What percentage do you charge before and after a lawsuit is filed?
  5. Are costs deducted before or after your fee, and do I owe anything if we lose?
  6. How do you handle medical liens and unpaid bills while the case is open?
  7. How long do you expect my case to take?
  8. How often will you update me, and how?
  9. Have you taken cases like this to trial?
  10. Is there anything that worries you about my case?

Bring the accident report, photos, medical records, insurance letters and any settlement offer. If you already have an offer, our guide on whether to accept the first settlement offer explains how to judge it.

Red flags: when to walk away

  • Someone contacts you first. ABA Model Rule 7.3 bars lawyers from soliciting clients through live person-to-person contact for money. A stranger who shows up at the hospital or calls right after a crash offering a lawyer is a warning sign.
  • Guaranteed results. No honest lawyer can promise a specific amount at the first meeting.
  • Pressure to sign immediately. You should be able to take the agreement home and read it.
  • Vague costs. If the lawyer cannot explain how costs are handled, expect surprises at the end.
  • Undisclosed referrals. If your case is being referred to another firm, Rule 1.5(e) requires that you agree in writing to the split, and the total fee must still be reasonable.
  • No time for you. If you cannot get the lawyer on the phone before signing, it will not get easier later.

Can you switch personal injury lawyers?

Yes. Under the ABA Model Rules, a client can discharge a lawyer at any time, with or without cause, and the lawyer must withdraw and hand over the file. You stay responsible for the reasonable value of the work already done, but in contingency cases that is usually paid out of the final fee. The first and second lawyers typically divide one fee, either by agreement or by a court deciding what each earned. Ask the new lawyer to explain how the previous lawyer’s lien will be handled before you switch.

How long does a personal injury case take?

Simple claims can settle in a few months. Represented auto injury claims took a median of almost 440 days to close in the Insurance Research Council’s study. Cases that go to litigation often take one to three years. Our guide to how long a settlement takes breaks down each stage.

Whatever you decide, do not wait too long to talk to a lawyer. Every state has a statute of limitations for injury lawsuits, and claims against government agencies can require written notice within months.

Frequently asked questions

How much does a personal injury lawyer charge?

Most charge a contingency fee of about 33% of a settlement reached before a lawsuit and around 40% if the case is litigated, plus case costs. You pay nothing if there is no recovery, unless your agreement says otherwise for certain costs.

Is 40% normal for a personal injury lawyer?

It is common once a lawsuit is filed or a case goes to trial, because the work and risk increase. Some states cap fees, and many lawyers will negotiate, especially for strong cases or large expected recoveries.

Do I pay my lawyer if we lose?

Not the fee. Whether you owe case costs after a loss depends on your written agreement, which must disclose any expenses you would still owe.

Can I negotiate a lawyer’s percentage?

Yes. Fees are not set by law in most cases. You can ask for a lower percentage, a sliding scale, or costs deducted before the fee is calculated.

Should I hire the lawyer I see on TV?

Advertising budget says nothing about results. Judge any lawyer on experience with your type of case, who will actually handle your file, communication and the written fee terms.

Is a free consultation really free?

Yes. Injury lawyers almost always offer free consultations and you are not obligated to hire them. Use it to compare at least two lawyers.

Can I settle without a lawyer?

Yes, many small claims are settled directly with insurers. Read our guide to how injury settlements are calculated and estimate your claim with the personal injury settlement calculator first.

posts.title: Do You Need a Car Accident Lawyer? When to Hire One (and When You Don’t)
posts.excerpt: Do you need a car accident lawyer? A clear guide to when hiring one is worth it, when you can settle on your own, what lawyers charge and how long you have.

meta.rank_math_description: When you need a car accident lawyer and when you don’t: serious injuries, disputed fault, uninsured drivers, fees, deadlines and what lawyers actually do.

seo.description: When you need a car accident lawyer and when you don’t: serious injuries, disputed fault, uninsured drivers, fees, deadlines and what lawyers actually do.
