posts.content:
Key points

  • You usually do not need a lawyer for a property-damage-only crash or a minor injury that heals quickly with clear fault.
  • Talk to a car accident lawyer if you were seriously hurt, fault is disputed, the other driver is uninsured or underinsured, or a truck, rideshare or government vehicle was involved.
  • Car accident lawyers work on contingency, usually around one-third of a settlement, and consultations are free.
  • In 2023, 15.4% of U.S. drivers were uninsured and 33.4% were uninsured or underinsured, according to the Insurance Research Council.
  • Deadlines matter: every state has a statute of limitations, and claims against government vehicles can need notice within months.

Most car crashes do not end up in court, and many do not need a lawyer at all. But some do, and the difference in what you recover can be large. U.S. traffic deaths fell to an estimated 36,640 in 2025, down 6.7% from 2024 (U.S. Department of Transportation, April 2026), yet millions of people are still injured in crashes every year and most of them deal with an insurance adjuster.

This guide helps you decide whether you need a car accident lawyer, what a lawyer actually does, what it costs, and when you can handle the claim yourself.

Do you need a car accident lawyer? A quick guide

When a car accident lawyer is worth it

1. Your injuries are serious or still being treated

The biggest part of an injury claim is often future medical care, lost earning capacity and pain and suffering. Adjusters are trained to value those conservatively. A lawyer gathers medical opinions on your prognosis before negotiating, rather than settling while you are still treating. Our car accident settlement calculator shows how injury type and treatment length change the range.

2. Fault is disputed

In most states, your compensation is reduced by your share of the fault. In a few contributory negligence states, even 1% fault can bar recovery. Lawyers preserve evidence that settles fault arguments, including dashcam and traffic camera footage, the cars’ event data recorders, witness statements and scene measurements. See how fault changes a payout with the comparative fault calculator.

3. The other driver has little or no insurance

More than one in seven drivers (15.4%) were uninsured in 2023, and one in three (33.4%) were uninsured or underinsured (Insurance Research Council, February 2025). When the at-fault driver’s limits are too low, recovery may depend on your own uninsured or underinsured motorist coverage. Read our guides to policy limits and UM/UIM coverage and hit-and-run and uninsured driver claims.

4. A commercial or government vehicle was involved

Truck crashes involve federal safety rules, driver logs and corporate insurers. Rideshare claims depend on whether the app was on and whether a ride was in progress. Crashes with city, county or state vehicles often require a formal notice of claim within a few months, far sooner than the usual lawsuit deadline.

5. The insurer is stalling, lowballing or asking for a recorded statement

You generally do not have to give the other driver’s insurer a recorded statement. Our guide on recorded statements explains why. If the offer seems low, a lawyer can value the claim properly and, if needed, file suit before the deadline.

When you can handle the claim yourself

If nobody was hurt, or your injury was minor and healed quickly, you can usually settle on your own:

  • Get the police report, photos, repair estimates and all medical bills and records.
  • Track every out-of-pocket cost, including mileage to appointments and lost pay (our lost wages calculator helps).
  • Send a written demand with your documents. Our demand letter generator builds one for you.
  • Do not sign a release until you are finished treating. A release ends the claim permanently.
  • If the offer seems unfair, test it with the settlement offer calculator or book a free consultation.

For the steps right after a crash, read what to do in the first 72 hours after a car accident.

What a car accident lawyer actually does

  • Investigates the crash, preserves video and vehicle data, and interviews witnesses.
  • Handles all calls and letters with insurers so you can focus on recovery.
  • Collects medical records and opinions to prove the full cost of your injuries.
  • Identifies every source of coverage, including the other driver, employers, your own UM/UIM, MedPay or PIP.
  • Negotiates medical liens down so more of the settlement reaches you.
  • Files a lawsuit before the statute of limitations runs out if the insurer will not pay fairly.

Car accident lawyer vs personal injury lawyer: is there a difference?

A car accident lawyer is a personal injury lawyer who focuses on vehicle crashes. The license is the same, but the day-to-day knowledge is not. Crash lawyers deal constantly with auto policies, UM/UIM and PIP coverage, vehicle data, accident reconstruction and the adjusters at the big auto insurers. For a truck crash, look for someone who also knows federal trucking rules. For a crash involving a bicycle or pedestrian, ask how many of those cases the lawyer has handled.

How much does a car accident lawyer cost?

Car accident lawyers almost always work on a contingency fee. You pay nothing up front, and the lawyer takes a percentage of the recovery, commonly about one-third before a lawsuit and up to 40% if the case is litigated. The agreement must be in writing and must say how case costs are handled (ABA Model Rule 1.5(c)). Use our attorney fee calculator to see what you would take home.

Is it worth the fee? The Insurance Research Council, an insurer-funded group, found that represented auto injury claimants received more in total but waited much longer, and kept slightly less per dollar of medical bills after fees ($1.40 versus $1.80) (IRC, July 2026). Represented cases also tend to be more serious and contested, so the comparison is not like for like. The practical rule: the more serious the injury and the more the insurer resists, the more a lawyer is worth.

How long do you have to hire a lawyer?

Each state sets a statute of limitations for injury lawsuits, commonly two or three years from the crash, though some are shorter and some longer. Government claims can require notice much sooner. No-fault states add their own rules about when you can step outside PIP and sue for pain and suffering (see no-fault states). Check your deadline with our statute of limitations calculator.

How to choose a car accident lawyer

Look for a lawyer who handles car crash cases every week, has taken cases to trial, will personally work on your file and puts the fee and costs in writing. Our full guide on how to choose a personal injury lawyer includes the questions to ask in a free consultation and the red flags to avoid. You can also search our Find an Expert directory.

Frequently asked questions

Is it worth getting a lawyer for a minor car accident?

Often not, if nobody was seriously hurt, fault is clear and your bills are small. It becomes worth it when injuries are ongoing, fault is disputed or the insurer is offering less than your documented losses.

How much does a car accident lawyer charge?

Usually a contingency fee of about 33% of a pre-suit settlement and up to 40% after a lawsuit is filed, plus case costs. You pay no fee if there is no recovery.

Do car accident lawyers offer free consultations?

Yes, almost all do. Use the consultation to ask what your claim is worth, who will handle it and how fees and costs work.

Can I hire a lawyer after I accept a settlement?

Generally no. Accepting a settlement usually means signing a release that ends the claim. Talk to a lawyer before you sign.

Should I talk to the other driver’s insurance company?

You can report the claim and give basic facts, but you usually do not have to give a recorded statement or sign a broad medical authorization.

What if I was partly at fault?

In most states you can still recover, reduced by your percentage of fault. A handful of states bar recovery if you were at fault at all, so get advice quickly.

How long does a car accident case take?

Simple claims can settle in months. Represented injury claims took a median of nearly 440 days to close in the Insurance Research Council’s study, and lawsuits can take longer.

Sources

  • U.S. Department of Transportation: 2025 traffic fatality estimate (April 1, 2026)
  • Insurance Research Council: Uninsured and underinsured motorists study (February 2025)
  • Insurance Research Council: Auto Injury Insurance Claims, A Study of Increasing Claim Severity (July 2026)
  • American Bar Association: Model Rule 1.5, Fees

This article is general information, not legal advice. Fault rules, insurance requirements and deadlines vary by state. Talk to a licensed attorney in your state about your situation.

blocks.html: You generally do not have to give the other driver’s insurer a recorded statement. Our guide on recorded statements explains why. If the offer seems low, a lawyer can value the claim properly and, if needed, file suit before the deadline.

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: When you can handle the claim yourself

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: If nobody was hurt, or your injury was minor and healed quickly, you can usually settle on your own:

blocks.name: core/list
blocks.html:
• Get the police report, photos, repair estimates and all medical bills and records.
  • Track every out-of-pocket cost, including mileage to appointments and lost pay (our lost wages calculator helps).
  • Send a written demand with your documents. Our demand letter generator builds one for you.
  • Do not sign a release until you are finished treating. A release ends the claim permanently.
  • If the offer seems unfair, test it with the settlement offer calculator or book a free consultation.

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: For the steps right after a crash, read what to do in the first 72 hours after a car accident.

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: What a car accident lawyer actually does

blocks.name: core/list
blocks.html:
• Investigates the crash, preserves video and vehicle data, and interviews witnesses.
  • Handles all calls and letters with insurers so you can focus on recovery.
  • Collects medical records and opinions to prove the full cost of your injuries.
  • Identifies every source of coverage, including the other driver, employers, your own UM/UIM, MedPay or PIP.
  • Negotiates medical liens down so more of the settlement reaches you.
  • Files a lawsuit before the statute of limitations runs out if the insurer will not pay fairly.

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: Car accident lawyer vs personal injury lawyer: is there a difference?

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: A car accident lawyer is a personal injury lawyer who focuses on vehicle crashes. The license is the same, but the day-to-day knowledge is not. Crash lawyers deal constantly with auto policies, UM/UIM and PIP coverage, vehicle data, accident reconstruction and the adjusters at the big auto insurers. For a truck crash, look for someone who also knows federal trucking rules. For a crash involving a bicycle or pedestrian, ask how many of those cases the lawyer has handled.

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: How much does a car accident lawyer cost?

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: Car accident lawyers almost always work on a contingency fee. You pay nothing up front, and the lawyer takes a percentage of the recovery, commonly about one-third before a lawsuit and up to 40% if the case is litigated. The agreement must be in writing and must say how case costs are handled (ABA Model Rule 1.5(c)). Use our attorney fee calculator to see what you would take home.

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: Is it worth the fee? The Insurance Research Council, an insurer-funded group, found that represented auto injury claimants received more in total but waited much longer, and kept slightly less per dollar of medical bills after fees ($1.40 versus $1.80) (IRC, July 2026). Represented cases also tend to be more serious and contested, so the comparison is not like for like. The practical rule: the more serious the injury and the more the insurer resists, the more a lawyer is worth.

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: How long do you have to hire a lawyer?

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: Each state sets a statute of limitations for injury lawsuits, commonly two or three years from the crash, though some are shorter and some longer. Government claims can require notice much sooner. No-fault states add their own rules about when you can step outside PIP and sue for pain and suffering (see no-fault states). Check your deadline with our statute of limitations calculator.

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: How to choose a car accident lawyer

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: Look for a lawyer who handles car crash cases every week, has taken cases to trial, will personally work on your file and puts the fee and costs in writing. Our full guide on how to choose a personal injury lawyer includes the questions to ask in a free consultation and the red flags to avoid. You can also search our Find an Expert directory.

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: Frequently asked questions

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: Is it worth getting a lawyer for a minor car accident?

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: Often not, if nobody was seriously hurt, fault is clear and your bills are small. It becomes worth it when injuries are ongoing, fault is disputed or the insurer is offering less than your documented losses.

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: How much does a car accident lawyer charge?

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: Usually a contingency fee of about 33% of a pre-suit settlement and up to 40% after a lawsuit is filed, plus case costs. You pay no fee if there is no recovery.

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: Do car accident lawyers offer free consultations?

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: Yes, almost all do. Use the consultation to ask what your claim is worth, who will handle it and how fees and costs work.

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: Can I hire a lawyer after I accept a settlement?

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: Generally no. Accepting a settlement usually means signing a release that ends the claim. Talk to a lawyer before you sign.

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: Should I talk to the other driver’s insurance company?

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: You can report the claim and give basic facts, but you usually do not have to give a recorded statement or sign a broad medical authorization.

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: What if I was partly at fault?

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: In most states you can still recover, reduced by your percentage of fault. A handful of states bar recovery if you were at fault at all, so get advice quickly.

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: How long does a car accident case take?

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: Simple claims can settle in months. Represented injury claims took a median of nearly 440 days to close in the Insurance Research Council’s study, and lawsuits can take longer.

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: Sources

blocks.name: core/list
blocks.html:
• U.S. Department of Transportation: 2025 traffic fatality estimate (April 1, 2026)
  • Insurance Research Council: Uninsured and underinsured motorists study (February 2025)
  • Insurance Research Council: Auto Injury Insurance Claims, A Study of Increasing Claim Severity (July 2026)
  • American Bar Association: Model Rule 1.5, Fees

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: This article is general information, not legal advice. Fault rules, insurance requirements and deadlines vary by state. Talk to a licensed attorney in your state about your situation.

seo.title: Asbestos Lawyer: How Mesothelioma Claims Work (2026)
seo.description: How asbestos and mesothelioma claims work: lawsuits, bankruptcy trust funds, VA benefits, filing deadlines, fees and how to choose an asbestos lawyer.
seo.focus: asbestos lawyer,mesothelioma lawyer,asbestos lawyers,asbestos trust fund,mesothelioma claim

posts.content:
Key points

  • An asbestos lawyer helps people with mesothelioma, asbestos-related lung cancer or asbestosis, and their families, recover compensation from the companies responsible for the exposure.
  • Mesothelioma usually appears 20 to 40 years after exposure, and sometimes much later, so most claims are about jobs, homes or products from decades ago.
  • Compensation can come from lawsuits against companies still in business, from asbestos bankruptcy trust funds, and from VA or workers’ comp benefits.
  • Deadlines are short and start at diagnosis, not exposure. In California, for example, you generally have one year (Code Civ. Proc. § 340.2).
  • Asbestos lawyers work on contingency, so there is nothing to pay up front.

An asbestos diagnosis usually comes long after the exposure that caused it. CDC researchers counted 45,221 deaths in the United States from 1999 to 2015 with malignant mesothelioma listed as a cause, with annual deaths rising from 2,479 in 1999 to 2,597 in 2015 (CDC, MMWR 2017). The same report notes that the time from first exposure to disease typically ranges from 20 to 40 years and can be as long as 71 years.

In 2024, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency finalized a ban on chrysotile asbestos, the only form still being imported, with phase-outs for remaining industrial uses (AIHA summary of the EPA rule). That ban protects future workers, but it does nothing for people already sick from past exposure. This guide explains how asbestos claims work, where the money comes from, the deadlines, and how to choose an asbestos lawyer.

Who can file an asbestos claim?

  • People diagnosed with mesothelioma, the cancer most strongly linked to asbestos, affecting the lining of the lungs, abdomen or heart.
  • People with asbestos-related lung cancer, asbestosis or other asbestos diseases, depending on the evidence of exposure.
  • Family members with secondhand exposure, for example from dust carried home on a worker’s clothes.
  • Surviving family or the estate, through a wrongful death claim, when a loved one has died. See our wrongful death settlement calculator for how these claims are valued.

Common exposure settings include shipyards, Navy ships, construction, insulation and pipefitting, power plants, refineries, auto brake work, and older homes and schools.

Where asbestos compensation comes from

Asbestos bankruptcy trust funds

Dozens of companies that made asbestos products went bankrupt and were required to set up trusts to pay current and future victims. The U.S. Government Accountability Office reported that 60 asbestos trusts had been established since 1988, with about $37 billion in total assets (GAO-11-819, 2011). Each trust has its own claim procedures, required proof of exposure and payment percentage, and trusts typically pay a fraction of a claim’s scheduled value.

A trust claim does not usually stop you from also suing companies that are still solvent. Many states now require plaintiffs to disclose their trust claims during a lawsuit, so an experienced asbestos lawyer coordinates both tracks from the start.

Veterans

The Navy and other branches used asbestos heavily for decades. Veterans may file a claim with the VA for asbestos-related disease connected to service (VA: asbestos exposure). VA benefits do not stop a veteran from filing trust claims or suing the private companies that made the products, but you generally cannot sue the federal government itself over military exposure.

How long do you have to file? Asbestos deadlines

Because asbestos diseases take decades to appear, the statute of limitations usually starts when you are diagnosed or disabled, or when you knew or should have known the disease was caused by asbestos. Most states allow one to three years from that point, and wrongful death claims usually run from the date of death.

California is a good example of how short this can be. Under Code of Civil Procedure § 340.2, an asbestos injury suit must generally be filed within one year after the later of the date of disability or the date the person knew, or should have known, that the disability was caused by asbestos exposure. A wrongful death suit must generally be filed within one year after the later of the death or the discovery that asbestos caused it.

Check your state’s general deadline with our statute of limitations calculator, but talk to an asbestos lawyer quickly, because special asbestos rules often apply.

What an asbestos lawyer does

  • Builds your exposure history. Asbestos cases turn on which products you were exposed to, where and when. Lawyers use work records, union and military records, product databases and testimony from former co-workers.
  • Identifies every defendant and trust. One worker may have been exposed to products from dozens of manufacturers.
  • Chooses where to file. Cases can sometimes be filed where the exposure happened, where you live or where a defendant is based, and the rules differ by court.
  • Moves fast when time is short. Many states let seriously ill plaintiffs ask for an expedited trial date. Lawyers can also record testimony early so the case can continue if the person dies.
  • Files trust claims. Each trust has its own forms, proof requirements and payment schedule.
  • Handles the estate side. If the person dies during the case, the claim may continue through the estate or as a wrongful death claim.

How much does an asbestos lawyer cost?

Asbestos and mesothelioma lawyers work on contingency. You pay nothing up front and the lawyer is paid a percentage of what is recovered, plus case costs, under a written agreement. Ask whether the percentage is different for trust claims and for lawsuits, and how costs are handled. Our attorney fee calculator shows how a percentage fee and costs affect your share.

How much is an asbestos claim worth?

There is no reliable public “average” mesothelioma settlement, because most settlements are confidential and each case combines payments from several defendants and trusts. What drives the value:

  • The diagnosis. Mesothelioma claims are usually valued higher than other asbestos diseases.
  • Age, health, earnings and family situation, including lost income and support for dependents.
  • How clearly the exposure can be tied to specific products and companies.
  • How many defendants are still solvent and how many trusts apply.
  • Where the case is filed and whether a jury trial is likely.

Be skeptical of advertisements that promise a specific figure. A good lawyer will explain the range for your facts after reviewing your work and medical history.

How to choose an asbestos lawyer

  • Choose a firm that handles asbestos cases as a core practice, with experience in both bankruptcy trust claims and trials.
  • Ask how many mesothelioma cases the firm has resolved, and who will be your day-to-day contact.
  • Ask whether the firm will travel to you if you are too ill to travel. Many do.
  • Confirm the fee percentage, costs policy and any co-counsel or referral arrangement in writing.
  • Check the lawyers’ licenses and discipline history with the state bar.

Our general guide on how to choose a personal injury lawyer covers the questions to ask in a free consultation and the red flags to avoid.

Frequently asked questions

Can I file a claim if the company that made the asbestos is bankrupt?

Often yes. Many bankrupt asbestos companies created trusts that pay victims. You may be able to file with several trusts and also sue companies that are still in business.

How long do I have to file a mesothelioma claim?

Usually one to three years from diagnosis, depending on the state, and often one year in states like California. Wrongful death deadlines generally run from the date of death.

Can family members file an asbestos claim?

Yes. Family members harmed by secondhand exposure can file their own claims, and surviving relatives or the estate can bring a wrongful death claim.

Do I need to know exactly where I was exposed?

No. Lawyers reconstruct your exposure from your work history, military service, homes and hobbies, and from records and witnesses.

Can veterans get compensation for asbestos exposure?

Veterans can apply for VA disability benefits and may also file trust claims and sue private product manufacturers. Suits against the federal government over military exposure are generally barred.

Does it cost anything to hire an asbestos lawyer?

Not up front. Asbestos lawyers are paid a percentage of the recovery, and you owe no fee if there is no recovery.

Is asbestos still legal in the United States?

The EPA finalized a ban on chrysotile asbestos in 2024, with remaining uses phased out over several years. Asbestos can still be found in older buildings and products.

Sources

  • CDC: Malignant Mesothelioma Mortality, United States, 1999–2015 (MMWR, 2017)
  • AIHA: EPA finalizes chrysotile asbestos ban (March 2024)
  • U.S. Government Accountability Office: Asbestos Injury Compensation, GAO-11-819 (2011)
  • California Code of Civil Procedure § 340.2
  • U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs: asbestos exposure

This article is general information, not legal or medical advice. Asbestos deadlines and rules vary by state. Talk to a licensed attorney about your situation as soon as possible after a diagnosis.

posts.content:
Key points

  • If a new car is a lemon under California’s Song-Beverly Act, the manufacturer must replace it or buy it back. The buyback (restitution) refunds what you paid plus taxes, fees and incidental costs, minus a usage offset.
  • The offset is: miles driven before the first repair visit for the defect ÷ 120,000 × the price paid for the vehicle. Miles after that first repair do not count against you.
  • A car is presumed a lemon if, within 18 months or 18,000 miles, a serious safety defect was repaired twice, the same defect was repaired four times, or the car was in the shop more than 30 days.
  • Manufacturers that opted into the 2025 reforms (AB 1755 and SB 26) follow new pre-suit notice, offer and mediation deadlines.
  • If you win, the manufacturer pays your attorney’s fees, so most lemon law lawyers charge nothing up front.

California’s lemon law, the Song-Beverly Consumer Warranty Act, is one of the strongest in the country. When a manufacturer cannot fix a defect that substantially impairs a new vehicle’s use, value or safety after a reasonable number of tries, it must offer you a replacement or a refund. Most people choose the refund, known as a buyback or restitution.

Use the calculator below to estimate your buyback, then read how each number is worked out, whether your car qualifies, and what changed in 2025.

Lemon law buyback calculator

California lemon law buyback estimate

Enter your numbers to estimate a Song-Beverly repurchase. Nothing you type is saved or sent anywhere.

Miles driven before first repair6,000
Usage offset (miles ÷ 120,000 × price)−$2,100
Price + taxes and fees + finance charges + incidentals$48,550
Estimated buyback (restitution)$46,450

If you financed the car, part of the buyback pays off your loan and the rest is refunded to you. This is an estimate under Civil Code § 1793.2(d)(2), not a guarantee. Courts decide disputed items.

The calculator opens with the worked example used later in this article. Replace the numbers with the figures from your purchase contract, loan statements and repair orders.

The California lemon law buyback formula

Under Civil Code § 1793.2(d)(2) and the standard jury instruction CACI 3241, restitution generally includes:

  • The price paid or payable for the vehicle, including charges for transportation and manufacturer-installed options, and including paid finance charges and any amount still owed on the loan.
  • Collateral charges: sales or use tax, license fees, registration fees and other official fees.
  • Incidental damages, such as towing, rental cars and repair costs you paid because of the defect.

From that total, the manufacturer may deduct an amount for your use of the car before the problem first appeared.

The mileage offset

The 120,000 figure treats a car as having a 120,000-mile useful life. CACI 3241 tells juries to leave out of the offset base any items supplied by someone other than the manufacturer, such as dealer add-ons, and the manufacturer has to prove the mileage it wants to deduct.

Worked example

A buyer pays $42,000 for a new SUV, including destination and factory options. Sales tax, registration and official fees come to $4,100. They have paid $1,850 in loan interest and $600 for a tow and a rental car. The SUV had 12 miles at delivery and first went in for the transmission problem at 6,012 miles.

If the buyer still owes on the loan, the manufacturer pays the lender first and refunds the rest to the buyer. A replacement vehicle is the alternative, with the same offset.

Does your car qualify as a lemon?

California law gives you a presumption, a head start in proving your case, if the problems began within 18 months of delivery or 18,000 miles, whichever comes first, and any of these happened (Civil Code § 1793.22(b); CACI 3203):

  • A defect likely to cause death or serious bodily injury was repaired two or more times, and you notified the manufacturer directly in writing.
  • The same substantial defect was repaired four or more times, and you notified the manufacturer directly in writing.
  • The vehicle was out of service for repairs for a total of more than 30 days.

The direct written notice is only required if the manufacturer clearly disclosed that requirement in the warranty or owner’s manual. The presumption is not the only way to qualify: a car can still be a lemon outside 18 months or 18,000 miles if it was covered by the warranty and the manufacturer had a reasonable number of repair attempts.

Used cars

In Rodriguez v. FCA US (Cal. Oct. 31, 2024), the California Supreme Court held that a used car sold with the balance of the original manufacturer’s warranty is not a “new motor vehicle” for the refund-or-replace remedy. That remedy covers used cars only when a manufacturer’s new car warranty is issued with the sale. Used-car buyers may still have other warranty claims.

What changed in 2025: AB 1755 and SB 26

Two laws reshaped how California lemon law cases move for manufacturers that opt in. AB 1755 was signed on September 29, 2024, and SB 26 on April 2, 2025 to streamline it (California Department of Consumer Affairs). The Department publishes the list of manufacturers that have opted in, and the election lasts five years. For those manufacturers:

  • Pre-suit notice. To seek civil penalties, you send the manufacturer a written repurchase or replacement demand at least 30 days before suing.
  • Fast deadlines. The manufacturer must offer restitution or replacement within 30 days of your notice and complete it within 60 days.
  • Early mediation. Once a lawsuit is answered, mediation must be scheduled within 90 days and held within 150 days, with limited early discovery (Bowman and Brooke summary).
  • Filing deadline. Suit must be filed within one year after the express warranty expires, and no more than six years after delivery, with extra time while the car is in for repairs.
  • Prompt payment. Agreed buybacks must be processed within 30 days of a signed release or daily penalties apply.

If your manufacturer did not opt in, the earlier procedures still apply. Check the Department of Consumer Affairs list or ask a lemon law attorney which rules govern your case.

Civil penalties and attorney’s fees

If a manufacturer willfully fails to comply, a court can add a civil penalty of up to two times your actual damages. A buyer who wins is also entitled to recover attorney’s fees and costs from the manufacturer (Civil Code § 1794). That fee-shifting rule is why most California lemon law attorneys charge clients nothing up front and nothing out of the buyback.

When to talk to a lemon law attorney

  • The manufacturer refuses a buyback or offers less than your calculation.
  • The offer deducts dealer add-ons, negative equity or extra mileage you think it shouldn’t.
  • You are not sure whether your manufacturer opted into the 2025 procedures, or which deadline applies.
  • Your car is used, leased or a motorhome, which raise special rules.

Keep every repair order, your purchase or lease contract, loan statements and receipts for towing and rentals. Those documents decide the numbers in the formula.

Frequently asked questions

How is the lemon law mileage offset calculated in California?

Take the miles driven from delivery to the first repair visit for the defect, divide by 120,000, and multiply by the price paid for the vehicle. For example, 6,000 miles on a $42,000 car is a $2,100 offset.

Do I get my down payment back?

Yes. Restitution covers what you have paid toward the vehicle, including the down payment and monthly payments, and the manufacturer pays off any remaining loan balance.

Are sales tax and registration fees refunded?

Yes. Sales or use tax, license, registration and other official fees are part of restitution under Civil Code § 1793.2(d)(2).

Are dealer add-ons refunded?

Items supplied by someone other than the manufacturer are left out of the offset base, and whether they are refunded is often disputed. Ask a lemon law attorney about your contract.

Does California lemon law cover leased cars?

Yes, new vehicles leased in California are covered. The restitution is based on what you have paid under the lease, minus the usage offset.

How long do I have to file a lemon law claim?

For manufacturers that opted into AB 1755, generally within one year after the warranty expires and no more than six years after delivery. Other deadlines may apply otherwise, so act quickly.

Do I need a lawyer for a lemon law buyback?

Not always, but because the manufacturer pays your attorney’s fees if you win, most buyers lose nothing by getting a free review before accepting an offer.

posts.title: Nursing Home Abuse Lawyer: Warning Signs, Your Rights and How Claims Work
posts.excerpt: Signs of nursing home abuse and neglect, the federal rights every resident has, how to report abuse, arbitration agreements, and how nursing home abuse claims and lawyers work.

meta.rank_math_description: Spot nursing home abuse and neglect, know the federal rights every resident has, report it the right way, and learn how nursing home abuse claims work.

seo.title: Nursing Home Abuse Lawyer: Signs, Rights & Claims (2026)
seo.description: Spot nursing home abuse and neglect, know the federal rights every resident has, report it the right way, and learn how nursing home abuse claims work.
seo.focus: nursing home abuse attorney,nursing home abuse lawyer,nursing home neglect lawyer,elder abuse lawyer,nursing home negligence

posts.content:
Key points

  • Nursing home abuse includes physical, sexual, emotional and financial abuse, and neglect such as untreated bedsores, dehydration, falls and overmedication.
  • Federal rules give every resident the right to be free from abuse and neglect, and require nursing homes to report suspected abuse to the state within 2 hours when it involves abuse or serious bodily injury (42 CFR 483.12).
  • If you suspect abuse, get the resident safe, document everything, and report it to the facility, the state survey agency and the long-term care ombudsman.
  • A nursing home cannot make you sign an arbitration agreement as a condition of admission, and you have 30 days to cancel one you signed.
  • Nursing home abuse lawyers work on contingency. Deadlines can be short, especially when a resident has died.

Families choose a nursing home because they need people they can trust. The evidence shows that trust is sometimes broken. The World Health Organization reports that in institutions such as nursing homes and long-term care facilities, 2 in 3 staff reported in surveys that they had committed some form of abuse in the past year (WHO fact sheet, June 2024). In the United States, the Government Accountability Office found that abuse deficiencies cited in nursing homes more than doubled, from 430 in 2013 to 875 in 2017 (GAO-19-433).

This guide explains the warning signs, the legal rights every resident has, what to do if you suspect abuse, how nursing home claims work and how to choose a nursing home abuse lawyer.

Types of nursing home abuse and neglect

One sign alone does not prove abuse. Older residents bruise easily and fall for many reasons. What matters is a pattern, explanations that do not fit the injury, or a facility that will not give you straight answers.

Your rights under federal law

Nursing homes that take Medicare or Medicaid must follow federal resident rights rules. Under 42 CFR 483.12:

  • Every resident has the right to be free from abuse, neglect, misappropriation of property and exploitation.
  • The facility must not use verbal, mental, sexual or physical abuse, corporal punishment or involuntary seclusion.
  • Physical or chemical restraints may not be used for discipline or staff convenience, only to treat a medical symptom, and then in the least restrictive way for the shortest time.
  • Suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation must be reported to the administrator and the State Survey Agency immediately: within 2 hours if the allegation involves abuse or serious bodily injury, and within 24 hours otherwise.
  • The facility must investigate and send the results to the State Survey Agency within 5 working days.

States add their own residents’ rights laws, and many have elder abuse statutes that allow extra damages or attorney’s fees.

What to do if you suspect nursing home abuse

  1. Make the resident safe. If there is immediate danger or a serious injury, call 911.
  2. Get a medical evaluation. Ask the resident’s doctor or an emergency room to examine and document injuries.
  3. Document everything. Take dated photos, write down what you saw and who you spoke to, and keep copies of care plans, medication lists and bills.
  4. Report it to the facility in writing. Address it to the administrator and the director of nursing, and keep a copy.
  5. Report it outside the facility. Contact your state survey agency (the state department that licenses nursing homes), your local long-term care ombudsman and Adult Protective Services. The Eldercare Locator can direct you to local offices.
  6. Check the facility’s record. Medicare’s Care Compare tool shows inspection results, staffing levels and penalties.
  7. Request records. Residents and their legal representatives can ask for the resident’s medical records. Do this early, before anything is lost.
  8. Talk to a lawyer before signing anything the facility or its insurer sends you.

Arbitration agreements in nursing home contracts

Many admission packets include a binding arbitration agreement that would move any dispute out of court. Under a 2019 federal rule for long-term care facilities, a nursing home cannot require you to sign one as a condition of admission or continued care. The agreement must say so plainly, must be explained in a way you understand, and must let you cancel it within 30 calendar days of signing (summary of the CMS rule). If you signed one, a lawyer can review whether it was valid and whether it applies to your claim.

How nursing home abuse claims work

Most claims are based on negligence: the facility failed to provide reasonable care and the resident was harmed. Depending on the state and the facts, a claim may also involve violations of residents’ rights laws, elder abuse statutes, medical malpractice rules or wrongful death.

Who can file

  • The resident, if able, or a legal representative such as an agent under a power of attorney or a court-appointed guardian.
  • The resident’s estate, if the resident has died, and family members through a wrongful death claim.

What compensation may cover

  • Medical treatment for injuries caused by the abuse or neglect, including hospital stays and wound care.
  • Pain and suffering and emotional distress (see our pain and suffering calculator).
  • Money taken through financial exploitation.
  • Funeral costs and loss of companionship in wrongful death cases.
  • Punitive damages in some states for reckless or intentional misconduct.

Some states cap damages in claims treated as medical malpractice, and Medicare or Medicaid may have a lien on any recovery. Our guide to medical liens explains how those are handled.

Deadlines

Each state sets its own statute of limitations, and claims treated as medical malpractice can have shorter limits and pre-suit requirements such as expert affidavits. Wrongful death deadlines usually run from the date of death. Check the general rule in your state with our statute of limitations calculator and talk to a lawyer promptly.

How to choose a nursing home abuse lawyer

  • Look for a lawyer who regularly handles nursing home and elder abuse cases, not just general injury claims.
  • Ask how they obtain facility records, staffing data and inspection reports, and whether they work with nursing and geriatric experts.
  • Ask how they handle arbitration agreements and Medicare or Medicaid liens.
  • Confirm the contingency percentage and how costs are handled, in writing.
  • Check the lawyer’s license and discipline history with your state bar.

Our guide on how to choose a personal injury lawyer lists the questions to ask in a free consultation. You can also search our Find an Expert directory.

Frequently asked questions

How do I report nursing home abuse?

Call 911 for emergencies. Otherwise report it in writing to the facility administrator, and to your state survey agency, the long-term care ombudsman and Adult Protective Services.

What are the most common signs of nursing home neglect?

Bedsores, dehydration, sudden weight loss, poor hygiene, repeated falls and untreated infections are among the most common signs.

How quickly must a nursing home report suspected abuse?

Under federal rules, within 2 hours if the allegation involves abuse or serious bodily injury, and within 24 hours otherwise, with investigation results due to the state within 5 working days.

Can I sue a nursing home if I signed an arbitration agreement?

Possibly. The agreement cannot be required for admission and can be cancelled within 30 days. A lawyer can check whether it is valid and covers your claim.

How much does a nursing home abuse lawyer cost?

Most work on contingency, taking a percentage of any recovery, so there is nothing to pay up front.

Can family members file a claim?

A legal representative can file for a living resident, and the estate or certain family members can file a wrongful death claim if the resident died.

How do I check a nursing home’s inspection history?

Use Medicare’s Care Compare website, which shows inspection findings, staffing and penalties for each certified facility.

Sources

  • World Health Organization: Abuse of older people, fact sheet (June 15, 2024)
  • U.S. Government Accountability Office: Nursing Homes, Improved Oversight Needed to Better Protect Residents from Abuse (GAO-19-433)
  • 42 CFR 483.12: Freedom from abuse, neglect and exploitation
  • National Law Review: CMS final rule on arbitration agreements in long-term care facilities (2019)
  • Medicare Care Compare
  • Administration for Community Living: Long-Term Care Ombudsman Program

This article is general information, not legal or medical advice. If someone is in immediate danger, call 911. Laws and deadlines vary by state; talk to a licensed attorney about your situation.

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: Under federal rules, within 2 hours if the allegation involves abuse or serious bodily injury, and within 24 hours otherwise, with investigation results due to the state within 5 working days.

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: Can I sue a nursing home if I signed an arbitration agreement?

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: Possibly. The agreement cannot be required for admission and can be cancelled within 30 days. A lawyer can check whether it is valid and covers your claim.

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: How much does a nursing home abuse lawyer cost?

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: Most work on contingency, taking a percentage of any recovery, so there is nothing to pay up front.

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: Can family members file a claim?

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: A legal representative can file for a living resident, and the estate or certain family members can file a wrongful death claim if the resident died.

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: How do I check a nursing home’s inspection history?

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: Use Medicare’s Care Compare website, which shows inspection findings, staffing and penalties for each certified facility.

posts.title: Pedestrian Accident Lawyer: Do You Need One After Being Hit by a Car?
posts.excerpt: Hit by a car while walking? What to do next, which insurance pays, how fault works, what affects a pedestrian accident settlement and when you need a lawyer.

meta.rank_math_description: Hit by a car while walking? Who pays, how fault works, insurance that covers pedestrians, settlement factors and when to hire a pedestrian accident lawyer.

seo.title: Pedestrian Accident Lawyer: When You Need One (2026)
seo.description: Hit by a car while walking? Who pays, how fault works, insurance that covers pedestrians, settlement factors and when to hire a pedestrian accident lawyer.
seo.focus: pedestrian accident lawyer,pedestrian accident attorney,pedestrian injury lawyer,pedestrian car accident lawyer,pedestrian accident law firm

posts.content:
Key points

  • Pedestrians who are hit by a car can usually claim against the driver’s liability insurance, and often against their own auto policy too, even though they were walking.
  • In no-fault states, your own personal injury protection (PIP) or a household member’s policy often pays medical bills first. If the driver fled or had no insurance, your uninsured motorist coverage may pay.
  • Drivers must use care around pedestrians, but a pedestrian’s own fault, such as crossing against a signal, can reduce compensation under comparative negligence rules.
  • A pedestrian accident lawyer is usually worth calling when injuries are serious, fault is disputed, the driver fled, or the driver’s policy limits are low.
  • Deadlines vary by state, and claims involving a city or state vehicle or road can require written notice within months.

Walking is the most exposed way to travel. The Governors Highway Safety Association estimates that 6,732 pedestrians were killed on U.S. roads in 2025, about 18 a day. That was a 7% drop from 2024 and the third straight annual decline, but still about 5% above the 2019 level (GHSA, July 2026). Federal data for 2023 counted 7,314 pedestrian deaths and an estimated 68,244 pedestrians injured, and pedestrians made up 18% of all traffic deaths (NHTSA Traffic Safety Facts).

If you were hit by a car while walking, the injuries are often severe, and the insurance picture can be more complicated than in a crash between two cars. This guide explains what to do after a pedestrian accident, who pays, how fault works, what affects a settlement and when you need a pedestrian accident lawyer.

What to do after being hit by a car as a pedestrian

  1. Call 911 and get medical care. Head, spine and internal injuries are not always obvious at the scene. Go to the emergency room or see a doctor the same day.
  2. Get a police report. Ask the officer for the report number. It records the driver, the vehicle, the insurance details and any citations.
  3. Collect evidence if you can. Photograph the scene, the crosswalk, signals, lighting, the car and your injuries. Get names and phone numbers of witnesses.
  4. Look for cameras. Nearby businesses, buses, doorbells and traffic cameras may have footage. It is often recorded over within days.
  5. Report the crash to your own insurer. Your auto policy may cover you as a pedestrian, and many policies require prompt notice, especially for hit-and-run claims.
  6. Be careful with the driver’s insurer. You can give basic facts, but you usually do not have to give a recorded statement. See our guide to recorded statements.
  7. Keep records. Save medical bills, receipts, pay stubs and a short journal of your pain and limitations.

Who pays when a pedestrian is hit by a car?

Several insurance policies can apply to one pedestrian accident. Which ones pay, and in what order, depends on your state and the policies involved.

If the driver’s limits are too low to cover serious injuries, your own underinsured coverage may add more. Our guides to policy limits and UM/UIM coverage and hit-and-run claims explain how those claims work, and the no-fault states guide covers when you can sue for pain and suffering.

Who is at fault in a pedestrian accident?

Drivers have a duty to watch for pedestrians, yield where the law requires it, obey speed limits and use extra care in crosswalks, near schools and at night. Common examples of driver fault include failing to yield in a crosswalk, turning without looking, speeding, distraction, and impaired driving.

Pedestrians have duties too. Crossing against a signal, stepping suddenly into traffic or walking on a freeway can shift some or all of the blame to the pedestrian. Federal data shows that 77% of pedestrian deaths happen in the dark and 74% happen away from intersections, which is why visibility and where you crossed are often disputed (NHTSA). Alcohol was involved, for the driver or the pedestrian, in 46% of fatal pedestrian crashes in 2023.

Most states reduce your compensation by your share of the fault, and a few bar recovery if you were at fault at all. Our guide to comparative negligence by state and the comparative fault calculator show how a fault split changes a payout.

State traffic laws matter here. In California, for example, the Freedom to Walk Act (AB 2147), effective in 2023, means pedestrians can no longer be ticketed for crossing outside a crosswalk unless there is an immediate danger of a collision (ABC7 News). A jaywalking ticket, or the lack of one, is not the final word on fault in a civil claim, but it is evidence an insurer will look at.

How much is a pedestrian accident settlement worth?

There is no reliable public average for pedestrian accident settlements. Pedestrians are often hurt more seriously than people inside a car, so claims can be large, but the payout depends on the facts:

  • The injuries and treatment, such as fractures, brain injury, surgery or permanent scarring.
  • Medical bills, future care and lost wages, including lost earning capacity.
  • Pain and suffering, often estimated with a multiplier of the economic losses.
  • Your share of the fault, if any.
  • The insurance available: the driver’s limits, your own UM/UIM and any commercial policy.
  • Liens from health insurers, Medicare or Medicaid that must be repaid from the settlement.

Get a starting range with our pedestrian accident settlement calculator, and read how injury settlements are calculated for the method behind it.

Do you need a pedestrian accident lawyer?

Not every pedestrian claim needs a lawyer. If you had a minor injury, recovered quickly, fault is clear and the insurer is paying your bills, you may be able to settle on your own. A pedestrian accident lawyer usually adds the most value when:

  • You were seriously hurt or are still being treated.
  • The driver says you stepped into the road, crossed against the signal or were hard to see.
  • The driver fled the scene or had no insurance, and you need to claim against your own policy.
  • The driver’s policy limits may be too low, and other coverage must be found.
  • A delivery, rideshare, company or government vehicle was involved.
  • Road design, missing sidewalks or broken signals may have contributed. GHSA found that 62.2% of 2024 pedestrian deaths happened where there was no sidewalk.
  • A family member was killed. See our wrongful death settlement calculator.

A lawyer can preserve camera footage and vehicle data before it is lost, gather medical opinions, deal with every insurer involved and negotiate liens down. Our guide on whether you need a car accident lawyer covers the same decision for drivers and passengers.

How much does a pedestrian accident lawyer cost?

Pedestrian accident lawyers almost always work on contingency. You pay nothing up front, and the lawyer takes an agreed percentage of the recovery, commonly about one-third before a lawsuit and more once a case is litigated. The fee agreement must be in writing and must say how case costs are handled (ABA Model Rule 1.5(c)). Use the attorney fee calculator to see what you would take home, and our guide on how to choose a personal injury lawyer for the questions to ask in a free consultation.

Deadlines for pedestrian accident claims

Every state has a statute of limitations for injury lawsuits, commonly two or three years, though some are shorter. Claims against a city, county or state, for a government vehicle or a dangerous road, can require a formal notice of claim within months. Uninsured motorist claims also have deadlines set by your policy. Check the general rule in your state with our statute of limitations calculator.

Frequently asked questions

Who pays if a pedestrian is hit by a car?

Usually the driver’s liability insurance, if the driver was at fault. Your own PIP, MedPay or uninsured motorist coverage, and your health insurance, may also pay depending on your state and policy.

Does my car insurance cover me if I am hit while walking?

Often, yes. In no-fault states PIP commonly covers you as a pedestrian, and uninsured motorist coverage can apply in hit-and-run cases. Check your policy and report the crash promptly.

Can I still recover if I was jaywalking?

In most states, yes, but your compensation may be reduced by your share of the fault. A few states bar recovery if you were at fault at all.

What if the driver drove away?

Report it to police right away and notify your insurer. Your uninsured motorist coverage may pay, and a lawyer can look for camera footage to identify the driver.

How long do I have to file a pedestrian accident claim?

It depends on the state, commonly two or three years for a lawsuit, with much shorter notice deadlines for claims against government agencies.

How much does a pedestrian accident lawyer charge?

Most charge a contingency fee, a percentage of the recovery, with no fee if there is no recovery.

Is a pedestrian accident lawyer different from a car accident lawyer?

Usually the same lawyers handle both, but ask how many pedestrian cases they have handled, since fault and insurance issues differ.

Sources

  • Governors Highway Safety Association: U.S. pedestrian deaths fall for third straight year (July 2026)
  • NHTSA Traffic Safety Facts: Pedestrians, 2023 data (DOT HS 813 727)
  • ABC7 News: California Freedom to Walk Act (AB 2147)
  • American Bar Association: Model Rule 1.5, Fees

This article is general information, not legal advice. Insurance rules, fault laws and deadlines vary by state. Talk to a licensed attorney in your state about your situation.

posts.excerpt: Waiting on SSDI or SSI? Eight ways to bring in money while your claim is pending, the 2026 work limits, how back pay works and how to ask SSA to speed up your case.

seo.title: Income While Waiting for Disability: 8 Options (2026)
seo.description: Waiting on SSDI or SSI? 8 ways to cover bills: SSI presumptive payments, state disability, SNAP, cash assistance, unemployment rules and part-time work limits.
seo.focus: what to do for income while waiting for disability,financial assistance while waiting for disability,can you get cash assistance while waiting for disability,how to make money while waiting for disability,loans while waiting on disability

posts.content:
Key points

  • Social Security disability decisions take months. SSA’s published averages in October 2026 were about 240 days for an initial decision and 291 days for a hearing decision.
  • SSDI has a five-month waiting period after your disability begins, but approved claims include back pay. SSI has no waiting period but is never paid for the month you apply.
  • While you wait, possible income sources include SSI presumptive disability payments, private or state disability insurance, workers’ comp, SNAP, cash assistance, unemployment and limited part-time work.
  • In 2026 you can earn up to $1,690 a month ($2,830 if blind) without it counting as substantial gainful activity, though any work can affect how SSA sees your claim.
  • Be wary of loans against future disability benefits. Social Security benefits generally cannot be signed over to a lender.

Applying for Social Security disability is often the start of a long wait. Social Security reported current average wait times of about 240 days for an initial disability decision, 243 days for reconsideration and 291 days for a hearing decision (SSA SecurityStat, October 2026). Rent, groceries and medical bills do not wait that long.

This guide covers eight realistic ways to bring in money while your SSDI or SSI claim is pending, the 2026 limits on work, how back pay works and how to ask Social Security to speed up your case.

How long you wait and what you get back

  • SSDI (Social Security Disability Insurance) has a five-month waiting period that usually starts on the date your disability began. The first payment covers the sixth full month and is paid the following month. If you are approved, SSDI can also pay up to 12 months of retroactive benefits before your application date (AARP summary of SSA rules). The waiting period was eliminated for ALS in 2020.
  • SSI (Supplemental Security Income) has no five-month wait, but “SSI benefits are not paid in the month that you first apply” (SSA Handbook § 2104).
  • Back pay is paid once you are approved and can be a large lump sum. Our SSDI back pay calculator estimates what you may be owed.

2026 Social Security disability numbers

Source: SSA 2026 COLA fact sheet. Some states add a supplement to the federal SSI payment.

8 options for income while waiting for disability

1. SSI presumptive disability payments

If you apply for SSI and your condition is so clear that you are very likely to be approved, Social Security can start paying before the final decision. These presumptive disability payments last up to six months, and you do not have to repay them if you are later found not disabled (SSA Handbook § 2188). Ask the SSA office whether your condition qualifies. You still have to meet SSI’s income and asset limits.

2. Private short-term or long-term disability insurance

Check whether you have disability coverage through your employer, a union or a policy you bought. Short-term policies typically pay for a few months and long-term policies start after an elimination period, often replacing a share of your salary. Many long-term policies require you to apply for SSDI and reduce their payment by what Social Security pays. Estimate a benefit with our long-term disability calculator.

3. State disability insurance or paid medical leave

California, Hawaii, New Jersey, New York, Rhode Island and Puerto Rico have long-running temporary disability insurance programs funded through payroll. A growing number of states also pay benefits for your own serious health condition through paid family and medical leave programs, including Washington, Massachusetts, Connecticut, Oregon and Colorado, with Delaware and Minnesota starting in January 2026 and Maine in May 2026 (Hylant summary of 2026 programs). These pay for a limited number of weeks, but they can bridge the first months.

4. Workers’ compensation

If your condition was caused by your job, file a workers’ comp claim. It can pay a weekly benefit, usually a share of your wages, while you are unable to work. Workers’ comp can reduce SSDI under an offset rule, so tell both agencies. See our workers’ comp weekly benefit calculator and our guide to workers’ comp vs personal injury claims.

5. SNAP food benefits and Medicaid

SNAP (food stamps) and Medicaid are based on income and household size, not on a disability decision, so you can apply right away. A 2025 federal law expanded SNAP time limits for adults without dependents to ages 18 to 64 and removed some exemptions (USDA guidance, July 2025). People who are medically certified as unable to work remain exempt from the work rules under federal SNAP law, so ask your doctor for documentation and tell the SNAP office about your condition.

6. Cash assistance and general assistance

Families with children may qualify for TANF cash assistance. Many states and counties run general assistance programs for adults without children, often aimed at people waiting on SSI. If you receive interim assistance and later win SSI, the state can be repaid from your SSI back pay with your written permission (SSA POMS on interim assistance). Dial 211 to find local programs, emergency rent help and utility assistance.

7. Unemployment benefits

Applying for unemployment does not automatically bar a disability claim, but it creates tension: unemployment requires you to say you can work and are looking for a job, while disability requires you to show you cannot work at the level SSA counts as substantial gainful activity. Judges can weigh that conflict. For SSI, unemployment counts as unearned income and reduces your payment. Talk to a disability lawyer before you apply for both.

8. Limited part-time work

You can work a little while your claim is pending, but keep earnings below the substantial gainful activity level, $1,690 a month in 2026 ($2,830 if blind). Earning above that usually leads to a denial for that period. Even work below the limit can be used as evidence of what you are able to do, so keep hours and duties modest and consistent with your medical records. For SSI, the first $65 of earnings plus half of the rest are excluded each month, along with a $20 general exclusion.

Should you borrow while waiting for disability?

Be careful. Companies that advertise loans or advances against future disability back pay often charge high fees, and Social Security benefits generally cannot be assigned or signed over to a lender under federal law. Safer options include hardship programs from your utility, landlord, lender or medical providers, a payment plan for medical bills, and help from family. If you take a loan, read the total cost carefully.

How to speed up a disability claim

Social Security fast-tracks some cases. These include terminal illness, conditions on the Compassionate Allowances list, veterans rated 100% permanent and total, military casualties, homelessness, people at risk of suicide or violence, and “dire need” (SSA HALLEX I-3-1-5). Dire need means you lack the income or resources to deal with an immediate threat to your health or safety, such as having no food, no access to needed medicine or medical care, or a home made uninhabitable by a utility shutoff. Ask in writing for a dire need review and attach proof, such as an eviction notice or shutoff letter.

Other practical steps: respond to every SSA letter on time, keep seeing your doctors, and make sure SSA has all your medical records. Missing records are one of the most common causes of delay.

Do you need a disability lawyer?

Disability lawyers and representatives are usually paid only if you win, from your back pay, and their fees are capped and must be approved by Social Security. A representative can gather medical evidence, request a dire need review and prepare you for a hearing. If your claim was denied, an appeal is often where representation matters most.

Frequently asked questions

Can I get cash assistance while waiting for disability?

Often, yes. Depending on your state and household, you may qualify for TANF, state or county general assistance, SNAP and Medicaid while your SSDI or SSI claim is pending.

Can I work while waiting for disability?

You can work a little, but keep earnings below $1,690 a month in 2026 ($2,830 if blind). Higher earnings usually mean SSA will find you are not disabled for that period.

Can I collect unemployment while applying for disability?

It is not automatically barred, but saying you can work for unemployment can conflict with your disability claim. Get advice before applying for both.

Do I have to pay back SSI presumptive disability payments?

Not if you are later found not disabled. Overpayments can still arise from non-medical issues, such as income or resources above the SSI limits.

How far back does SSDI back pay go?

Up to 12 months before your application date, depending on when your disability began, after the five-month waiting period.

How long does a disability decision take?

SSA’s averages in October 2026 were about 240 days for an initial decision, 243 days for reconsideration and 291 days for a hearing decision.

Are there loans for people waiting on disability?

Key points

  • Social Security disability decisions take months. SSA’s published averages in October 2026 were about 240 days for an initial decision and 291 days for a hearing decision.
  • SSDI has a five-month waiting period after your disability begins, but approved claims include back pay. SSI has no waiting period but is never paid for the month you apply.
  • While you wait, possible income sources include SSI presumptive disability payments, private or state disability insurance, workers’ comp, SNAP, cash assistance, unemployment and limited part-time work.
  • In 2026 you can earn up to $1,690 a month ($2,830 if blind) without it counting as substantial gainful activity, though any work can affect how SSA sees your claim.
  • Be wary of loans against future disability benefits. Social Security benefits generally cannot be signed over to a lender.

blocks.html: Applying for Social Security disability is often the start of a long wait. Social Security reported current average wait times of about 240 days for an initial disability decision, 243 days for reconsideration and 291 days for a hearing decision (SSA SecurityStat, October 2026). Rent, groceries and medical bills do not wait that long.

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: This guide covers eight realistic ways to bring in money while your SSDI or SSI claim is pending, the 2026 limits on work, how back pay works and how to ask Social Security to speed up your case.

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: How long you wait and what you get back

blocks.name: core/list
blocks.html:
• SSDI (Social Security Disability Insurance) has a five-month waiting period that usually starts on the date your disability began. The first payment covers the sixth full month and is paid the following month. If you are approved, SSDI can also pay up to 12 months of retroactive benefits before your application date (AARP summary of SSA rules). The waiting period was eliminated for ALS in 2020.
  • SSI (Supplemental Security Income) has no five-month wait, but “SSI benefits are not paid in the month that you first apply” (SSA Handbook § 2104).
  • Back pay is paid once you are approved and can be a large lump sum. Our SSDI back pay calculator estimates what you may be owed.

blocks.name: core/image
core/heading
blocks.html: 2026 Social Security disability numbers

blocks.name: core/table
core/paragraph
blocks.html: Source: SSA 2026 COLA fact sheet. Some states add a supplement to the federal SSI payment.

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: 8 options for income while waiting for disability

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: 1. SSI presumptive disability payments

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: If you apply for SSI and your condition is so clear that you are very likely to be approved, Social Security can start paying before the final decision. These presumptive disability payments last up to six months, and you do not have to repay them if you are later found not disabled (SSA Handbook § 2188). Ask the SSA office whether your condition qualifies. You still have to meet SSI’s income and asset limits.

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: 2. Private short-term or long-term disability insurance

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: Check whether you have disability coverage through your employer, a union or a policy you bought. Short-term policies typically pay for a few months and long-term policies start after an elimination period, often replacing a share of your salary. Many long-term policies require you to apply for SSDI and reduce their payment by what Social Security pays. Estimate a benefit with our long-term disability calculator.

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: 3. State disability insurance or paid medical leave

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: California, Hawaii, New Jersey, New York, Rhode Island and Puerto Rico have long-running temporary disability insurance programs funded through payroll. A growing number of states also pay benefits for your own serious health condition through paid family and medical leave programs, including Washington, Massachusetts, Connecticut, Oregon and Colorado, with Delaware and Minnesota starting in January 2026 and Maine in May 2026 (Hylant summary of 2026 programs). These pay for a limited number of weeks, but they can bridge the first months.

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: 4. Workers’ compensation

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: If your condition was caused by your job, file a workers’ comp claim. It can pay a weekly benefit, usually a share of your wages, while you are unable to work. Workers’ comp can reduce SSDI under an offset rule, so tell both agencies. See our workers’ comp weekly benefit calculator and our guide to workers’ comp vs personal injury claims.

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: 5. SNAP food benefits and Medicaid

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: SNAP (food stamps) and Medicaid are based on income and household size, not on a disability decision, so you can apply right away. A 2025 federal law expanded SNAP time limits for adults without dependents to ages 18 to 64 and removed some exemptions (USDA guidance, July 2025). People who are medically certified as unable to work remain exempt from the work rules under federal SNAP law, so ask your doctor for documentation and tell the SNAP office about your condition.

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: 6. Cash assistance and general assistance

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: Families with children may qualify for TANF cash assistance. Many states and counties run general assistance programs for adults without children, often aimed at people waiting on SSI. If you receive interim assistance and later win SSI, the state can be repaid from your SSI back pay with your written permission (SSA POMS on interim assistance). Dial 211 to find local programs, emergency rent help and utility assistance.

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: 7. Unemployment benefits

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: Applying for unemployment does not automatically bar a disability claim, but it creates tension: unemployment requires you to say you can work and are looking for a job, while disability requires you to show you cannot work at the level SSA counts as substantial gainful activity. Judges can weigh that conflict. For SSI, unemployment counts as unearned income and reduces your payment. Talk to a disability lawyer before you apply for both.

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: 8. Limited part-time work

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: You can work a little while your claim is pending, but keep earnings below the substantial gainful activity level, $1,690 a month in 2026 ($2,830 if blind). Earning above that usually leads to a denial for that period. Even work below the limit can be used as evidence of what you are able to do, so keep hours and duties modest and consistent with your medical records. For SSI, the first $65 of earnings plus half of the rest are excluded each month, along with a $20 general exclusion.

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: Should you borrow while waiting for disability?

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: Be careful. Companies that advertise loans or advances against future disability back pay often charge high fees, and Social Security benefits generally cannot be assigned or signed over to a lender under federal law. Safer options include hardship programs from your utility, landlord, lender or medical providers, a payment plan for medical bills, and help from family. If you take a loan, read the total cost carefully.

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: How to speed up a disability claim

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: Social Security fast-tracks some cases. These include terminal illness, conditions on the Compassionate Allowances list, veterans rated 100% permanent and total, military casualties, homelessness, people at risk of suicide or violence, and “dire need” (SSA HALLEX I-3-1-5). Dire need means you lack the income or resources to deal with an immediate threat to your health or safety, such as having no food, no access to needed medicine or medical care, or a home made uninhabitable by a utility shutoff. Ask in writing for a dire need review and attach proof, such as an eviction notice or shutoff letter.

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: Other practical steps: respond to every SSA letter on time, keep seeing your doctors, and make sure SSA has all your medical records. Missing records are one of the most common causes of delay.

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: Do you need a disability lawyer?

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: Disability lawyers and representatives are usually paid only if you win, from your back pay, and their fees are capped and must be approved by Social Security. A representative can gather medical evidence, request a dire need review and prepare you for a hearing. If your claim was denied, an appeal is often where representation matters most.

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: Frequently asked questions

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: Can I get cash assistance while waiting for disability?

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: Often, yes. Depending on your state and household, you may qualify for TANF, state or county general assistance, SNAP and Medicaid while your SSDI or SSI claim is pending.

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: Can I work while waiting for disability?

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: You can work a little, but keep earnings below $1,690 a month in 2026 ($2,830 if blind). Higher earnings usually mean SSA will find you are not disabled for that period.

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: Can I collect unemployment while applying for disability?

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: It is not automatically barred, but saying you can work for unemployment can conflict with your disability claim. Get advice before applying for both.

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: Do I have to pay back SSI presumptive disability payments?

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: Not if you are later found not disabled. Overpayments can still arise from non-medical issues, such as income or resources above the SSI limits.

blocks.name: core/heading
blocks.html: How far back does SSDI back pay go?

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: Up to 12 months before your application date, depending on when your disability began, after the five-month waiting period.

blocks.html: How long does a disability decision take?

blocks.name: core/paragraph
blocks.html: SSA’s averages in October 2026 were about 240 days for an initial decision, 243 days for reconsideration and 291 days for a hearing decision.

posts.title: RV Lemon Laws: Are Motorhomes, Campers and Motorcycles Covered?
posts.excerpt: Do lemon laws cover RVs, travel trailers and motorcycles? How states treat motorhomes and living quarters, the federal warranty backup and how to file an RV lemon law claim.
